en: The Sūtra of the Radiant Praise, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Radiant Praise. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter One: The Radiant Praise.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, together with a great community of five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from defilement, and had attained mastery;
whose minds were liberated in peace, who were well-delivered through wisdom, who had reached benevolent harmony, and who served as great guides.
Having accomplished what was to be done and perfected what was to be established, he has cast off the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, and eliminated the afflictions of beginning and end;
through equal liberation, he has transcended all conceptualizations and attained the perfection of deliverance—except for one person, the worthy Ānanda, who is training for the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus, as well as bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, all of whom were present;

together with various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained the various dhāraṇīs and achieved samādhi, who cultivated the practice of emptiness and honored the signless, who did not dwell on various vows yet attained equal patience (samarthya), and who, having mastered the infinite, attained the five supernormal powers;

whose speech was quick and clever and free from indolence, who had relinquished the heart that craved worldly gain and home, whose preaching of the Dharma was not for the sake of offerings, who had reached the profound and wondrous Dharma and crossed over to the ultimate, who had attained fearlessness and transcended the works of Māra, who were liberated from the obstructions of all the skandhas, and who expounded upon the causes and conditions of the direction of their resolve.

Having cultivated the vows of diligent practice throughout incalculable kalpas, wherever his mind is directed, he is always the first to greet others with joy and inquiry, remaining free from fetters and resentment.
Entering into countless assemblies, his majestic power is towering and sublime, such that he is without fear or difficulty; he recollects events from immeasurable billions of kalpas.

When he expounds the sutras and teachings, clarifying their manifold meanings, he views them as being like illusions, transformations, mirages, the moon in water, dreams, shadows, echoes, or images in a mirror—his valor is peerless.

With subtle wisdom, they know the thoughts and actions that arise within the minds of sentient beings; they transcend conceptual discrimination, harbor no malice in their intent, and are diligent in fulfilling the practice of patience. They clearly understand those who are to be delivered, embrace infinite vows for the purification of Buddha-lands, and remain constantly in samādhi. With their eyes, they behold countless Buddha-worlds, attaining mastery in skillful means, and they entreat immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Whether advancing or retreating, they are able to resolve various views and attachments; with a concentrated mind, they find joy in themselves and comprehend hundreds of thousands of practices.
Such are the virtues of all these bodhisattvas—their names include the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
...the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, the Bodhisattva Mahāsubhūti, the Bodhisattva Naradatta, the Bodhisattva Kātyāyana,
the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, the Bodhisattva Indradatta, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Sumati,
the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva An...
The Bodhisattva Void-Vision, the Bodhisattva Established-Vow, the Bodhisattva Circumambulation,
the Bodhisattva Constant-Diligence-Responsive, the Bodhisattva Non-Remote, the Bodhisattva Increasing-Sun, the Bodhisattva Selfless,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Gradual-Pinnacle, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal-Pinnacle, and the Bodhisattva Constantly-Raised-Hand.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Constant-Hand Lowering Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva—such hosts of bodhisattvas are beyond limit;
they cannot be numbered, numbering hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, all possessing wondrous virtues, pure, and identical with the Truth.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon a natural lion throne, assuming the full lotus posture with his body erect, directing his mind toward a specific object and establishing his intention.

There is a samādhi named King of Concentrated Mind; by means of this timely samādhi of spontaneous right reception, one universally enters all states of concentrated mind, gathering and sustaining them with equanimity, and directing oneself toward them.
The Buddha, having entered samādhi with a mind of profound tranquility, surveyed this world with his eye of the Way;
his body remained serene as he smiled, emitting sixty trillion hundred thousand rays of light from the soles of his feet,
ten billion hundred thousand rays from each of his ten toes, and two billion hundred thousand rays from both sides of his torso.
From his knees, he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light; from his two feet, he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light;
from his two shoulders, he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light; from his two elbows, he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light;
from his navel, he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light; from his head, he emitted one billion hundred thousand rays of light; and from his two hands, he emitted...

There were ten billion hundred thousand rays of light; from his two arms he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light, from his two eyebrows he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light,
from his neck he emitted one billion hundred thousand rays of light, from his two eyes he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light,
from his two ears he emitted two billion hundred thousand rays of light, and from his nose he emitted one billion hundred thousand rays of light.
From his body, he emitted four hundred billion hundreds of thousands of rays of light; from his forty teeth, he emitted forty billion hundreds of thousands of rays of light;
from the mark between his eyebrows, he emitted one billion hundreds of thousands of rays of light;
and from the mark of the protuberance on his crown, he emitted sixty trillion hundreds of thousands of rays of light, illuminating this trichiliocosm so that there was nowhere they did not reach.
The light universally illumined Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction;
likewise, it was so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Any sentient beings who encountered this light had their minds become tranquil and composed, and all of them resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately smiled with joy, emitting various rays of light from all his pores, which illuminated this trichiliocosm, pervading everywhere throughout the ten directions without exception.

In as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, all sentient beings who are illuminated by this light become entirely tranquil and abide in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

At that time, the World-Honored One then manifested the light of the Tathāgata’s pure, true, and wondrous volitional nature, illuminating this trichiliocosm and extending universally to Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions; should any sentient beings encounter this light, they shall all ultimately attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One extended his tongue from its base until it completely covered the Buddha-field, emitting countless billions of hundreds of thousands of rays of light that illuminated this trichiliocosm and pervaded the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Within that radiance, golden jewel lotuses spontaneously sprang forth; upon each of these lotuses sat a Buddha in the full lotus posture, preaching the Dharma and expounding the six pāramitās.
It was likewise so throughout all the ten directions.
If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma discourse, they shall all ultimately attain firm abiding in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne; there is a samādhi named "Lion’s Delight," and by entering into right reception through the concentration of this samādhi, he manifested his divine powers, displaying majestic radiance in accordance with their respective forms and appearances.

The trichiliocosm shook in six ways; even its furthest boundaries trembled, moving harmoniously from the center to the edges with tranquility, gentleness, and softness, out of compassion for all classes of sentient beings, so that they might obtain peace, security, happiness, and freedom from affliction.

At that time, those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals within the trichiliocosm—those who were unrefined, terrified, and oppressed—spontaneously had their rebirths in the three woeful paths severed. Having been liberated, they all came of their own accord and attained birth as humans, or among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

At that time, the devas who had just been born there, whether among humans or in the heavens, immediately recognized their past lives; filled with joy and delight, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and paid homage with palms joined. This was likewise the case for all those in the ten directions, without any distinction.

At that time, among the classes of sentient beings in this trichiliocosm, those who were blind regained their sight and beheld forms; those who were deaf gained the power of hearing and perceived all sounds; those whose wills were disordered and minds confused had their hearts restored;

and those who were deluded and agitated immediately attained meditative concentration. Those who were naked were spontaneously clothed; those who were famished were spontaneously satiated; those suffering from thirst required no further longing; those who were ill were healed; and those with physical defects had their faculties made complete.
Those who were utterly exhausted were spontaneously relieved, and those long dependent upon the body were no longer dependent upon it.

All sentient beings attain a mind of equanimity, looking upon one another in turn as fathers and mothers, elder and younger brothers, and elder and younger sisters; each with a single heart, they are equal and without partiality or deviance, all practicing a mind of loving-kindness.
All living beings cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action, their pure Brahma-conduct being free from the dust of defilement.
All the people obtain peace and security, and the peace they attain is like that of a bhikṣu who has realized the third dhyāna.
At that time, sentient beings attained wisdom and were fully endowed with goodness, joy, and disciplined concentration; they were free from base inferiority and had achieved harmony and elegance.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne within the trichiliocosm, most transcendent and peerless, his majestic spiritual power towering and sublime, his radiance brilliant and resplendent, free from all fear. His holy brilliance shone forth and his venerable countenance was complete, universally illuminating the Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the lands of the World-Honored Ones in the eight directions, above, and below—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—just as Mount Sumeru surpasses all other mountains, its light pervading everywhere.
Thereupon, having received the intent of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One spontaneously issued a holy command so that all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm might behold him together.

At that time, in this world, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Pure Abodes, the Brahmā heavens, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the Nirmāṇarati, the Tuṣita, the Yāma, the Trāyastriṃśa, and the Cāturmahārājika heavens, as well as the inhabitants of the trichiliocosm, naturally perceived themselves approaching the Tathāgata. They all spontaneously obtained celestial flowers for adornment, celestial incense, blended celestial perfumes, and pounded celestial fragrances, along with celestial blue lotuses, water lilies, and fresh blossoms—exquisite celestial flowers complete with stems and leaves. Each set out and brought these to the Tathāgata; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and scattered them over him. Furthermore, taking in their hands various flowers from the waters and lands of the human realm, they went to the World-Honored One to present as offerings.

The various flowers scattered as offerings by the devas and humans remained suspended in the void; throughout the trichiliocosm, they transformed into palaces and natural multi-storied towers. From these palaces hung celestial flowers, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, which fluttered and swayed, appearing with brilliant clarity everywhere. These floral fragrances adorned the Buddha-land of the trichiliocosm, becoming naturally majestic; their forms and myriad colors were like purple-polished gold, and this same splendor and fragrance extended throughout the eight directions, above and below.
Thereupon, all the people in the cities of Jambudvīpa beheld the Tathāgata’s manifested body and its inconceivable, wondrous transformations;
each thought to themselves: "Today, the Tathāgata sits before me."
In all Buddha-lands it was likewise; each thought to themselves:
"Today the Tathāgata is sitting before me, preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, upon his lion throne, smiled again with joy and further illuminated the trichiliocosm, his great light blazing brilliantly.

The people of this land all behold together the Buddha-lands of the east, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas dwell with their assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;

furthermore, all sentient beings in those Buddha-worlds of the east, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise see from afar this Buddha-land, Śākyamuni Buddha, seated with his community of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas preaching the sutras.
It is the same for the eight directions and the zenith and nadir; they all see this from afar, exactly and without distinction.

Thereupon, passing through Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, there was a peripheral land named Ratnāvasthāna. Its Buddha was named Ratnakāra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there for the sake of all sentient beings, likewise preaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

At that time, in that buddha-world, there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabha. Beholding the great radiance and the great trembling of the earth, he immediately went to the Tathāgata Ratnakāra and prostrated himself, asking:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!..."
For what cause and condition does this great radiance illuminate this buddha-field and the great earth tremble?
The bodies of the Tathāgatas appear spontaneously; there must surely be a significant meaning behind this.
That Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, saying: "Noble son!

If you wish to know, there is a world called Sahā, extremely far to the west. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who is currently present, preaching the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
"This is the light of his majestic spiritual power.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha addressed the Tathāgata Ratnakāra:
"Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!"
I wish to go there to see the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, to prostrate and pay him homage;

as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the *kumārabhūta* youths, and others who have attained the ultimate *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*, whose minds are sovereign and who have attained the *pāramitās*, [namely] the Śākya-mukta-āgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnakāra addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāsa, saying:
"Go, son of good family!
You know the time."
The Tathāgata Ratnakāra bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha a golden lotus with a thousand petals, saying:
"Take it, son of good family!
Use this precious lotus to scatter as an offering to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."

“Good son! Those who wish to go and cultivate the practice of tranquility, and those bodhisattvas born in that realm of endurance (*sahā-lokadhātu*), encounter great hardships and are difficult to meet.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha accepted the golden lotus and, together with an incalculable number of hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayuta* bodhisattvas—men and women, great and small, lay and ordained—made offerings to the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, of the eastern quarter; they served and took refuge in them, presenting flowers, incense, blended perfumes, and powdered incense.
Next, he proceeded to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, O Great Sage!
The Tathāgata Ratnavastu sends his greetings with great respect, inquiring whether you are at ease and whether your practice is proceeding in peace.
He has also sent this golden lotus flower.
The Buddha accepted the lotus flower and immediately scattered it afar toward the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction.

At that moment, the flowers pervaded all the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction; in each, a Buddha sat upon a naturally golden lotus flower, preaching the Dharma and likewise expounding these six pāramitās.
Any sentient beings who hear this teaching shall all, at that very moment, ultimately and firmly abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Men and women, great and small, shall all prostrate at the feet of the Buddha and, each according to their merit, make offerings to the *Tathāgata*, the *Arhat*, the *Samyak-saṃbuddha*.

To the south, at the furthest limit beyond as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a buddha-world named Free from All Sorrow; its Buddha is named Aśokaśirṣa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Vigataśoka (Free from Sorrow) who took leave of his Buddha. The Buddha bestowed upon him a lotus flower, and together with countless bodhisattvas, he traveled through various lands making offerings to the Buddhas. He then came to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, prostrated and made offerings, and withdrew to sit at one side to listen to the sutra.

To the west, at a distance from here equal to the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world named *Jiran* (Tranquil). Its Buddha is named *Bāolóng Duō Ājié, Āluóhē, Sāniè Sānfó* (Ratnābhaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha).

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Icchānta, who took his leave of his Buddha. The Buddha bestowed upon him lotus flowers, and together with countless other bodhisattvas, he traveled through various lands making offerings to the Buddhas. He then came to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, prostrated himself in worship, and sat to one side to listen to the sutra.

To the north, at a distance from here equal to the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world named Jie-sheng (Victorious). Its Buddha is named Sheng-zhu-gen-duo (Victorious over All Faculties) Ajita, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Dānavara. He took leave of his Buddha, who bestowed upon him lotus flowers; accompanied by countless bodhisattvas, he traveled through various lands making offerings to the Buddhas, until he arrived at the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. There he prostrated and made offerings, then withdrew to sit and listen to the sutra.

Below this world, at a distance of as many *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a world named Renxian (Bhadra). Its Buddha is named Xianshou Duojie, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Padmottara, who took leave of his Buddha. The Buddha bestowed upon him lotus flowers, and together with countless bodhisattvas, he traveled through various lands making offerings to the Buddhas. He then proceeded to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, prostrated himself in worship, and withdrew to sit and listen to the sutra.
Above this world, at a distance of as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a world named *Prīti*, whose Buddha is named *Ratimukha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha*.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Śukhābhyudgata, who took leave of his Buddha. The Buddha bestowed upon him a lotus flower, and together with countless other bodhisattvas, he traveled through various lands making offerings to the Buddhas. Arriving at the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, he prostrated and made offerings, then withdrew to sit and listen to the sutra.
The four intermediate directions were likewise thus, equal and without distinction.

At that time, throughout this trichiliocosm, there immediately fell rains of various precious flowers, incense, banners, and canopies; fragrant trees and flowering trees were spontaneously adorned, just like the Buddha-land of Padmavati, where the Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Samantapuspa resides, and where the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra dwells and travels.

The sons of the gods, such as Susīma, along with the assembly of other great bodhisattvas of infinite majesty and power bestowed by the World-Honored One, as well as all other devas and the people of the world, all came together in assembly.
All the Māras, Brahmās, along with the assembly of Śrāvakas, Gandharvas, Asuras, spirits, and human beings, all gathered together in great numbers.
For these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, while they were in their youth, the merit of the food and drink they consumed was spontaneously provided.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"If there should be any bodhisattva mahāsattva here, they should diligently cultivate and study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, fully endowed with all qualities and having thoroughly understood all dharmas, train in the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and practices non-abiding, they then fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);
they cause it not to be deficient, and in whatever they give, they have no attachment or aversion, thereby fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).”
By reason of these causes and conditions, one never dwells in either transgression or non-transgression;
one shall also fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) and give rise to no anger;
one should study the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), whereby one will receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
By exerting all diligence through body and mind, and without giving rise to any outflows, one shall fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā.
For this reason, there is nothing to be sought after or craved.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom, he then personally fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, giving rise to that which is without anything to arise.”

Furthermore, one should fully attain the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);
cause them all to be fully endowed with the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), and the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

One shall decisively and gradually fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), the four formless samādhis, and the eight doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), entering them through right reception. Taking these as liberation, there is no conceptualization: no internal thoughts, no thought of making offerings, no thought of light, no thought of crimson or red, no thought of decay, no thought of blueness, and no thought of being bitten, wounded, or rotted by insects.
Furthermore, they have no distracted thoughts, no thoughts of withered bones, no thoughts of scattering like stars, and no thoughts of location.
They are entirely free from all such conceptions, constantly setting their will upon the Buddha, recollecting the sutras, recollecting the Sangha, and recollecting the precepts.

The intention lies in bestowing grace; the resolve is directed toward the various heavens. There is the intention of coming and going, the intention of death, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering and pleasure, the perception that there is nothing but the body, and the perception of beginning and end. One has no perception of anything in all worlds being worth delighting in; there is the perception of all habitual tendencies and the perception of their total cessation. Regarding the wisdom of the Path, the wisdom of exhaustion, the wisdom of non-feverishness, the wisdom of non-arising, and the wisdom of phenomena—within these various scriptural teachings, there is neither the wisdom of grasping nor the wisdom of self. There is no internal wisdom, yet there is the wisdom of the subtle mind. One thoroughly understands all forms of wisdom; as for what is called wisdom, it is entirely through the contemplation of the practice of samādhi.

For those who abide in the concentration of non-perception, non-thought, and non-activity, there is no difference; yet the faculties differ, and with different faculties come different modes of activity.

Furthermore, there is another practice that is difficult to attain: the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
If one wishes to thoroughly understand all these conditions, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom;
if there are those who wish to be fully endowed with the wisdom of all paths, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom;
if one wishes to thoroughly understand the endowment of wisdom and to be complete in all supernormal knowledges, one should practice the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to clearly understand all things and draw near to the complete eradication of worldly afflictions, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice the prajñāpāramitā.
"In this way, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and trains in the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha spoke again to Śāriputra:
"If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to enter into tranquility, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to dwell in the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the roots of the mental faculties and the conduct of all sentient beings, he should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to surpass the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the gate of dhāraṇī and, even if a man encourages and assists in the giving of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, to transcend them, he should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to surpass the precepts and prohibitions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and to encourage and assist their mental intentions, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If they wish to be fully endowed with samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should study the *prajñāpārmitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish and manifest dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti, and to encourage, assemble, and resolve the objects of the mind’s thoughts, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to encourage and assist in giving, and to distinguish the infinite and immeasurable accomplishment of merit, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully accomplish infinite and immeasurable morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

The Buddha spoke again to Śāriputra: "If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to fully establish the practice of the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā; who wish that in all their births they may see all Buddhas and personally attain Buddhahood;

who wish to accomplish the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics and be fully endowed with the nature of a bodhisattva; or who, as a *kumārabhūta* (true youth), wish to stand upon this ground without being separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and who wish that whatever wholesome roots they aspire to and contemplate—such as making offerings to the Tathāgatas, upholding and obeying their commands—shall be immediately fulfilled: they should study the prajñā-pāramitā."

If one wishes to fulfill all that sentient beings desire in their hearts—whether it be food and drink, clothing, vehicles, incense, flowers, blended perfumes, ointments, bedding, lamps, hand towels, shoes, or socks—so that they may be fully supplied with whatever wealth they require, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to bring to fulfillment as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and to exhort and establish them in the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā, they should study the prajñā-pāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

by means of a single root of goodness, accords with the virtues of the Tathāgata such that they are neither exhausted nor diminished, even until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the prajñāpāramitā, all the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, throughout the eight directions, above and below, will together chant and proclaim that person's merits."

In the mere instant that one resolves the mind [on enlightenment], if one wishes to travel to this realm or to the worlds of the ten directions—such as the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the rivers of the eastern quarter—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to address all Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—with every sound, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish the buddha-fields so that they are never interrupted; if he wishes to abide in internal emptiness, or external emptiness, or internal-and-external emptiness; if he wishes to abide in the emptiness of emptiness, or great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of all things, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned; if he wishes to abide in true emptiness, the emptiness of non-sacrifice, the emptiness of non-conditions, the emptiness of conditions, the emptiness of the natural marks, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unobtainable, the emptiness of non-being, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of the nature of formlessness, or the emptiness of the majestic power of conditions regarding the characteristics of all formations—then he should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to draw near to all Tathāgatas, who wishes to contemplate and understand all dharmas, and who wishes to comprehend that all dharmas abide in the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi), should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish the perfection of wisdom should abide in this manner. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to calculate and know the number of sands, stones, trees, flowers, all atoms, and the various unresolved doubts within a trichiliocosm, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to know the exact number of drops in all the great oceans, rivers, streams, springs, and sources within a trichiliocosm, while doing so without harming the creatures that dwell in the sea, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, suppose all the fires within the trichiliocosm were to blaze up simultaneously, like the conflagration at the end of an eon; if one wishes to extinguish them all at once on every side so that no fire remains, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to extinguish all the winds in the trichiliocosm— winds that at times blow through the lands, tearing them apart and shattering Mount Sumerus until nothing remains, like fine dust utterly vanishing, as if burning reeds or burning thistle— should they wish to extinguish the fires of the triple world with a single finger, whether a finger of the hand or a toe of the foot, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to pervade the entire void of the trichiliocosm with his body by sitting cross-legged throughout it, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if he wishes to manifest transformations with sovereign mastery, neither near nor far, neither large nor small, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to take all the Mount Sumerus of the trichiliocosm and, with a single hand, lift those Mount Sumerus and place them in various other immeasurable buddha-worlds— without any thought of coming or going, and without increase or decrease— should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to gather at one time and simultaneously all the Buddhas— the Gods among Gods— as well as their śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas from as many Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River, in order to make offerings to them, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a single garment, incense, flowers, powdered incense, ointment, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, makes offerings to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of śrāvakas, and serves and takes refuge in them when they gather together at one time, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the vision and knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*); and if they wish for them to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), up to the fruit of parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*) and enter parinirvāṇa, they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*)."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, if it concerns the perfection of giving, they should train in this way: 'By such giving, one obtains a great fruit of retribution; by such giving, one is born into the families of nobles, brahmins, or great clans of elders;
by such giving, one is born above the Four Heavenly Kings, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.'"

A donor who gives in this manner relies upon that giving to contemplate the first, second, third, and up to the fourth dhyāna; the concentration of the sphere of infinite space and its meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and the meditative absorptions of samādhi.

Such a donor gives rise to the Eightfold Noble Path and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), and the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
If one understands this, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā* therein. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they always employ skillful wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*) in whatever they give, in order to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the six pāramitās?
The Buddha replied:
"The donor has no thoughts of attachment, and the recipient does not forget the kindness shown; this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
To be free from transgression and not to use the precepts for self-adornment; this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
Constantly maintaining patience and harboring no anger or resentment toward sentient beings is the perfection of forbearance (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Diligently striving without indolence with the desire to deliver all beings is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To have a mind that is tranquil and free from agitation is the perfection of dhyāna.
To understand emptiness through wisdom and not conceive of a self is the perfection of prajñā.

To state the essentials and explain them further: that there is neither transgression nor non-transgression, and even no absence of non-transgression, is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
To be free from malice and resentment is the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
To exert oneself in body and mind without weariness is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
To give rise to non-distraction and the absence of conceptualization is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
To understand all phenomena without attachment is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to achieve the realization of the meaning of the merits of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones— past, future, and present— should study the perfection of wisdom.

Those who wish to transcend and deliver all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas; who understand that the dharmas of the past, future, and present reach back to a rootless origin and that the arising of all dharmas does not originate from a fundamental limit (*koṭi*); those who wish to attain this state; those who wish to practice the dharmas of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas; those who wish to serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; those who wish to be fully endowed with the immeasurable retinues and followers of the Buddhas; those who wish to obtain the assembly of Bodhisattvas as their kin; those who wish to purify and complete the merit of all blessings; those who wish to achieve the mind of giving without any sense of receiving; those who do not give rise to thoughts of violating the precepts; those who have no mind of anger, no mind of indolence, and do not wish to arouse a distracted mind, nor wish to arouse a mind of delusion—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish sentient beings in the merit of giving, and to exhort them to cultivate and maintain the precepts and wisdom, he should study the *prajñāpāramitā* regarding the meritorious virtues that are to be generated."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring forth the five eyes should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
What are the five eyes?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye—
one should study the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra:

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, as well as in the eight intermediate directions and above and below, and wishes to hear with the divine ear all the sūtras and dharmas they preach, and furthermore wishes to know the thoughts in the minds of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear and never cease to hear the Dharma being preached by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who are universally present throughout the ten directions, until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and wishes to see the buddha-fields of those Buddhas; or if they wish to follow and see the present Buddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions and all that exists within their fields, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to understand and comprehend the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata— namely, the *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, and *upadeśa*— and wishes to master, study, and recite those which have not been heard by the śrāvakas, they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Tathāgatas of the eight directions, above, and below, and retain them all in mind without loss; and if he wishes to uphold what has been retained and preach it for the sake of the assembly and others, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to inquire about the meaning of what has been taught regarding the past and the future, and having heard it, wishes to explain it to others, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to illuminate the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where it is so dark and obscure that even the brilliance of the sun and moon cannot be seen, and wishes to illuminate these as well as the worlds of the ten directions, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to transform and enlighten as many Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River, as well as the ignorant and dark realms throughout the ten directions— where the name of the Buddha is not heard, the sutras are not heard, and the Sangha is not seen— and if he wishes to transform and enlighten the various classes of sentient beings by establishing them in right view, enabling them to behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma and the teachings, and encounter the noble assembly, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause all sentient beings in the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, as well as in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions— those who are born blind to obtain sight to behold forms, the deaf to attain hearing, the insane to regain their senses, the naked to obtain clothing, the hungry to receive food, and the thirsty to obtain water and drink— and desires that they all receive this grace through his own power, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there are those among the multitudes of beings in this trichiliocosm who dwell in the evil destinies— whether in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals— and I wish to bestow grace upon them so that these common folk may attain their proper place, and likewise throughout the eight directions and above and below, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in the precepts, in samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; from the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, up to the realization of pratyekabuddhahood and the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and furthermore, if they wish to cultivate the majestic deportment and ritual etiquette of a tathāgata, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate in this way:
'Even if there is something that my body cannot perceive, yet I wish to examine it, I must study the prajñāpāramitā.'"

"Even if my body were but four inches in height, and I were to traverse every inch of ground with my toes, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up through the heavens of the desire realm, the form realm, and the Akaniṣṭha heaven—surrounded by an infinite number of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of followers—I would go to the site of the Bodhi tree at the place of practice and study the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sits beneath the Bodhi tree, the devas from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to those of the Pure Abodes come without distinction to provide him with perfect offerings. Whether he is about to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and *abhisaṃbudhyate*, or whether he is walking, coming and going, standing, sitting, or lying down, the ground beneath him spontaneously becomes diamond (*vajra*).”
"If you wish to attain this, you should study the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they should form this contemplation:"
"On what day shall I go forth to leave my kingdom and abandon my home, so that on that very day I may realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attain *abhisaṃbodhi*;

and having attained *abhisaṃbodhi*, on that very day turn the wheel of Dharma; and by turning the wheel of Dharma, cause countless, immeasurable classes of sentient beings to remove dust and leave behind defilement, so that their Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena becomes pure; and may immeasurable, limitless multitudes of living beings attain the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), and may immeasurable, limitless sentient beings with blood in their veins attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva forms the mental aspiration to attain: "

"When I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and reached the state of an A-vai-san-bu (Avaivartika Buddha), there will be an infinite number of bhikṣus, a holy assembly of śrāvaka disciples; some, by expounding the Dharma but once, shall attain arhatship while seated upon a single seat.
All the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall reach the stage of avaivartika and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There will be an infinite, incalculable, and immeasurable multitude of bodhisattvas, whose lifespans are limitless and whose radiance shines afar without bound."
"One should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieve *abhisambuddhi*, and desires that in his buddha-field there shall be no sound even of the names 'lust,' 'anger,' or 'delusion'; if he wishes for all sentient beings to obtain such physical forms as are fully perfected in the *prajñāpāramitā*; if he wishes for the excellence of their giving, the joy of their discipline, the wondrousness of their wisdom, and the goodness of their cultivation of the holy life; and if he wishes for the joy of wandering in accordance with the Dharma while not dwelling among sentient beings—he should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the prajñāpāramitā with this thought: 'May I attain the perfection of noble penetration; yet, though enriched by the True Dharma, may there be no sound whatsoever. Thus should they train."
The mind makes this vow, saying:
"May my pure reputation cause all classes of sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā. Chapter Two: Accordance with Emptiness (*Śūnyatā-anuloma*) The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and gives rise to such virtues, the Four Heavenly Kings immediately rejoice: "We shall protect this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the Prajñāpāramitā. They will protect him from the hands of kings, ministers, thieves, robbers, and enemies; they will protect him from the hands of those who harbor malice toward him, and they will protect him from the hands of those who wish to harm him through curses, incantations, or sorcery. Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a being, a soul, or a person. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental objects, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he perceive the unconditioned. He does not perceive the past, nor the future, nor the present. He does not perceive the world of sentient beings, nor the world of vessels. He does not perceive the Buddhas of the past, nor the Buddhas of the future, nor the Buddhas of the present. He does not perceive the Dharma, nor the Saṅgha. He does not perceive the emptiness of internal phenomena, nor the emptiness of external phenomena, nor the emptiness of both internal and external phenomena. He does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, nor the great emptiness, nor the emptiness of ultimate reality, nor the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, nor the emptiness of that which transcends limits, nor the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor the emptiness of nature, nor the emptiness of all phenomena, nor the emptiness of characteristics, nor the emptiness of non-characteristics, nor the emptiness of the unapprehendable. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the four fearlessnesses, nor the four grounds of self-confidence, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He does not perceive the path of the Stream-enterer, nor the fruit of the Stream-enterer, nor the path of the Once-returner, nor the fruit of the Once-returner, nor the path of the Non-returner, nor the fruit of the Non-returner, nor the path of the Arhat, nor the fruit of the Arhat, nor the path of the Pratyekabuddha, nor the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the path of the Bodhisattva, nor the fruit of the Bodhisattva, nor the path of the Tathāgata, nor the fruit of the Tathāgata. He does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor the perfection of morality, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditation, nor the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the emptiness of all dharmas. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor the four foundations of mindfulness, nor the four right efforts, nor the four bases of psychic power, nor the five faculties, nor the five powers, nor the seven factors of enlightenment, nor the eightfold noble path. He does not perceive the four dhyānas, nor the four immeasurables, nor the four formless attainments. He does not perceive the eight liberations, nor the nine successive stages of meditative concentration. He does not perceive the ten powers, nor the four fearlessnesses, nor the four grounds of self-confidence, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He does not perceive the Great Compassion, nor the Unhindered Wisdom, nor the Knowledge of the Destruction of Outflows. He does not perceive the knowledge of the past, nor the knowledge of the future, nor the knowledge of the present. He does not perceive the knowledge of the minds of others, nor the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. He does not perceive the knowledge of the recollection of past lives, nor the divine ear, nor the knowledge of death and rebirth, nor the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all afflictions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all views, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all conceptualizations. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all habitual tendencies, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all fetters, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all bonds. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all obscurations, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all hindrances, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all delusions. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all ignorance, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all craving, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all attachment. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all grasping, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all clinging, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all conceit. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all pride, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all arrogance, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all haughtiness. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all vanity, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all self-importance, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all egoism. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all self-centeredness, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all possessiveness, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all appropriation. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all identification, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all attachment to signs, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all conceptual proliferation. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all discursive thought, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental activity, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental formations. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental constructions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental imputations, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental superimpositions. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental fabrications, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental elaborations, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental constructs. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental projections, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental extensions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental expansions. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental diffusions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental dispersals, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental distractions. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental wanderings, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental deviations, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental aberrations. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental perversions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental inversions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental distortions. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental errors, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental misapprehensions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental misconceptions. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental delusions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental confusions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental obscurations. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental veils, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental coverings, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental shrouds. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental barriers, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental obstructions, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental impediments. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental hindrances, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental obstacles, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental blockages. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental confinements, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental enclosures, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental prisons. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental cages, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental traps, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental snares. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental nooses, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental bonds, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental fetters. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental chains, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental links, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental joints. He does not perceive the knowledge of the destruction of all mental connections, nor the knowledge of the destruction of all mental associations

"We shall establish four alms bowls; those which the Four Heavenly Kings previously offered to the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, we shall likewise present to those who study the Dharma."
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven also leaped for joy, as did those of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens, saying:
"We shall all serve and make offerings to this son of good family; the bodies of the Asuras shall thus diminish, while the bodies of the various devas shall increase."
Throughout the trichiliocosm, reaching upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, there was none who did not leap for joy, saying:
"We entreat and exhort you to turn the wheel of Dharma."
"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they thereby increase and benefit others, fully accomplishing the six pāramitās.
Sons and daughters of good family will then feel joy and delight."

"We shall practice the loving-kindness of parents toward their children, and the loving-kindness of wives, children, relatives, and friends toward one another; we shall love our parents, brothers, wives, children, and dear friends, and shall look upon them with reverence and joy."

The Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, shall ensure that the Bodhisattva does not encounter worldly desires; they will resolve to go forth to attend upon him and pay him homage, saying:
"We too shall cause him to attain the pure conduct of the Brahmā heavens and to leave behind defiled conduct; by refraining from practicing sexual desire, he shall be reborn in the Brahmā heavens."

"There is no such thing as being heedless while weaving heedfulness; those who possess form cannot advance to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, a bodhisattva abandons household affairs through pure brahmacarya and thereby attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and *abhisambuddhi*; one does not attain the Buddha-way through defilement."
The venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Regarding the dharma of a bodhisattva, must they necessarily have parents, a wife and children, and close friends and acquaintances?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“If there is a bodhisattva, he must necessarily have parents, yet he should not have a wife or children; or, having first resolved his mind upon awakening and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, he becomes a *kumārabhūta* (a perpetual celibate), until he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”
There may be bodhisattvas who, through *upāyakauśalya*, practice the five desires and only thereafter leave the household life to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and become a Buddha.

It is like a skillful and clever illusionist and his disciple who, having mastered the arts of illusion, conjure the five objects of desire; they then amuse themselves with these five pleasures, engaging in play and laughter as their practice.
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Would that illusionist ever become habituated to the five desires?
Śāriputra replied: "No, O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said, “So it is,

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the five desires through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform and guide sentient beings, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is not defiled by those five desires.”

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva extols sensual desires through countless means; yet there are also those who revile them, saying that sensual desire is a blazing fire, that sensual desire is a defilement, that sensual desire is an enemy, and that sensual desire is a foe.
"In this way, Śāriputra,
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, makes distinctions regarding these five objects of desire.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive a bodhisattva, nor do they perceive the word 'bodhisattva'; they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive the word 'practicing the perfection of wisdom,' nor do they perceive non-practice."
Why is this? Because the designation "Bodhisattva" is naturally empty.

That which is empty has no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is not distinct from the emptiness of form, nor is it distinct from the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Just as form is empty, so too are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness empty.
That which is called "emptiness" means that form is empty, and sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise of their own nature.

Why is this so? It is because what is called a "bodhisattva" is merely a provisional designation; what is called the "Path" is likewise a provisional designation; and what is called "emptiness" is likewise a provisional designation.
That Dharma is spontaneous, neither arising nor ceasing, and free from affliction; it has nothing upon which to rely and no dispute or contention.
If there is a bodhisattva whose practice is such as this, they see neither that which arises nor that which ceases; they see neither that upon which to lean nor that which is contested.
Why is this so? Deceptive and fraudulent designations are established based on the conceptualization of travelers; it is due to such mental recollection that these phenomena arise.
Based upon what are these designations established?
It is merely based on empty words.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands this clearly, they are then practicing the prajñāpāramitā; they do not perceive any names or designations whatsoever. Having nothing to see, yet not being in a state of non-seeing, they have no reliance; this is to be practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
Chapter Three: Practice of Emptiness, Part One. The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should form this contemplation:
‘The designation "bodhisattva" and what is called "Buddha" are likewise merely provisional designations.’”
What are called name-and-form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely provisional designations;
they all arise from the notion of "self.

This so-called self is, in reality, non-existent. There is no self, no person, no life-principle, no lifespan, nor any sentient beings down to the smallest crawling insect; there is neither mind nor thought.

If one considers that which is produced through conditioning—those things naturally practiced, encountered, seen, known, and perceived—all such categories are unobtainable, empty, and without attachment.
"All are merely provisional designations; they are nothing but empty words.

In this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive sentient beings; even though there is nothing to be seen, they do not have the notion of seeing, nor do they perceive the words upon which these [designations] rely.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they act in accordance with the instructions of the Tathāgata as they practice the prajñāpāramitā.
Having set aside the Tathāgata [as their primary object], their wisdom surpasses that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they give rise to the practice of emptiness without becoming deluded.
Why is this? Because in what that person cultivates, they do not perceive any characters upon which to rely.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said:

"Suppose, Śāriputra, that monks such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fill Jambudvīpa, as densely as a forest of bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, hemp, or flax; though they were fully endowed with wisdom, they could never equal a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, not even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or a hundred-millionfold—they could not bear comparison."
Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is intended to deliver all classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the wisdom they cultivate in a single day surpasses all the wisdom possessed by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bhikṣus such as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana; it is not matched by the practice of those who have not yet attained the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Setting aside these bhikṣus such as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana in this trichiliocosm—for example, even if the lands of the Buddhas in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were entirely filled with bhikṣus such as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and this were extended throughout the ten directions—these would not equal for a single day the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. This wisdom surpasses the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and hundreds of billions of times; it is beyond comparison.
Thereupon, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“Indeed, whether it be the wisdom of a śrāvaka, or the wisdom of a srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, tathāgata, arhat, or samyaksaṃbuddha—if one calculates all such wisdom that exists, it is without destruction, without contention, and without arising; it is naturally empty.”
"O Heaven among Heavens!
As for that which is indestructible, free from contention, unarisen, and naturally empty—can it possibly attain any degree of distinction or differentiation?"
"How is it that a bodhisattva practices wisdom for a single day and yet surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"What do you think, Śāriputra? For what purpose does a bodhisattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?"

The wisdom practiced throughout a single day, the vows established, and the cultivation of illusory arts performed out of compassion—all these are for the sake of all classes of sentient beings; having fully understood all phenomena, they transform the multitudes of living beings, desiring to bring them to nirvana.
“Would the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever be able to establish such wisdom based on conditions?
He replied, “No, O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said, "What do you think, Śāriputra? Do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever have this thought:
'We shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, having transformed sentient beings, lead them to the realm of nirvāṇa so that they may be extinguished and liberated'?"
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:
"For this reason, you should further understand that even a single member of this assembly of Buddhas would never entertain such a thought:

'Shall we not practice the six *pāramitās*, transform sentient beings, and adorn and purify Buddha-fields; shall we not fulfill the ten powers of a *tathāgata*, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, so as to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and deliver, liberate, and lead to extinction immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable classes of sentient beings?'"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! The Buddha said:
“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva resolves in his mind, saying:
‘I shall practice the six pāramitās, fulfill all dharmas, realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and deliver immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings.’”
The Buddha said:
"It is like the palace of the sun, which exerts its radiance and illuminates the land of Jambudvīpa all at once, leaving no place unpenetrated."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās, they become endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they transform, instruct, and liberate immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable classes of sentient beings.
The venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and thereby attain the stage of avaivartika while purely cultivating the path to buddhahood?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“In this regard, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the six pāramitās and transcends the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he thereby surpasses the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and abides in the stage of avaivartika.”
The venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become the supreme field of merit among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment, as Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās until they sit beneath the Bodhi tree, they are always the supreme source of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
Why is this? If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas appear, they naturally give rise to the true and wondrous Dharma;
they fulfill the ten wholesome actions and further accomplish the five precepts, establish the eightfold equanimity and the eightfold fast, and [practice] the four dhyānas.
The four immeasurable minds, the four formless samādhis, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path appear in the world; as do the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
When such categories of merit from various virtues arise and manifest in the world, one then distinguishes the lineages of gentlemen, brahmins, elders, and haughty clans of great families;
as well as those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the thirty-three abodes, the Heaven of Perception, and the Heaven of Non-perception; and the Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, Anāgāmins, and Arhats.
Arhats, pratyekabuddhas, tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas distinguish these matters through this very [wisdom].
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring the accumulations of merit (puṇyaskandha) to complete purity?
The World-Honored One replied:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva has nothing among those who provide merit that is not purified and brought to completion.
Why is this? Because when one reaches the ultimate realization of emptiness, that constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fulfillment of those who provide merit.”
Why is this so? Śāriputra, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a person of giving.
What is it that is given? One gives the gift of the wholesome Dharma to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
What is meant by the "wholesome Dharma"?

The matters of the ten wholesome actions; the five precepts and the six *pāramitās*; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the transformation and edification of those at the stages of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha*; and the bodhisattvas (*tathāgata*, *arhat*, *samyaksaṃbuddha*) who practice giving.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
What practices does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate so as to be practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"In this regard, if a bodhisattva practices the emptiness of form, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they practice the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is likewise practicing [the perfection of wisdom]."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands and knows that the eye is empty, this constitutes practice. To understand that the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness;

the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness; the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness; the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness; and the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness are empty—this constitutes practice."
One who understands that suffering is empty also understands that its arising is empty, its cessation is empty, and the eightfold path is empty; this constitutes practice.

One who understands that ignorance is empty also understands that volitional formations are empty, consciousness is empty, name-and-form is empty, the six sense bases are empty, contact is empty, feeling is empty, craving is empty, grasping is empty, existence is empty, birth is empty, and old age and death are empty; this constitutes practice.
To understand that all dharmas are empty is practice.
To be able to understand that all things—whether spontaneous, conditioned, or unconditioned—are empty is practice.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, understanding that they are fundamentally pure and empty, and that their own essential nature is likewise so, this is practice.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom: they should understand these seven kinds of emptiness; this is what constitutes practice.

By means of these seven kinds of emptiness, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā*. Form has neither correspondence nor non-correspondence, neither practice nor non-practice; one does not form such views, nor does one see sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having correspondence or non-correspondence, practice or non-practice. One does not see that the dharma of form arises or ceases, nor does one see that the dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness arise or cease. One does not see that the dharma of form has anything upon which it relies or attaches, nor anything with which it contends; one does not see that the dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness have anything to which they attach or anything with which they contend. One does not see oneself dwelling or roaming together with form, nor does one see oneself dwelling or roaming together with sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. One does not see oneself dwelling together with birth and death, nor does one see oneself not dwelling together with birth and death.
Why is this? Because there is never any dharma that exists together with it; all dependently originated phenomena are fundamentally pure and empty. Śāriputra!
If form is emptiness, then there is no form; if sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, then there is no consciousness.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"That which is empty has neither arising nor ceasing."
If form is empty, then there is no form; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, then there is no consciousness.

If form is empty, then there is no seeing; if feeling is empty, then there is no affliction; if perception is empty, then there is no conceptualization; if mental formations are empty, then there is no creation; and if consciousness is empty, then there is no discrimination.
Why is this so? Śāriputra, form is distinct; it is not identical with emptiness.
Emptiness is not different, and form is not to be discriminated.
Form is naturally empty; form is itself emptiness. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not distinct from it, nor is emptiness different from them.
If emptiness is not different [from form], consciousness is also not different; consciousness is naturally empty, and thus consciousness is emptiness.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“That which is empty does not arise and does not cease; it has nothing upon which to rely or cling, nothing with which to dispute, no increase and no decrease; it has no past, no future, and no present.”
