In that [state], there is also no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is also no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is also no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena—none of these exist there.

There is no ignorance that is not extinguished and no ignorance that does not cease; there is no consciousness, no name-and-form, no six sense bases, no contact, no feeling, no craving, no clinging, no existence, no birth, no aging, no sickness, and no death; nor is there the extinction or removal of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
That is neither suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path.
That is neither attainment, nor is there a time for it.

Therein is no fruit of the stream-enterer, no fruit of the once-returner, no fruit of the non-returner, no fruit of the arhat, no awakening of a pratyekabuddha, no attainment of the Way, and no Buddha-way.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā in this manner, that is indeed the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā; they do not perceive whether the prajñāpāramitā is appropriate or inappropriate, practiced or not practiced; they do not perceive giving, nor morality, patience, diligence, meditation, or wisdom—they do not perceive these six pāramitās.
One does not perceive whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are appropriate or inappropriate, or whether they are practiced or not practiced;

one does not perceive whether the eye is appropriate or inappropriate, or whether it is practiced or not practiced; one does not perceive whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are appropriate or inappropriate, or whether they are practiced or not practiced;
one does not perceive whether forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are appropriate or inappropriate, or whether they are practiced or not practiced.
One does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as being either appropriate or inappropriate, or as being practiced or not practiced;

one does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold path as being either appropriate or inappropriate, or as being practiced or not practiced;

one does not perceive the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either appropriate or inappropriate, or as being practiced or not practiced.
One does not perceive the Tathāgata’s wisdom of suchness as either appropriate or inappropriate, nor as practiced or unpracticed.
Śāriputra, this is the practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā; this is indeed what should be practiced.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, emptiness does not contend with emptiness, nor does emptiness proceed with emptiness;
signlessness does not contend with signlessness, nor does signlessness proceed with signlessness; wishlessness does not contend with wishlessness, nor does wishlessness proceed with wishlessness.”
The wishless does not contend with the wishless; the wishless does not proceed together with the wishless.
Emptiness does not correspond with emptiness; signlessness does not correspond with signlessness; the wishless does not correspond with the wishless.

Why is this so? Emptiness has neither practice nor non-practice; signlessness likewise has neither practice nor non-practice; wishlessness likewise has neither practice nor non-practice. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā is able to act in this manner, this is what constitutes true practice.
The Buddha spoke again to Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he attains the crossing over into emptiness through the natural mark of all dharmas.”
Having already attained the crossing over of emptiness, one does not contend with form (*rūpa*) nor engage in any activity;
one does not contend with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor engage in any activity;
one does not contend with past form, nor does one perceive past form.
One does not contend with past form, nor does one perceive future form;
one does not contend with future form, nor does one perceive present form;

one does not contend with present form, nor does one contend with past feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one contend with future or present feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one perceive past, future, or present feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not contend with the past regarding the future, nor do they contend with the future regarding the past; they do not contend with the present regarding the past or the future, nor do they contend with the past or the future regarding the present. Not perceiving the three periods of time as being distinct from the practice of the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom—practicing in this manner is what constitutes true practice."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, his practice is such that it accords with what ought to be practiced; he does not dispute his practice with the past sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), nor does he perceive any past sarvajñatā. How could there be any dispute regarding the practice of past sarvajñatā? "
One does not contend with future omniscience (sarvajñatā) in one's practice, nor is there anything practiced; furthermore, how could there be future omniscience that contends with practice?

Nor does one dispute the practice of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) with respect to the present, nor does one perceive the *sarvajñatā* of the present; how then could there be a dispute regarding the practice of *sarvajñatā*?
To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner is truly to practice.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice with regard to the form of sarvajñatā, nor does he perceive the form of sarvajñatā; he does not perceive the feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness of practicing with regard to the sarvajñatā of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive the feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness of sarvajñatā itself."

One does not practice with the eye of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), nor does one perceive the eye; likewise, one does not practice with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind of sarvajñā, nor does one perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One does not practice the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of form, nor does one perceive form.
Not perceiving form, one does not practice the omniscience of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharmas*), nor does anything manifest therein.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“One who can practice the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner is indeed practicing it correctly. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not adhere to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) for the sake of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor do they perceive the perfection of giving; the same applies to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of omniscience, nor do they perceive the perfection of wisdom for the sake of omniscience.

Nor does one follow the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) of sarvajñatā, nor does one perceive the four foundations of mindfulness of sarvajñatā; nor does one follow the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga), or the eightfold path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga) of sarvajñatā, nor does one perceive the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, or the path of sarvajñatā.

Nor does one follow the ten powers (bala), the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) of sarvajñatā, nor is there anything perceived, nor does one perceive the various powers and qualities of a Tathāgata of sarvajñatā.
To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner is indeed to practice.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not practice *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and the Buddha; nor does the Buddha practice *sarvajñatā*. He does not practice *sarvajñatā* and the Path; nor does the Path practice *sarvajñatā*."
Why is this? The Buddha is omniscience (sarvajñatā), and omniscience is the Buddha;
the Path is omniscience, and omniscience is the Path.
"The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise thus.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā in such a manner as this is truly practicing it."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice the existence of form, nor does he practice the non-existence of form; he does not practice the existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he practice the non-existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not reckon form as permanent, nor does he reckon form as impermanent; he does not reckon form as suffering, nor does he reckon form as pleasure; he does not reckon form as having a self, nor does he reckon form as being without a self. It is the same for the five aggregates and the six sense-fields."

One practices the perfection of wisdom by not reckoning the five aggregates as empty or non-empty, not reckoning the five aggregates as having marks or being markless, and not reckoning the five aggregates as having vows or being vowless.

Now, my practice is likewise without anything received, without anything practiced, and without anything grasped; it is neither practicing nor non-practicing, neither receiving nor non-receiving, and neither grasping nor non-grasping.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā is able to act in this way, this indeed constitutes practice.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditation; rather, they practice the perfection of wisdom [for its own sake].
One practices the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of the stage of non-retrogression, but for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
one practices the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of purifying buddha-fields.
One practices the Prajñāpāramitā not for the sake of the ten powers of the Tathāgata;
one practices the Prajñāpāramitā not for the sake of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Because of the non-appropriation of non-ultimate emptiness, the non-appropriation of internal emptiness, the non-appropriation of external emptiness,
the non-appropriation of internal-and-external emptiness, the non-appropriation of the emptiness of emptiness; because of the non-appropriation of great emptiness,
the non-appropriation of true emptiness, the non-appropriation of conditioned emptiness, the non-appropriation of unconditioned emptiness, and the non-appropriation of ultimate emptiness.
It is not because of the emptiness of non-existence, nor because of the emptiness of primordial purity, nor because of the emptiness of natural characteristics,

nor because of the emptiness of all phenomena, nor because of the emptiness of non-arising, nor because of the emptiness of non-ceasing, nor because of the emptiness of formlessness, nor because of the emptiness of spontaneity.
Because form and formlessness are empty, because there is no absence of the fundamental source, because it is not by means of the dharma-realm,
and not by means of the limit of reality, one practices the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they neither destroy nor perceive any phenomena.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the supernormal power of psychic travel;
they do not practice it for the sake of the divine eye, nor for the sake of the divine ear, nor for the sake of knowing the minds of others, nor for the sake of recollecting past events.
Why is this? When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not even perceive the *prajñāpāramitā*; how much less could one behold the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva?
One who can practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner is indeed practicing it correctly.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, his mind does not give rise to such thoughts as: "
"I shall, by means of my supernormal power, go to the east to visit as many Tathāgatas as there are sands in the Ganges River and prostrate myself before them in worship. Nor does he think:
"I shall go to the eight directions, above, and below."
"It is likewise thus, exactly the same without any difference.
One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner is one who should practice it. Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not think to themselves:

"I shall hear with my divine ear everything that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, proclaim; I shall perceive and see the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings; I shall recollect their past places of dwelling and wandering; and with my divine eye, I shall see the locations where all living beings reside."
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, for one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, this is indeed how it should be practiced. It is thus, Śāriputra!"
One who practices in this manner brings liberation to immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of sentient beings.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to act thus, neither Māra nor his retinue can find an opportunity to cause harm.
Furthermore, the people of other world-systems, hearing of his virtue from afar, all pay him homage.

Moreover, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the rivers in the east, and throughout the eight directions, above and below, all together protect this Bodhisattva, so that he shall never fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

From the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, all together shall protect this bodhisattva mahāsattva, so that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them may find such an opening; whatever they initiate and whatever they ought to do, they shall obtain present merit.
Why is this? Because they direct a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* is able to act in this way, that is what constitutes the proper practice.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they attain the gates of *dhāraṇī* and the gates of *samādhi* with little effort; they swiftly draw near to the *tathāgata*, *arhat*, *samyaksaṃbuddha*, and in every birth they always encounter and see the Buddhas, never being separated from them until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said:
"One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā in such a manner is practicing what should be practiced.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not think to themselves:
"Do these dharmas exist?
As for what are called dharmas, are they all appropriate or inappropriate?"
"Is it equal or unequal? Why is this so?
At that time, the practitioner does not perceive any phenomena as being appropriate or inappropriate, practiced or unpracticed, equal or unequal.
The Buddha said:
“One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā in such a manner is indeed practicing it correctly. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not think to themselves:
"I shall swiftly understand the realm of all phenomena up to the state of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet there is no such thing as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Why is this? Even that which attains the dharma-realm is itself without anything to be awakened to.
If one who practices the prajñāpāramitā can act in this manner, then it is the practice that accords with reality.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any diseases or any emptiness and stillness within phenomena or the dharma-realm."
One who can practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner is practicing in accordance with what should be practiced. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not think to themselves:
"All dharmas and the dharma-realm consist of various kinds, yet one does not calculate them as distinct.
One who can practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner is able to practice in accordance with it.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not think to themselves:
'Regarding these dharmas and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is observing and non-observing, seeing and non-seeing.'"
Why is this? It is because they do not perceive any inherent existence in phenomena, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination regarding phenomena that could be grasped.
To practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in such a manner is what constitutes the proper practice.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell on the dharma-realm while practicing the matter of emptiness, nor does that matter of emptiness dwell on the dharma-realm."
One who practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner is indeed practicing what should be practiced. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not conceive of the eye-element as being empty of emptiness, nor do they feel anxiety regarding the eye-element.
Form does not depend on emptiness, and emptiness does not depend on form;
the realm of form does not depend on emptiness, and the realm of emptiness does not depend on form;
the realm of eye-consciousness does not depend on emptiness, and the realm of consciousness does not depend on the emptiness of eye-consciousness.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*).
The mind-element does not depend on emptiness, and the emptiness-element does not depend on the mind;
the dharma-element does not depend on emptiness, and the emptiness-element does not depend on dharmas.
"The consciousness element does not worry about space, and the space element does not worry about consciousness. The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
This is the foremost practice, namely the practice of emptiness.

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is able to practice emptiness does not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they are able to purify buddha-fields, transform and enlighten sentient beings, swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and achieve abhisaṃbodhi.
When one calculates all practices of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the practice of *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme, the longest, the highest, bottomless, and peerless.
Why is this? Because the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* is the supreme practice; it is the practice of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice in this way and maintain this resolve; thus they will swiftly draw near to the stage of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they open the way for the liberation and benefit of countless, incalculable sentient beings.
Yet they do not harbor the thought:
"I am practicing the prajñāpāramitā; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall grant me a prediction of enlightenment."
Nor does he think: "I have attained intimacy;
I have received the prediction."
"I shall purify the Buddha-field, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and turn the wheel of Dharma. Why is this so?

As for that practitioner, they do not cling to the dharma-realm, nor do they dwell in empty stillness, nor do they perceive any separate dharmas; they should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, and the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, will grant them the prediction of enlightenment and their attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not give rise to the notion of a person, do not give rise to the notion of a self, do not give rise to the notion of a life-span, do not give rise to the notion of a soul, do not give rise to the notion of a multitude of beings, and do not give rise to the notion of one who sees and knows.
Why is this? Because when one reckons that the self and sentient beings neither arise nor cease, and further reckons that the person is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing—
then for that which neither arises nor ceases, what is there to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they give rise to nothing and belong to the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*; because sentient beings are empty, sentient beings are unobtainable, and sentient beings are quiescent, they practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices emptiness performs the foremost practice.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practicing the Prajñāpāramitā are able to act in this way, they transcend all conditioned practices.
Setting aside these practices that are to be followed, they engage in the practice of great loving-kindness and the practice of great compassion.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this, they never give rise to thoughts of greed or envy; they have no thought of violating the precepts, no thought of malice, no thought of indolence, no thought of distracted mind, and no thought of false wisdom.
The Sūtra of Radiant Praise, Scroll One.
The Sūtra of Radiant Praise, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Three, Part Two: "The Practice of Emptiness.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this prajñāpāramitā, from what state do they pass away to be reborn here?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom has passed away from a buddha-field in another direction and been born here.”
If one transmigrates from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born among humans, or comes from among humans to be born here, they will swiftly attain this practice of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā achieve accomplishment in this present life; such persons quickly draw near to the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate.
Thereafter, they will ultimately perfect the Prajñāpāramitā;
they will constantly encounter and behold the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, never being separated from the Buddhas in whatever land they reside.

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having manifested the transformation and disappearance of their bodies from the Tuṣita Heaven as those in their final birth before Buddhahood, do not lose the six pāramitās; wherever they go, they fully possess all the gates of dhāraṇī and swiftly approach the gates of samādhi.
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva passes away from among humans and is reborn again in the human realm, this bodhisattva is one who is irreversible (avaivartika).”

That person, observing those faculties to be tranquil and stilled, is unable to swiftly attain the meditative concentration of the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can they approach the gates of the *dhāraṇīs* or the gates of *samādhi*.
Again, Śāriputra asked:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this prajñāpāramitā reaches the end of his life here, where will he be reborn?”
The Buddha said:

"When their life here comes to an end, they will travel from one buddha-field to another, wherever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently reside, never being separated from those Gods among Gods."

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, lacking upāyakauśalya, cultivate the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna and practice the six pāramitās; by virtue of these meditative absorptions, they are reborn in the long-lived heavens.

"Even if, after passing away from that life, they were to obtain a human body and encounter the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, their faculties would be tranquil and settled, yet they would not be sharp-witted.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who practices the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna and practices the prajñāpāramitā, yet lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). Subsequently, abandoning those dhyānas, he is born in the desire realm; this bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s faculties will be tranquil and settled, yet not sharp-witted."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, do not depart from the prajñāpāramitā;

they enter meditative absorption by contemplating the wisdom of emptiness, enter meditative absorption by reaching the wisdom of consciousness and mind, enter meditative absorption by reaching the wisdom of non-functionality, and enter meditative absorption by reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

Having transcended these four heavens, they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path; they practice great compassion and possess *upāyakauśalya*. In whatever place they are born, they do not follow the teachings of the dhyānas, nor do they rely on loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity, nor do they conform to the formless meditations. They are sovereign over their births, and in every place where they are born, they constantly see the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Not departing from the Prajñāpāramitā, during this *vibhajya-kalpa*, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the state of an Arhat-Buddha.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; who practice the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni) beyond these four heavens; and who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga). Yet, while practicing great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and possessing skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they do not enter meditative absorption (dhyāna-samādhi), and thus they do not attain mastery over their place of rebirth."
That person is born into this realm of desire among the families of nobles, aristocrats, brahmins, or householders, desiring to transform sentient beings and bring them benefit.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, who practice the four immeasurable minds, and who contemplate the wisdom of emptiness, the wisdom of consciousness, the wisdom of non-utility, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having transcended these four heavens, they cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and practice great compassion and skillful means (upāya-kauśalya). Without following the teachings of the dhyānas to take birth [in those realms], such persons are born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
"Born in those realms, they teach and transform sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, behold the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and do not depart from the Way and its teachings.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā and possess upāyakauśalya (skillful means), cultivating the first dhyāna and practicing the four immeasurable minds."
Thereupon, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Heaven of Brahmā’s Retinue, the Heaven of Brahmā’s Ministers, the Heaven of Brahmā’s Glory, and the Heaven of Great Brahmā.

Residing in those Brahmā and Mahābrahmā heavens, he traveled from one buddha-field to another. To all the lands manifested by the Buddhas where they attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, reached *abhisambodhi*, and turned the wheel of Dharma, that bodhisattva mahāsattva exhorted and assisted the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is in his final birth before buddhahood practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), manifests the practice of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, as well as the samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; he proceeds to the wisdom of emptiness, the wisdom of consciousness, the wisdom of non-activity, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having transcended these four heavens, he cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and practices great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). He practices the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness; such is the place where a bodhisattva freely wanders and takes birth.”

That person shall personally behold the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and having cultivated the pure Brahma-conduct in the presence of those Buddhas, shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. There, he shall act as a guide for others; like a boat that ferries across, his faculties shall be flawless and ever-abiding in tranquil concentration. Surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of devas, he shall descend together with them to this world, attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the six supernormal powers, he is not reborn in the heavens of desire, the heavens of form, or the formless heavens; rather, he travels from one buddha-field to another, bowing his head and serving all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the six supernormal powers, he enjoys himself as he travels from one buddha-field to another. In whichever buddha-field he dwells, he hears neither the voices of śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas, nor even their names.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the six supernormal powers, he finds delight therein and travels universally throughout the ten directions, going from one buddha-field to another. In whichever buddha-lands he arrives, his lifespan is exceedingly long, such that its limit in kalpas cannot be measured.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the six supernormal powers and delights therein, he travels from one buddha-field to another. In whichever buddha-lands he arrives where there is no Buddha-dharma nor assembly of noble ones, he shall sing praises and provide detailed explanations concerning the virtues of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.”

Sentient beings, hearing the sounds of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha at the appropriate time, will harbor joy in their hearts; after the end of their lives, they shall all be reborn in lands where a World-Honored Buddha currently resides.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not attain the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, nor the four immeasurables, the brahma-conduct, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, will never be born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
rather, wherever they are born, it is among sentient beings who seek renown."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), from the first resolution he proceeds toward extinction and tranquility; attaining non-retrogression and abiding on the stage of immovability, he shall reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path and realize supreme perfect enlightenment.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"From the first moment of generating the aspiration, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path, achieves supreme perfect enlightenment, and immediately turns the wheel of Dharma. For the sake of immeasurable and incalculable classes of sentient beings, he guides them, benefits them, and provides them with aid, and only thereafter does he enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"After his parinirvāṇa, his Dharma will remain for one kalpa or even longer than a kalpa.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, from the first moment he resolves his mind,

the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) together with incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, traveling from one buddha-field to another, being born in buddha-lands of pure and adorned realms."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he attains the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the formless absorptions, delighting therein; he attains the first dhyāna.”
Rising from the first dhyāna, he enters the samādhi of profound stillness and dwells in right reception (*samyaksamādhi*).
Rising from the dhyāna of cessation, he proceeds through to the fourth dhyāna and dwells in contemplation.

Rising from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the dhyāna of cessation and stillness; rising from the dhyāna of cessation and stillness, he proceeds to the dhyāna of infinite space; rising from the dhyāna of infinite space, he dwells in the dhyāna of cessation; rising from the dhyāna of cessation, he proceeds to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enters meditative absorption; rising from the dhyāna of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells in the dhyāna of cessation and stillness.
This, Śāriputra, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, manifesting through skillful means the samādhis and meditative attainments in which they engage.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path, up to the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, yet does not attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, or the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood.”

Practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, he employs skillful means and expedients to transform sentient beings through the Eightfold Noble Path, enabling them to attain the fruit of Stream-entry, the fruit of Once-returning, the fruit of Non-returning, the fruit of Arhatship, and the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The wisdom of the fruits of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is compared to the bodhisattva’s attainment of dharma-patience;
thus one knows that the bodhisattva’s practice of non-retrogression is this pāramitā of wisdom.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and dwells in the six perfections, and while in the Tuṣita Heaven has fully perfected all the various emptinesses (śūnyatā), that bodhisattva mahāsattva should know this: he shall become a Buddha among the number of bodhisattvas in the Bhadrakalpa.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path, up to the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—and when there are beings practicing the Buddha-way who do not yet establish themselves in the Four Noble Truths—that bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who stands as a candidate for the state of being born only once more before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they pass from one buddha-field to another, traveling extensively through various lands; wherever they arrive, they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to establish themselves in the Buddha-way.”
That bodhisattva mahāsattva, after incalculable and innumerable kalpas, shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“The bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfections (pāramitā) and constantly practices diligence for the sake of sentient beings; he never gives rise to thoughts or speaks words that are without benefit.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and is constantly diligent in his desire to rescue sentient beings, he travels from one buddha-field to another, transforming and enlightening the multitudes so that they may transcend their toil and suffering, and sever the paths of the three evil realms of retribution."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), practicing the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) while surrounded by a retinue, he guides and leads sentient beings toward eternal peace. To those who are hungry he gives food; to those who are thirsty he gives drink; to those without clothing he gives clothes; to those without incense he gives incense, blended incense, and powdered incense; as well as bedding, servants, vehicles, gold, silver, and the seven treasures. Regarding whatever means of livelihood they seek, he never opposes them, but accords with their needs.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he transforms his own body to be like that of a Tathāgata and enters the hells, preaching the Dharma for those within the hells;
he likewise expounds the principles of the teachings to those among the animals and the hungry ghosts."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), they transform their own body and mind so that they are like the image of a Buddha. They cross over to buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, preaching the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; they prostrate before the Tathāgatas and purify those buddha-lands, and all who hear this teaching give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.”

In this manner, they travel throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, observing all Buddha-lands and selecting superior beings to purify their own lands, so that these five matters may be more sublime than those of the Buddhas [of other lands].
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is fully accomplished as one who is in his final birth before Buddhahood.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); at the appropriate time, he fulfills the thirty-two marks of a great man (dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa). His faculties are sublime and he attains complete penetration. By means of these faculties of diligence, he is seen with reverence and affection by countless people, causing immeasurable classes of sentient beings to give rise to hearts of joy and delight, gradually leading those in the three miserable realms (triyapāya) to attain liberation (nirvāṇa)."
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should purify their body, speech, and mind.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, his faculties are supremely refined and his physical form is upright and handsome; he does not praise himself, nor does he speak of the faults of others, but constantly examines his own transgressions and does not litigate the deficiencies of others."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the perfection of giving and the perfection of ethical discipline, and has already attained stability in these two perfections, they gather and take hold of the most exalted positions of countless wheel-turning sage kings, beyond all measure."

Wherever that Wheel-Turning Sage King may be, he beholds countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; he then prostrates himself in salutation and serves and makes offerings to those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), he expounds the light of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. Having illuminated himself, he never loses this radiance of the Dharma until he reaches the unsurpassed, right, and true path and attains supreme perfect enlightenment.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva brings great illumination to all the Buddha-dharmas.
For this reason, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should always cultivate with diligence the protection of body, speech, and mind, ensuring that body, speech, and mind do not commit any transgression or failure.
The worthy Śāriputra said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivate all practices, guarding body, speech, and mind so as to commit no transgression?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects within his own mind:
‘This is what is produced by that body, what is brought forth by the body, and what is established; this is speech, and these six are the mind.’”
Whatever his mind intends is successfully accomplished.
This is how the bodhisattva mahāsattva guards body, speech, and mind.
When the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he neither attains a body, nor attains speech, nor attains a mind.

Suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and attains control over body, speech, and mind; yet if there arises within that very control of body, speech, and mind a mind of greed and envy, then there will likewise arise a mind that violates the precepts, a mind of anger, a mind of indolence, a mind of distraction, and a mind of false wisdom.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“One who practices in such a manner should not be called a bodhisattva.

It is only when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, purifying the defilements of body, purifying the defilements of speech, and purifying the defilements of mind so that they are without deficiency, that one is called a bodhisattva.”
The venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the defilements of body, speech, and mind?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Suppose that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend a self-body, nor does he apprehend speech or mental volition.
The Buddha said, "So it is, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies body, speech, and mind.
Should there be any flaws or evils in body, speech, or mind, they arise from the pursuit of gain and offerings.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, practices the path toward the retribution of the ten wholesome deeds and does not give rise to the thoughts of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, then such a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly purifies the defilements of body, speech, and mind.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and seeks the path of the Buddha, they practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, and the perfection of single-minded concentration.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva seek the path to buddhahood?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, suppose one could not obtain the actions of body, speech, or the mental intentions; could not obtain the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of concentration, or the perfection of wisdom; could not obtain the state of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; could not obtain the state of a bodhisattva; and could not obtain the path of the Buddha.”
"Therefore, when a bodhisattva seeks the path of the Buddha, they find nothing to be attained in any dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has practiced the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), there is a place of arrival, yet there is no place arrived at, and none can find an opportunity against them."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, there is both reaching and no reaching, such that no one can find an opportunity to gain advantage?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he does not dwell upon form, nor does he dwell upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not dwell upon the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; nor does he dwell upon forms, sounds, or odors.”
Regarding the phenomena of taste and tangibility, one does not attend to the eye, nor to forms, nor to eye-consciousness;
one does not attend to the ear, nor to sounds, nor to ear-consciousness; one does not attend to the nose, nor to odors, nor to nose-consciousness;
one does not attend to the tongue, nor to tastes, nor to tongue-consciousness; one does not attend to the body, nor to tangibility.

One does not dwell upon the seven factors of awakening or the eightfold path; one does not dwell upon the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom;

one does not dwell upon the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor does one dwell upon their dissemination or their coming and going.
“...the stage of non-returning, the stage of non-attachment, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed, right, and true path, attaining supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are able to fulfill and increase the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); wherever they go, there is nowhere to which they have gone, and no one can find an opportunity to gain advantage over them."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the perfection of wisdom and is fully endowed with all supernormal knowledges. By means of the principles practiced through that wisdom, he never falls into the state of remainderlessness (anupadhiśeṣa); he is not loathed by the multitude, nor is he impoverished, nor does he undergo rebirth in the realm of form after his death."
"For this reason, they destroy themselves and [bring ruin] to the devas, the people of the world, and the asuras.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“The wisdom upon which the bodhisattva mahāsattva relies allows him to see the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction; he hears the Dharma they preach, beholds their assemblies of noble ones, and perceives the utterly pure dharmas of those buddha-fields.”

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva follows this compliant wisdom, they have no conception of a Buddha, no conception of a bodhisattva, no conception of a śrāvaka, and no conception of a pratyekabuddha; nor do they conceive of a buddha-field as being for their own sake.

Why is this so? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, they do not apprehend the perfection of giving; they practice the perfections of morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, yet they do not apprehend the perfections of morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, or wisdom. It is through this wisdom that they attain the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—this is the wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
By employing this wisdom, one fulfills the root of all dharmas, yet remains without any conceptualization regarding any dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s perfection of wisdom purifies the five eyes.”
"What are the five eyes?
They are the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva purify the fleshly eye?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may, by means of the fleshly eye, see four thousand li;
some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may, by means of their own fleshly eye, see eight thousand li;
and there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by means of the fleshly eye, see Jambudvīpa.”
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with their fleshly eyes, see two Jambudvīpas;
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with their fleshly eyes, see the four continents;
and there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with their fleshly eyes, see a thousandfold world system.
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who see two thousand worlds with their physical eyes;
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who see a trichiliocosm with their physical eyes.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to attain the purity of the fleshly eye.
Śāriputra asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva attaining the purity of the divine eye?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The bodhisattva mahāsattva knows all the divine eyes of the various deities in the heavens of the Four Great Kings."
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know all that is seen by the eyes of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
The Bodhisattva’s divine eye perceives everything from the Four Great Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; the Bodhisattva knows them all.

With this divine eye, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva beholds Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, knowing the births and deaths of sentient beings therein; likewise, he beholds the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, this is the purified divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Śāriputra asked again:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
How is it that the wisdom-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is purified?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“As for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses the eye of wisdom, he does not form such thoughts as:
‘Dharmas exist; there are conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, formed and formless dharmas, worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas, outflows and those without outflows.’”
"The Bodhisattva who possesses the eye of wisdom beholds all phenomena; there is nothing, however immeasurable or innumerable, that he does not see or hear.
This is the purification of the eye of wisdom of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
Śāriputra asked again:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
What is the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In this regard, the bodhisattva mahāsattva employs the Dharma-eye to make such distinctions:
'This practice is faith; this practice is the Dharma; this practice is emptiness; this practice is signlessness; this practice is wishlessness.'"
By means of these gates of liberation, one attains the five faculties and the samādhi of non-seeing.
Having attained the samādhi of non-seeing, one gives rise to the wisdom of the knowledge of deliverance; having attained the wisdom of the knowledge of deliverance, one severs the three fetters.
What are these three?
First is attachment to the body, second is doubt, and third is the violation of precepts; these are the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
One who can eliminate attachment to the body, is free from doubt, and does not violate the prohibitions has no fetters. One who has no fetters is one who spreads [the Dharma] among people.
When one travels by this path, lust, ill will, anger, and delusion are attenuated; such a person is called a "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin).
When one proceeds along this same path with greater diligence, lust, ill will, anger, and delusion are completely severed; such a person is called a "non-returner" (anāgāmin).

He applies himself with even greater diligence on the path; with diminished desire for the realm of form and no desire for the formless realm, he eradicates ignorance and conceit. Such a person is called one who is unattached; such a person is called one who practices emptiness.

Being empty regarding the gates of liberation, one attains the five faculties and achieves the samādhi of non-seeing; by means of the samādhi of non-seeing, one gives rise to the wisdom of deliverance and reaches the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, this person has attained the five faculties through the gate of liberation from ideation; to speak of the essentials, they have reached non-attachment—this is the purity of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye.

If a bodhisattva is able to discern and understand that all phenomena which arise through conjunction ultimately converge upon the principle of extinction, and perceives the extinction of all phenomena as the attainment of the five faculties—this is called the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva discerns in this way:

'This bodhisattva who has first resolved his mind practices the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of single-mindedness, and the perfection of wisdom, as well as the faculty of faith and the faculty of vigor. Through these faculties, he is fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and his own person is always established upon the root of virtuous qualities.'"

These bodhisattvas are born among the nobility, the gentry, the brahmins, and the elders; or they are born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

Born in that heaven, manifesting before those who dwell there, they transform and guide sentient beings, causing all living creatures to enter into peaceful conduct and purify Buddha-lands; they encounter the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, making offerings and serving him, never falling into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva will regress; that one will not regress until reaching the unsurpassed, right, and true path, attaining supreme perfect enlightenment.
This is the purification of the Dharma-eye of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva discerns in this way.
A bodhisattva who has received the prediction shall attain the unsurpassed path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment."
"Such-and-such a bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path;
such-and-such a bodhisattva has nothing established or created;
such-and-such a bodhisattva is non-retrogressive, while such-and-such a bodhisattva is not non-retrogressive."
Such-and-such a bodhisattva is fully endowed with supernormal powers; such-and-such a bodhisattva is not fully endowed with supernormal powers;

such-and-such a bodhisattva, being fully endowed with supernormal powers, travels to Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction to prostrate before, pay homage to, and serve the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
such-and-such a bodhisattva has not yet attained supernormal powers; such-and-such a bodhisattva shall attain supernormal powers.
"The lands of certain bodhisattvas shall be pure, while the lands of certain bodhisattvas shall not be pure;
certain bodhisattvas shall transform sentient beings, while certain bodhisattvas shall not;
certain bodhisattvas shall be praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

Such-and-such a bodhisattva will have the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, standing near before them; such-and-such a bodhisattva will not have the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appearing before them.
Such-and-such a bodhisattva’s lifespan will be limited; such-and-such a bodhisattva’s lifespan will be immeasurable.
Such-and-such a bodhisattva’s assembly of bhikṣus will be limited; such-and-such a bodhisattva’s assembly of bhikṣus will be limitless.
A certain bodhisattva shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, taking a multitude of bodhisattvas as his saṃgha;
another bodhisattva, when he attains Buddhahood, shall have no assembly of bodhisattvas;
yet another bodhisattva shall achieve it through arduous and ascetic practices, while another shall achieve it through peaceful and tranquil practices.
"This bodhisattva will ultimately reach the end and exhaust the beginning; this bodhisattva will not ultimately reach the end and exhaust the beginning.
This bodhisattva shall sit beneath the tree of enlightenment; this bodhisattva shall not sit beneath the tree of enlightenment.
This bodhisattva shall encounter the trials of Māra; this bodhisattva shall have no trials of Māra."
“Such, Śāriputra, is the purification of the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the purification of the Buddha-eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“The cause employed by the bodhisattva mahāsattva is the resolve for the unsurpassed path; it is the samādhi of correct reception likened to a vajra. He is fully endowed with all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as great kindness and great compassion. Thus, the eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva universally penetrates all Buddha-dharmas; regarding all Buddha-dharmas, there is nothing he does not see and nothing he does not hear. It is without limit and nothing remains unpenetrated.”

It is so, Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieves supreme perfect enlightenment, he is then able to fully attain the purity of the Buddha-eye.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the five eyes should practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). Why is that?

Therefore, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) all enter into every dharma of virtuous merit; they fully comprehend and understand the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas.
Therefore, Śāriputra! One who attains an impartial mind and practices to this extent will then rescue and sustain all dharmas.
You should contemplate the perfection of wisdom; this perfection of wisdom is the biological mother of the five eyes.
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva studies these five eyes and thereby attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path, achieving supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who cultivates the supernormal powers up to the perfection of liberation; through countless causes and conditions of supernormal power, he abides in this stage, manifesting various forms from a single body and then returning again to a single body."

Thereupon, walls, barriers, mountains, and lofty hills were passed through without obstruction, as if moving through empty space; where there are currents of water, they pass like mist, just as a flying bird travels through the air.
He enters and exits the earth; he emerges without opening and enters without hole, as if entering water.

He walks upon the surface of the water as if upon the ground. His body emits flaming light like a great fire. The brilliance and majestic power of all these suns and moons are so sublime as to be difficult to approach, yet he touches them with his palm and grasps their radiance, exercising complete mastery over them.

Though his body reaches the Brahma Heaven, he does not become conceited on account of his supernormal powers; his mind is neither arrogant nor unrestrained, nor does it harbor any conceptualizations. His supernormal powers are likewise ungraspable, and he is free from pride or self-indulgence.
That which arises is without conceptualization and without thought; its arising is naturally empty. That which is naturally empty is quiescent, and that which is natural does not arise at all.

Furthermore, one who does not give rise to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) nor the practice of the bases of psychic power, but instead focuses exclusively on the matters of the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the basis for the realization of the bases of psychic power through the wisdom of the supernormal knowledges.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the divine ear so that it transcends the ears of gods and humans, he hears every single sound and the voices of all gods and humans; yet he does not conceive of the category of the divine ear, nor does he form the thought:
'I am hearing those sounds.'"
Furthermore, there is nothing to be attained.
Natural emptiness is naturally tranquil; that which is natural neither arises, nor is it attained, nor is it conceptualized, nor does one think to oneself:
"I have obtained the divine ear."

"Merely by being intent upon the matters of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); this is the practice of the supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*)."

The Buddha told Śāriputra: “That bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the reality and the inclinations of the mental thoughts of other sentient beings: whether there is a mind of desire or no mind of desire; a perception of desire or no perception of desire; a mind of anger or a perception of anger; a mind free from anger or a perception free from anger; a mind of delusion or a perception of delusion; a mind free from delusion or a perception free from delusion; a mind with attachment or a mind without attachment; that which is grasped or that which is not grasped; whether it is raised or lowered; a violent mind or a peaceful mind; a great mind or a small mind; a concentrated mind or an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind or an unliberated mind; whether that mind has already been defiled or is about to be defiled; and whether that mind has already conceived a defiled perception or is about to conceive a defiled perception.”

Just as one who thoroughly understands and discriminates between the real and the unreal, and possesses the unsurpassed mind that contemplates the unsurpassed, yet has nothing to contemplate and nothing to conceive. Why is this so?

All minds are mindless; that from which all minds arise is without conceptualization. Thus, one realizes through wisdom the dwelling-places of the past, which are verified by insight; it is for this reason that one traverses those dwelling-places by means of supernormal powers, and it is by means of these that one masters them.

With single-minded mindfulness, one can recall events of a hundred days, a hundred months, and a hundred years; one can fully recall and remember events of one eon, a hundred eons, incalculable eons, countless hundreds of eons, countless thousands of eons, and incalculable billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis.

"In such a place, his name was such-and-such, his clan was such-and-such, his birth was thus, his food and drink were likewise, his long residence was as follows, his lifespan was long or short, his experiences were of suffering, pleasure, good, or evil; having passed away from there, he was born in such-and-such a place—thus did this person of this assembly describe that [being]."
"He is able to recollect and remember his countless past dwellings and travels, yet he does not harbor thoughts regarding the supernatural powers he has attained.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of wisdom is such as this, it constitutes the wisdom that recollects and remembers the clear verification of supernatural powers from former dwellings and travels; this is the practice of the wisdom of supernatural powers."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"That bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the divine eye, beholds the beginning and end of the birth and death of sentient beings—their roots of goodness and roots of evil, their misfortunes and blessings, their virtues and vices, their inclinations toward peace or suffering, and their subtleties or defilements; through their own actions, he fully understands them all."

I pity this person, who has clearly committed evil through body, speech, and mind, being fully possessed of evil conduct; having slandered the noble ones and adhered to false views, by reason of these causes and conditions, their body and life are shattered, and they proceed toward suffering and fall into hell.

These beings, such as these virtuous ones, practice goodness in body, goodness in speech, and goodness in mind; they are complete in all their deeds, do not slander the noble ones, and adhere to right view. Because of these practices, when their bodies perish at the end of their lives, they proceed to a state of peace and are reborn in the heavens.

He beholds those in the eight directions, above, and below who are to be pitied; he perceives that they have committed evil through their bodies, spoken evil through their mouths, and conceived evil in their minds, being fully possessed of such evil conduct, slandering the noble ones, and adhering to false views.
For this reason, their bodies were shattered and their lives ended, leading them to suffering and a fall into hell.

Yet these noble and holy beings among the classes of sentient beings practiced virtue in body, spoke virtue in speech, and conceived virtue in mind; they were fully endowed with all manner of goodness, did not slander the sages and worthies, and faithfully adhered to right view.
By virtue of this practice, his body was shattered at the end of his life, and he proceeded toward peace and security, ascending to be born in the heavens.
He beheld the eight directions, above and below; his supernormal powers had reached such a state that they were likewise so throughout, and he beheld the ten directions without any obstruction.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the knowledge of the thoughts and mental activities of others, he knows them for one day, one hundred days, one year, one hundred years, one kalpa, one hundred kalpas, one thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, incalculable kalpas, and incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, up to the infinite.”

Regarding the immeasurable thoughts of all Buddhas in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—thoughts that are beyond measure and limit, and whose minds are free from obscuration or obstruction—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom of supernatural power that realizes through clear evidence the thoughts in the minds of others and their past dwellings; it is the practice of the wisdom of supernatural power.

The Buddha told Śāriputra: “A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows from whence his own body has come—whether it be one life, a hundred lives, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or incalculable hundreds of millions of lives; whether it be one kalpa, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or incalculable hundreds of millions of kalpas. He knows their good and evil, their misfortunes and blessings, the destinations of their good and evil deeds, their parents, brothers, kinsmen, wives, and children; their power, nobility, wealth, and pleasure; their poverty, lowliness, suffering, and hardship; their folly and wisdom, their failure and success; and their names and clans. This is the wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva who knows from whence his body has come, having been witnessed and certified by the divine spirits throughout his ancient wanderings and dwellings.”
Through the practice of supernormal wisdom, one naturally perceives the five paths; throughout the ten directions, there is no obstruction or hindrance.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the realization of supernormal powers through the wisdom that exhausts outflows, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor do they conceive of other divergent dharmas, nor do they conceive of:”
"Even when I attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path and became fully awakened,
I did not harbor thoughts of pride or negligence regarding the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows or the wisdom of supernormal powers."

If one were to establish the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and if one were to explain that the twelve links of dependent origination have no root and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment have no beginning, thereby teaching and transforming all beings.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom and the supernormal powers, having achieved such fullness, there is great benefit; he attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path and becomes a most perfectly awakened one.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom while abiding in the perfection of giving; they see that which can adorn and purify all paths as ultimately empty, and from that realization they give rise to and experience the practice of benevolent virtue."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom while abiding in the perfection of precepts; they fulfill and purify all the paths of the sages, reaching the ultimate emptiness wherein there is neither faith nor lack of faith, neither arising nor non-arising, establishing the meaning of the Dharma such that it is forever without birth."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be a bodhisattva who practices the *pāramitā* of wisdom while abiding in the *pāramitā* of patience. Fully perfecting and purifying all the paths of the sages, they realize ultimate emptiness; they give rise to forbearance, harbor no anger or resentment, and understand that there is no fundamental basis, for all things are entirely empty."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“There may be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and abides in the perfection of vigor; one who is fully endowed with the purification of all supernormal powers and has reached the ultimate of true emptiness; whose body and mind are diligent and focused single-mindedly on the One Meaning; whose practiced vigor is free from all outflows, having established this progress.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“There may be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and dwells in the perfection of single-mindedness, fully perfecting and purifying all the paths of the sages and reaching the ultimate of true emptiness; his mind is undisturbed, neither elevated nor depressed, neither arising nor ceasing, as he establishes this dhyāna.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and abide in the perfection of wisdom; they fully perfect and purify all the transcendent ways, realize ultimate emptiness, eliminate the mind of false views, inspire those lacking wisdom, and give rise to that which is without anything to bestow."

The Buddha told Śāriputra: "In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and dwells in the six perfections. He fully accomplishes and purifies all the paths of the sages, reaching the ultimate of true emptiness. As for those who come or do not come, there is neither coming nor going; he is without that which is received. He does not practice giving nor is he stingy; he does not observe precepts nor violate them; he does not practice patience nor harbor anger; he does not exert vigor nor is he indolent; he does not practice dhyāna nor is he distracted; he does not possess wisdom nor is he ignorant. Regarding that which is given, he has no thought of it and no conceptualization of it—whether it be generosity or stinginess, upholding precepts or violating prohibitions, patience or malice, vigor or indolence, single-mindedness or distraction, wisdom or folly."

One does not dwell upon abuse, nor does one dwell upon songs of praise; one does not even contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). There is no one who gives rise [to anger], no one who feels hatred, and no one who reviles; nor does one dwell upon the existence of speech, nor dwell upon existence, nor dwell upon non-existence.
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom is called ‘Renowned Virtue’; it is beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
Having fulfilled these virtues, they transform and guide sentient beings, purify the buddha-lands, practice great compassion, and attain the various paths of universal wisdom.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s perfection of wisdom always gives rise to an impartial mind toward all sentient beings.”
Once one is able to direct an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, one then attains equality with respect to all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Having attained equality with respect to all phenomena, one is then able to establish equality among all sentient beings. When all phenomena manifest in accordance with the proper time, one will be seen, loved, and respected by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as well as by the bodhisattvas, all śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, who will honor and revere one.

Furthermore, in whatever place they are born, their eyes never see anything improper; their ears do not hear evil sounds; their noses do not smell foul odors; their mouths do not encounter unpleasant tastes; their bodies do not experience coarse or harsh sensations; and their minds are free from unwholesome states.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) in this manner, they shall never lose the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to enlightenment.

When the Buddha had spoken this chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom, three hundred bhikṣus who were all practitioners of the path took necklaces and scattered them over the Buddha, and they resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
The Venerable Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"For what cause and condition do you smile?"
"There must be a reason for this smile.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These three hundred bhikṣus shall become buddhas after sixty-one kalpas; they shall be named Mahāyaśas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
Thereupon, when their lives come to an end, they shall be reborn in the land of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya.

Sixty thousand gods of the desire realm shall, during the era of Maitreya Buddha, leave the household life to become śramaṇas; following the holy intent of the Buddha, they shall behold a thousand Buddhas in that world, and as they act for the sake of sentient beings throughout the eight directions and above and below, each shall likewise behold a thousand Buddhas and their various lands.

Furthermore, they beheld this Sahā world as pure, adorned, and without flaw, just like the worlds of those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Thereupon, ten thousand people each made a vow:
"We shall each give rise to the intention for practice, desiring to be present in the Buddha-land of the present."
At that time, the Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the good man, smiled once more.
Ānanda knelt upright and asked the Buddha again:
"For what cause and condition do you smile?"
"There must be a specific intention behind this smile. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see these ten thousand people establishing their vows?"
He replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to him:

"When these ten thousand people pass away from this life, they shall be reborn in a Buddha-land where they will never be far removed from the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; thereafter, they shall attain Buddhahood, being named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Pure Adornment."
