4. Chapter on Praising Equality. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Four: Praising Equality. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and others—along with countless other bhikṣus who were noble, possessed of supernormal powers, and fully enlightened—as well as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upāsakas, and upāsikās, all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”
A practitioner who acts in this way possesses the great, boundless, and subtle *pāramitā* of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, which none can surpass;
the most transcendent *pāramitā*, which none can exceed;
the most venerable *pāramitā*, which maintains sovereign power and is called a *pāramitā* that none can equal.
The unsurpassed pāramitā, which none can surpass;
the immeasurable pāramitā, which none can surpass;
these peerless pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose deliverance is infinite.
The peerless *pāramitā* is the infinite crossing of emptiness.
Indeed, World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already crossed to the other shore by means of the emptiness of marks; they have crossed by means of the *pāramitā* of signlessness, which is the absence of thought; and they have crossed by means of the *pāramitā* of wishlessness, which is the absence of attachment.
All dharmas are empty, for they are all naturally non-existent.
Because the perfection of emptiness is naturally empty, it is the perfection of the fulfillment of all virtues that leads to the ultimate limit.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
All the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are beyond being opposed;
there is no practice of perfections—this is what is called the perfection of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to equalize that which is equal and unequal; when his giving is provisionally able to fulfill the equal-and-unequal *pāramitā*, he is then able to reach and return to equality, having attained the equal-and-unequal, until he reaches *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Just as a Bodhisattva practices the *dāna-pāramitā* as he ought to do, so too can he bring about the equal-and-unequal through the *śīla-pāramitā*, as well as the *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñā-pāramitās*.
O God among Gods!

It is not merely by possessing the Prajñāpāramitā that one can attain what is equal to the unequaled; rather, regarding the true Dharma—whether it be form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—and whether it be the turning of the wheel of Dharma, all are equal and without anything to which they could be compared.

The Buddhas of the past, the Gods among Gods, as well as all the Buddhas of the future and the present, have all practiced this Prajñāpāramitā and turned the wheel of Dharma that is equal to the unequaled.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to transcend all dharmas should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should pay homage to them; gods, humans, and asuras shall all prostrate themselves and pay homage to those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha then addressed these countless śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and mahāsattvas: “So it is, so it is!
O sons of good family!”
One should pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas;
all devas, humans, and asuras who practice the Prajñāpāramitā shall all come to take refuge in them.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva appears in the world to manifest among humanity, or if they appear in the heavens, manifesting as a gentleman, a noble clansman, a brahmin, or a householder; or if they appear as a universal monarch (cakravartin); or if they appear in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; or if they appear in the world as a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat; or if they appear in the world as a pratyekabuddha, a tathāgata, an arhat, or a samyaksaṃbuddha.”
The Buddha said, “For this reason, Śāriputra,

it is only because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas appear that they are able to obtain and provide for sentient beings food and drink, clothing, bedding and seats, dwellings, lamps and torches, bright moon pearls and jewels, crystal and lapis lazuli, jade, gold and silver, coral and amber, and carnelian and agate.”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“It is not for this reason that I have appeared in the world; rather, it is so that by upholding these words, I may rescue and protect the world, bringing it peace and security.”
The various musical performances gathered by the devas and humans are all brought forth and manifested by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Why is this? Because when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās and abide in these six pāramitās, they personally practice giving in order to exhort sentient beings to do so; their practice of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom is likewise the same, as they exhort the multitudes to cultivate the prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva brings peace to all classes of sentient beings.
Chapter Five: The Bestowal of Prophecy (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta) of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Thereupon, the World-Honored One extended his tongue from its root and covered the trichiliocosm.
From the root of his tongue, he emitted an infinite radiance of light that illuminated the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction.

At that moment, in as many Buddha-lands in the east as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, countless and incalculable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas beheld this light; each went from their own Buddha-land to personally inquire of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, regarding this matter:
"O Heaven among Heavens!..."
"What is this majestic spiritual power that causes the light to shine universally throughout this land?
At that time, the assembly of Tathāgatas in those lands each addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
"O sons of noble family!..."

If you wish to know of this transformation: to the west, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, there is a buddha-field named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has extended his tongue and emitted light that illuminates as many worlds of the World-Honored Ones as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in the eastern direction, causing it to shine universally throughout the ten directions.
The reason for this is that he is expounding the Prajñāpāramitā for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of that land each addressed their own Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, O Great Sage!”
"We wish to go and prostrate ourselves before the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and we also wish to hear and examine the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said to him:
"Go, son of good family!
Choose your own time; do as you wish."

Then the bodhisattvas, having requested and received permission from the Buddha, each took various canopies, banners, and streamers; incense, flowers, and decorative ornaments; blended perfumes and powdered incenses; and golden and silver flowers. They proceeded to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and each scattered the canopies, banners, streamers, incense, flowers, ornaments, blended perfumes, powdered incenses, golden flowers, and silver flowers that they had brought over the Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
From the eight directions, above, and below, there were also incalculable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, each of whom addressed the World-Honored One from within their own lands, saying:
"From where does this majestic radiance come?"
The Buddhas replied:

"There is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who emits from the root of his tongue a radiance of merit that illuminates each of the Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this is his majestic splendor."
Then each of those bodhisattvas addressed their respective buddhas,
saying, “We wish to go and pay homage to Śākyamuni and see the bodhisattvas there. The buddhas replied:
"Go, son of noble family!
Choose the time according to your benevolence and as you desire.
Then the assembly of bodhisattvas, each bringing offerings, went to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, prostrated themselves, and paid him homage.

They proceeded from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each bringing celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial powdered incense, celestial blended incense, blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses—all these being the subtle and exquisite fragrant flowers of the heavens—each holding them as they went to the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, the devas above and the various bodhisattvas each brought fragrant flowers, blended incenses, and powdered incenses, making offerings to and scattering them over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, the flowers and incense that were scattered rose into the void and transformed into palaces situated in the four directions; suspended in mid-air facing the four quarters, they were exquisitely clear and composed entirely of various jewels that bring joy to all people.
In that assembly of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, they all joined their palms in homage and took refuge in the Buddha, asking the World-Honored One:
"O Heaven among Heavens!

We pray that in future ages our bodies may likewise obtain the benefits of the Dharma as those of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; and that the assembly of our śrāvakas shall likewise be such that we may expound the sutras and the Dharma for all those gathered, just as you have now proclaimed."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the sons of good family, beheld that all dharmas are eternally without arising and without activity; seeing that no dharma whatsoever can be attained and perceiving the patience of their minds, the Buddha smiled at that moment.
The worthy Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Buddha smile?
A smile must have its purpose."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In this assembly today, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of people have all attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). After sixty-eight billion kalpas in the future, they shall become Buddhas, titled *Buddha*, *Tathāgata*, *Arhat*, *Samyaksaṃbuddha*, *Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*, *Sugata*, *Lokavid*, *Anuttara*, *Puruṣadamyasārathi*, *Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*, and *Bhagavān*. The kalpa shall be named Puṣpakārya, and the world shall be called Vyūhapuṣpa.”
Chapter Six: The Analysis of Emptiness (*Śūnyatā-vibhaṅga*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
"Are you not capable of generating the *prajñāpāramitā* as a condition for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, such that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may thereby come into being?"
Thereupon, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the śrāvakas, and the devas and humans each thought to themselves:
"Is Subhūti now, by means of his own eloquence, teaching the prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
"Is it by riding upon the holy intent of the Buddha that you speak?
Furthermore, Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great śrāvakas, and the devas and humans, said to the worthy Śāriputra:
"Whatever a disciple of the Buddha may say, its radiant discernment is entirely due to the majestic power of the Tathāgata."
"Whatever dharmas the Tathāgata has taught, all those dharmas are fundamentally without dispute.
Sons of good family, you should study these dharmas; those who study and realize these dharmas will all accord with the realm of realization of the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
The various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Prajñāpāramitā; it is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Because when the Dharma is preached, there is none who does not rejoice.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti, "This is what is called a bodhisattva.
Then Subhūti addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“O God among Gods! Regarding what is called a ‘bodhisattva,’ what is meant by a ‘bodhisattva’?
Within this Dharma, for what reason does the term ‘bodhisattva’ exist?”
I do not even perceive the dharma of a bodhisattva; what, then, is meant by "bodhisattva"?
O World-Honored One among Gods!
Since I never perceive the *prajñāpāramitā* nor the bodhisattva, how can I speak of the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
"By what principle should one expound the Prajñāpāramitā to instruct and guide the bodhisattvas?
The Buddha told the venerable Subhūti:

"That which is called 'Prajñāpāramitā' and 'bodhisattva' are merely provisional designations. Their names are nameless; those names do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they abide in between the two."
For example, Subhūti! A person who is seen is merely a provisional designation; that person has no name.
That dharma neither arises nor ceases; it is a name given according to worldly convention through the coming together of causes and conditions.
However, the sounds and words concerning self, person, or life-span;

the classes of sentient beings—whether crawling, breathing, flying, or wriggling; their deeds, their creations, their endeavors and encouragements, their views, their observations, and their knowledge—all these are merely provisional designations. All are neither arising nor ceasing;
and the same applies to all that can be spoken or taught by gods and humans.
Thus it is, Subhūti! The designation "Prajñāpāramitā" and the name "Bodhisattva" are all merely provisional names; they are neither arising nor ceasing.
Even the names spoken by the Tathāgata, the God among Gods, are likewise equal and without distinction.
For example, Subhūti! All that constitutes my form within is also a dharma that is merely a provisional name; it is a designation established through conventional reliance.
These provisional designations are dharmas that neither arise nor cease; one who wishes to understand this convergence of causes and conditions perceives it only as vocal sound.

The dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also provisional designations; the names given to these dharmas neither arise nor cease, yet they appear through the provisional reliance upon causes and conditions, manifesting as vocal sound.

Thus it is, Subhūti! Regarding what is called the *prajñāpāramitā*, the term "bodhisattva" and the name "bodhisattva" are merely designations; as for the phenomena upon which they depend, those dharmas neither arise nor cease.

That which is called the Bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā and the name "Bodhisattva" are both entirely without external dependence; they exist as words through the reliance upon causes, conditions, and designations.

The eye is, in fact, elusive, empty, and tranquil; even down to provisional names, phenomena are merely entrusted to characters, and these too neither arise nor cease—they exist as vocal sounds through the reliance upon causes, conditions, and provisional designations.
That which is called the emptiness of the eye: that eye has no interior, no exterior, and does not abide between the two;

the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so. Phenomena (*dharma*) are mere designations; these phenomena neither arise nor cease; they exist as vocal sounds through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
As for that which is called "mind," Subhūti, the mind is neither within nor without, nor does it abide in between the two.
As for that which is called "form," Subhūti, it is merely a provisional designation for dharmas; it neither arises nor ceases, nor is it internal, external, or abiding in between the two.

The eye-element is also a mere designation, a name lent by way of dharmas; likewise for what are called the eye-element, form-element, and eye-consciousness-element; the ear-element, sound-element, and ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, odor-element, and nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, taste-element, and tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, tangibility-element, and body-consciousness-element; and the mind-element, dharma-element, and mind-consciousness-element. These dharmas exist as borrowed designations through speech and sound, yet these dharmas have no interior, no exterior, and do not abide in between the two.

Thus it is, Subhūti! That which is called "bodhisattva" and "prajñāpāramitā" are merely provisional designations based on dharmas; these designations neither arise nor cease, yet they exist as names through reliance [upon conditions] and are expressed as sounds.
The Prajñāpāramitā and the designation "Bodhisattva"—their names have no interior and no exterior, nor do they abide between the two.
For example, Subhūti, that which is called the "interior" is my own body; because of the designation "head," its name is merely a sound, and it is further named the "neck."
The five aggregates, the two arms, the back, the navel, the flanks, the two kneecaps, and the two feet are merely provisional designations.

Relying on the sound of the head, one speaks by means of the designation "conditioned phenomena. When one examines these phenomena, they neither arise nor cease. One should understand that all these existing things are established as mere provisional designations and verbal sounds; when one examines their names, they neither arise nor cease, having no interior, no exterior, and no dwelling in between.

Thus it is, Subhūti! Both "prajñāpāramitā" and the name "bodhisattva" are all mere designations. These dharmas neither arise nor cease; they exist entirely as provisional constructs, manifesting only as sounds and words. Their names likewise neither arise nor cease; they have no interior, no exterior, and do not abide in between the two.

For example, Subhūti! Beyond this, there are grasses, trees, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; all these are considered to exist only as provisional designations with verbal expressions. These names are nameless; these names neither arise nor cease. They are provisionally established as names with verbal expressions, yet when one examines these names, they are neither internal nor external, nor do they abide between the two.

Thus it is, Subhūti! Both the Prajñāpāramitā and the name "Bodhisattva" are all merely provisional designations based on dharmas; these dharmas neither arise nor cease, and their names have no interior or exterior, nor do they abide in between the two.
For example, Subhūti! All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past were merely given provisional names; those of the future and the present are likewise so.
Subhūti, it is like an echo, or like a reflection in a mirror, a magical illusion, a transformation, or a mirage.

Thus the Tathāgata explains that all dharmas are like transformations; they exist only as provisional designations. These designations neither arise nor cease; they exist as verbal expressions based upon names. Those names have no interior and no exterior, nor do they abide in between the two.

Thus it is, Subhūti! What are called "bodhisattva" and "prajñāpāramitā" are merely provisional designations. These designations neither arise nor cease; they have no interior and no exterior, nor do they abide in between the two.

Thus it is, Subhūti! What are called "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" and "prajñāpāramitā" are merely provisional designations arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions; what are designated as "skillful means" and what are designated as "Dharma" are all but false attributions.
One should train in this manner in the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*: not abiding in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and having no perception thereof;
not abiding in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*); not abiding in names;
not beholding name-and-form as permanent, not seeing name-and-form as blissful, and not seeing name-and-form as suffering. One does not see name-and-form.

There is that which has an internal aspect, yet one does not perceive name-and-form; there is that which has an external aspect, yet one does not perceive name-and-form; there is emptiness, yet one does not perceive name-and-form;
there is the transformation of signlessness, yet one does not perceive name-and-form; there is the state of wishlessness, yet one does not perceive name-and-form;
there is profound stillness, yet one does not perceive name-and-form; there is the state of vagueness, yet one does not perceive it. One does not perceive [it].

While name-and-form exists, there are sensual defilements; yet one does not see name-and-form as something that gives rise to disputes, nor does one see name-and-form as something that arises, nor does one see name-and-form as something that ceases.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element; the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, the odor-element, and the nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, the taste-element, and the tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, the tangible-object-element, and the body-consciousness-element; the mind-element, the mental-object-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—all are likewise thus: they are compounded by causes and conditions and exist as mere provisional designations; such are the five aggregates.

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and the bodhisattva path, they regard both the practice and its designation as neither existent nor non-existent; they do not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor do they abide in the realm of the unconditioned, and they perceive nothing at all.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they have no conceptualizations regarding any phenomena; there is neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate. Furthermore, they do not conceptualize that they are practicing the perfection of wisdom, but dwell in the state of non-conceptualization while practicing the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

When practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom," nor does one perceive the designation "bodhisattva. Furthermore, one does not perceive the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisamvidah*), or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the name "perfection of wisdom," nor does one perceive the bodhisattva, nor does one perceive the name "bodhisattva."
Who can see the bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly understands and discerns the root of all dharmas and the characteristics of all dharmas, regarding the root of all dharmas and the characteristics of all dharmas, they are neither attached nor contentious.
Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not rely on names nor create designations for dharmas.
Regarding the path of the Buddha as well, they do not take recourse in names as mere false attributions, but fully comprehend them all.
He does not rely on form, nor does he rely on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not rely on the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he rely on eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, or tongue-consciousness.

He does not rely on the consciousness of bodily contact with subtle textures, nor does he rely on the consciousness of mental objects; he does not rely on the phenomena of the five aggregates conditioned by the eye, remaining without reliance.

He does not give rise to sensation—neither suffering, nor pleasure, nor that which is neither suffering nor pleasure—and even regarding the causes and conditions conditioned by the consciousness of the mind, wherein there arise sensations of suffering, pleasure, or that which is neither suffering nor pleasure, he has no reliance whatsoever upon them.

They do not rely upon or cling to the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), nor do they rely upon or cling to the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*). They do not rely upon or cling to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), nor the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), nor the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), nor the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), nor the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), nor the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). They do not rely upon or cling to marks (*nimitta*), nor do they rely upon or cling to the body of a bodhisattva.

They do not rely upon or cling to the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), nor the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*), or the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
They do not rely upon or cling to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), nor do they rely upon or cling to the perfection of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) by which the mind is liberated.
Nor does he rely upon or cling to the internal or the external, nor does he rely upon or cling to that which lies between the two;

nor does he rely upon or cling to internal emptiness, nor does he rely upon or cling to external emptiness, nor does he rely upon or cling to formless conditions, nor does he rely upon or cling to natural emptiness, nor does he rely upon or cling to the transformation and edification of sentient beings, nor does he rely upon or cling to the adornment and purity of Buddha-fields, nor does he rely upon or cling to *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely non-existent.
That which one might become attached to is itself without attachment, and there is nothing whatsoever that can be grasped.
Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is without attachment to any phenomena, they practice the perfection of wisdom;

the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are thereby increased and strengthened, and they enter into tranquility to attain the bodhisattva path.
They enter into the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and become fully endowed with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
being thus endowed with supernormal powers, they travel through the Buddha-fields to teach and transform sentient beings;
having transformed sentient beings, they then make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and are able to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields.
Having already been able to adorn and purify the buddha-fields, they are beheld by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

At that time, the bodhisattvas likewise see from afar the Buddhas, the Great Sages; desiring to attain the roots of merit and goodness, they should then make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, prostrating and taking refuge in them. Thus they shall attain spontaneous and immeasurable virtue, drawing near to the Buddhas and obtaining the opportunity to hear the sūtras they preach. Having attained the hearing of the Dharma without interruption, they shall reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unexcelled perfect enlightenment, as well as all the gates of *dhāraṇī* and all the gates of *samādhi*.

Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the practice of the perfection of wisdom, they analytically understand that all dharmas are merely provisional designations based on causes and conditions.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is form the bodhisattva?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:
"No, O God among Gods! How so, Subhūti? Is the eye the Bodhisattva?"
"Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the Bodhisattva? He replied, "No, O God among Gods!"
“Are form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena the bodhisattva? He replied, “No, O God among Gods!”
He asked again:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the eye, form, and visual consciousness the bodhisattva?
Are the ear and sound, nose and odor, tongue and taste, body and tangibles, and mind and mental phenomena the bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is the earth element the bodhisattva?”
He replied: “No, O God among Gods!
Are the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element the bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! Subhūti, what do you think? Is ignorance the Bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! Are consciousness, name-and-form,
the six sense bases, contact, craving, sensation, feeling, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, and suffering the Bodhisattva?”
He replied: "No, O God among Gods! Subhūti, what do you think:
could there be some distinct form that constitutes a bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No,
O God among Gods! Could there be any other sensation,
perception, mental formations, or consciousness that constitutes a bodhisattva?”
He replied: "No, O God among Gods!
Could there be any other eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind that constitutes a bodhisattva?"
He replied: "No, O God among Gods!
Could there be any other form, sound, odor, taste, tactile sensation, or mental phenomenon that constitutes a bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods!

Could there be a bodhisattva who is distinct from eye-form-consciousness, ear-sound-consciousness, nose-odor-consciousness, tongue-taste-consciousness, body-tangible-object-consciousness, and mind-dharma-consciousness?”
He replied, “No,
O God among Gods! Could there be anything other than the twelve links of dependent origination— from ignorance through to sickness, old age, and death— that constitutes a bodhisattva?”
He replied: "No, O God among Gods!
Subhūti, what do you think: is form, being without a fundamental basis, the bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! Are the five aggregates,
the six sense-fields, the eighteen elements, the four great elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination, being without a fundamental basis, the bodhisattva?”
He replied: “No, O God among Gods! Subhūti, what do you think:
could there be one who is a bodhisattva without having the fundamental [nature]?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What meaning did you understand, Subhūti, and by what observation did you answer?
The Buddha said:
“Form is not the bodhisattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the bodhisattva.”

The six sense-bases, the eighteen elements, the four great elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination—from ignorance through birth, old age, sickness, and death—are not the Bodhisattva. That which is without origin is not the Bodhisattva; likewise, that which is other than what is without origin is also not the Bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, O God among Gods!
Since the self, the person, and the life-span are likewise unapprehendable, how can one be designated as a 'bodhisattva'?"

What is meant by regarding the afflictions of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the beginning and end of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the bodhisattva?
What is meant by regarding form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as distinct from the bodhisattva?
What is meant by designating one who is distinct from the six sense-fields, the eighteen elements, the four great elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination as a bodhisattva?
What is meant by designating that which is without fundamental basis as a bodhisattva?
"How can that which is called 'difference' be without a basis for it to be a bodhisattva?
It has no location.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the *prajñāpāramitā* should contemplate that sentient beings, persons, and things are non-existent and unobtainable; likewise, the *prajñāpāramitā* itself is non-existent and unobtainable. It is in this manner that a bodhisattva should train.”
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is one who speaks of form with their mouth a bodhisattva?
He replied, "No, O God among Gods!"
“Is one who speaks of sensation, perception, mental formations, volitional formations, and consciousness a bodhisattva?
He replied: “No, O God among Gods!”
“Is one who reckons form as permanent, and reckons feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as permanent, a bodhisattva?
He replied: “No, O God among Gods!”
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is one who conceives of form as impermanent, and who conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent, a bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! Subhūti, what do you think?
Would one who speaks with their mouth of the pleasure of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be a bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is one who speaks with their mouth that ‘form is suffering, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering’ a bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Would one who says with their mouth, ‘Form is mine; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are mine,’ be a bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is one a bodhisattva by saying with one’s mouth: ‘Form is not mine; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not mine’?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is one who verbally says that form is empty, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, a bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is one who speaks with their mouth that ‘form is without perception, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without perception’ a bodhisattva?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is one a bodhisattva by verbally declaring that form is wishless, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wishless?”
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked: “What do you think, Subhūti?

Would one who says with their mouth that form is not empty, not without perception, and not without resolve; and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not empty, not without perception, and not without resolve—would such a person be a bodhisattva?”
He replied, "No, O Heaven among Heavens! Subhūti, what do you think?
Are the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, the eighteen elements, the four great elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination, being non-existent, the bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"By what principle do you observe that you instead say that the five aggregates, the six sense-fields, the eighteen elements, the four great elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the afflictions of beginning and end, suffering and pleasure, good and evil, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, existence and non-existence—all these are not the Bodhisattva?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
Since form (rūpa) is ultimately unattainable even when sought, how much less can one who merely speaks the word ‘form’ be considered a bodhisattva!”

It is the same for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: even when sought to the ultimate extent, permanence cannot be found; how much less could impermanence be found as something that should constitute a bodhisattva!
Since suffering and pleasure are ultimately unattainable, how much less can one claim by word of mouth that "suffering and pleasure" constitute a bodhisattva!
Since that which belongs to a self is ultimately unattainable upon thorough investigation, how much less can one claim by word of mouth that "self" or "non-self" constitutes a bodhisattva!
It is the same for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Since form, in its ultimate nature, cannot be apprehended, how much less can one claim that "form is empty" by means of speech to be a bodhisattva!
It is the same for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Ultimately, even perception cannot be found; how much less can one claim by word of mouth that "form is without perception" constitutes a bodhisattva!
It is the same for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Since one ultimately cannot find anything to be sought or wished for, how much less can one claim with words that "form is wishless" as being the bodhisattva!
"It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to study the prajñāpāramitā should study it in this way:

when one realizes that the form spoken of by the mouth is ungraspable, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, signless, wishless, and ungraspable, then one is studying the prajñāpāramitā.
Regarding what Subhūti said just now—that within the Dharma he has never perceived anyone who is a bodhisattva—Subhūti!
You should know that a dharma cannot see a dharma; a dharma cannot see the dharmadhātu; and the dharmadhātu does not see a dharma.

It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): the realm of form does not see the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), nor does the dharma-realm see the realm of form; the eye-faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) does not see the dharma-realm, nor does the dharma-realm see the eye-faculty.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

The mind-element does not see the dharma-element, and the dharma-element does not see the mind-element. The eighteen elements do not see the dharma-element, and the dharma-element does not see the eighteen elements. The conditioned element does not see the unconditioned element, and the unconditioned element does not see the conditioned element; furthermore, the conditioned element cannot be dualized.
The unconditioned realm cannot be named; the unconditioned is not dualistic, and the conditioned likewise cannot be named. Thus it is, Subhūti!
One who practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner perceives nothing whatsoever among all phenomena.
Having perceived nothing, they are neither terrified nor afraid, neither distressed nor fearful; their mind is neither cowed nor resentful.

Why is this so? Subhūti, because one does not perceive form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not perceive the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; one does not perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; one does not perceive desire for form, nor even desire for dharmas—of these, nothing is perceived.

One does not perceive greed, anger, or delusion; one does not perceive ignorance, nor does one perceive anything from volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, up to old age, sickness, death, and so forth—there is nothing to be seen.
He does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a person or a life-span.

He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm. He does not perceive śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; he does not perceive the dharmas of bodhisattvas, nor does he perceive a Buddha, nor does he perceive the Dharma, nor does he perceive the assembly of bodhisattvas.
"Having no longer perceived any phenomena, one is neither terrified nor afraid, neither distressed nor fearful,
and the mind is not timid. Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying, "So it is, World-Honored One!"
"For what reason, Subhūti, does the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become timid or weak, and remain without attachment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the dharmas that are objects of mental attention, nor does he perceive anything; for this reason, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become timid or weak, and remains without attachment."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become terrified?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva does not harbor fear in the mind, nor does he have any [dualistic] perception; for this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is without terror.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva have no attainment regarding all dharmas?”
"Does one practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Regarding all that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices as the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend that perfection of wisdom, nor do they apprehend the mind of a bodhisattva."
"This is what constitutes the present instruction for a bodhisattva.
*The Sūtra of Radiant Praise*, Fascicle Two.
*The Sūtra of Radiant Praise*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: On the Realization of Emptiness. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Seven:
On the Realization of Emptiness, Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā should study the prajñā-pāramitā.
One who wishes to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā should study the prajñā-pāramitā.”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to eliminate form, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if they wish to eliminate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who wish to eliminate the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
those who wish to eliminate forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena should study the Prajñāpāramitā;

those who wish to eliminate eye-form-consciousness, ear-sound-consciousness, nose-odor-consciousness, tongue-taste-consciousness, body-tangible-consciousness, and mind-phenomena-consciousness should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to eliminate the contact of the eye, the contact of the ear, the contact of the nose, tongue, body, and mind, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to eliminate the habitual tendencies of the conditions of contact—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to eliminate the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate doubt and transgressions of the precepts should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to eliminate desire and all attachments to the realm of form and the formless realm should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate the attachments arising from the bonds of the meeting of causes and conditions and the locations where [retribution] is received, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to eliminate the four fruits—the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat—should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate the four sorrows, the four attachments, the four evil sensations, and the four perversions should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

One who wishes to eliminate the five hindrances, the six sense bases, the seven consciousnesses, the eight wrong paths, the nine afflictions, and the karma of the ten non-virtuous actions—whether of merit or demerit—should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to transcend the ten wholesome paths of action, the four dhyānas, the four truths, and the five supernormal powers; and wishes to transcend the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate [the conceptualization of] the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, all the foundations of mindfulness, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to and enter the meditative absorption of the *bodhyanga-samādhi* should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

One who wishes to discern the *ākāśa-jñāna-samādhi*, the *vijñāna-jñāna-samādhi*, the *ākiṃcanya-jñāna-samādhi*, the *saṃjñā-asaṃjñā-jñāna-samādhi*, and the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish the Lion’s Play Samādhi and the Lion’s Roar Samādhi, and wishes to attain the gateways of dhāraṇī, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who wish to attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Ratnasāgara Samādhi, and the Prajñāmudrā Samādhi of right concentration should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain the Candraprabha Samādhi, the Candradhvaja-koṭi Samādhi, and the Sarvadharmapraveśa Samādhi of right concentration should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Seal of Illumination, the Samādhi that Gives Birth to All Dharmas, and the Right Concentration of the Samādhi of Emerging from the Banner of Offerings and the Evil, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the vajra-like samādhi, the samādhi of entering all dharma-gates, the samādhi of the king of concentrated minds, and the meditative absorption of the imperial seal, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the samādhi of pure power, the samādhi of transcending all equalities, the samādhi of entering into the destination of the arising of all dharmas, and the samādhi of entering the verbal sounds of all dharmas, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain the Samādhi of Contemplating the Ten Directions, wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Seal of the Dhāraṇī-Door of All Dharmas, and the Samādhi of the Seal of Equality of All Dharmas (the *Dan* manuscript calls it the "Seal of Governing Creation"), and wishes to abide in the Samādhi of Right Reception in the Sphere of Emptiness, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who wish to attain the Samādhi of Adorned Purity, the Samādhi of the Bodhimaṇḍa, and the Samādhi of Transcendent Supernatural Powers and Right Attainment should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the Samādhi of Transcendence and the Samādhi of the Banner of Equality and Protection, and wishes to reach the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of these samādhis as well as the gates of other samādhis, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, O God among Gods, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cause all classes of sentient beings to fulfill their aspirations should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, O God among Gods!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the perfection of the roots of merit, so that by virtue of those perfected roots of goodness he does not fall into the evil destinies, does not encounter lowly births, does not descend to the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and does not dispute over the supreme dharmas of bodhisattvas, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
The venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not dispute regarding the supreme Dharma? Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not possess *upāyakauśalya*, nor gives rise to the *upāyakauśalya* that is non-arising, yet practices the six *pāramitās* while understanding the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the non-arising [of phenomena], and enters the gates of samādhi without falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, yet does not deliver others—this cessation of concentration of the bodhisattva is called the 'non-purified birth' of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "What is meant by a bodhisattva being 'unrefined'? Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Therefore it is said that those who are not pure and virtuous are those who are attached to dharmas.
It is further said: "Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the emptiness of form yet perceive that perception and consciousness have something upon which they rely; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Abiding in emptiness, they perceive that perception and consciousness have something upon which they rely; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attachment to the "patience in accordance with the Dharma," which gives rise to a lack of purity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva establishes form within the signless (*animitta*), yet knows that perception and consciousness have something upon which they rely;
he establishes form within the wishless (*apraṇihita*), yet knows that perception and consciousness have something upon which they rely.
This is the attachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva to the patience that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).
It is the same for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

To establish [the view] that there is nothing at all, yet to perceive that consciousness has something upon which it relies—namely, eye-form-consciousness, ear-sound-consciousness, nose-odor-consciousness, tongue-taste-consciousness, body-tangible-consciousness, and mind-phenomena-consciousness—and to perceive that consciousness has something upon which it relies: this is the attachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva to the patience that accords with the Dharma.

Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. Form is suffering; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering. Form is non-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self. Yet, by establishing oneself upon these, one gives rise to conceptual attachments that have something to rely upon.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s attachment to the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*), whereby birth and death are not yet purified.

One should sever this form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; since this form is not [inherently] form, one thereby eliminates form, and it is the same for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is what is meant by cessation, and one should establish the realization thereof.

This is not the realization attained through the extinction [of defilements]; one should cultivate this path. This constitutes the precepts for the cessation of stained dust and contention; one should practice this and not practice that. This is what a bodhisattva ought to practice, and this is what a bodhisattva ought not to practice; this is the bodhisattva path.

This is how a bodhisattva studies the precepts: they should not study by thinking, "This is a bodhisattva’s dāna-pāramitā," "This is a bodhisattva’s śīla-pāramitā," "This is a bodhisattva’s kṣānti-pāramitā," "This is a bodhisattva’s vīrya-pāramitā," "This is a bodhisattva’s dhyāna-pāramitā," "This is a bodhisattva’s prajñā-pāramitā," "This is a bodhisattva’s upāya-kauśalya," "This is a bodhisattva’s lack of upāya-kauśalya," "This is a bodhisattva’s entry into tranquility," or "This is a bodhisattva’s failure to produce purity."
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

“To speak of a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* while dwelling in and establishing such dharmas, yet perceiving that perception and consciousness have something upon which they rely—this is called the attachment to the 'patience in accordance with the Dharma' (*anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it gives rise to a lack of purity.”
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "What is meant by the bodhisattva mahāsattva being tranquil?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:

"In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive internal emptiness, they do not perceive external emptiness, they do not perceive internal-and-external emptiness,
they do not perceive the emptiness of the emptiness of internal-and-external emptiness, they do not perceive the non-existence of the emptiness of internal-and-external emptiness,
they do not perceive internal-and-external emptiness, they do not perceive the emptiness of the great emptiness, [they do not perceive] the emptiness of the great emptiness..."
One does not perceive emptiness; one does not perceive the great emptiness within ultimate true emptiness; one does not perceive ultimate true emptiness within the great emptiness;
one does not perceive ultimate true emptiness within conditioned emptiness; one does not perceive ultimate true emptiness within conditioned emptiness;
one does not perceive unconditioned emptiness within conditioned emptiness; one does not perceive conditioned emptiness within unconditioned emptiness; [one does not perceive] unconditioned...
The emptiness of the beginningless and endless does not perceive the emptiness of the unconditioned;
the emptiness of the beginningless and endless does not perceive the emptiness of non-discrimination; the emptiness of non-discrimination does not perceive the emptiness of the vast wilderness;
the emptiness of non-discrimination does not perceive the emptiness of original purity; the emptiness of purity does not perceive the emptiness of non-discrimination.
The emptiness of distinction does not perceive the emptiness of natural thought; the emptiness of natural thought does not perceive the emptiness of original purity;
the emptiness of natural marks does not perceive the emptiness of all dharmas; the emptiness of all dharmas does not perceive the emptiness of natural marks;
the emptiness of all dharmas does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence. Non-...
The emptiness of all things does not perceive the emptiness of all dharmas; the emptiness of non-existence does not perceive the emptiness of nature;
the emptiness of nature does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence; the emptiness of the emptiness of nature does not perceive the emptiness of the emptiness of non-existence;
and the emptiness of the emptiness of non-existence does not perceive the emptiness of the emptiness of nature.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is able to act in this way, that bodhisattva reaches the state of profound stillness.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā should train in this way and act accordingly: they should not dwell upon form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise—within consciousness, they should not dwell upon consciousness;
they should not dwell upon the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
One should not dwell upon thoughts of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
one should not dwell upon thoughts of the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, or prajñā-pāramitā.

Furthermore, one should not rely upon or become attached to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four immeasurable minds, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not form a conceptual attachment to being a "bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, they should maintain a mind of equality and non-equality, and enter into a subtle and wondrous state of mind.
Why is this? Because that mind is no-mind; the mind is fundamentally pure.
That which is fundamentally pure is spontaneously joyful, lucid, and clean.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti,
"In what way is the mind clear, bright, and pure?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:

“Suppose, Śāriputra, that the mind neither joins with nor separates from desire; neither joins with nor separates from anger; neither joins with nor separates from delusion; it does not abide in causes and conditions, being without fetters or bonds; it neither revolves nor fails to revolve; it neither joins with nor separates from any doubts or the sixty-two views; and it neither joins with nor separates from the mental activities of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this, Śāriputra, is [the bodhisattva’s practice].”
“The mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fundamentally pure, luminous, and purified.
The venerable Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Does such a mind exist?”
"His mind is no-mind.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "What do you think, Śāriputra?"
Is there a mind? How could such a mind exist, and how can one know whether there is a mind or no mind?
Is it possible to apprehend it?
"Is it possible to obtain?
He replied, "No, O virtuous one!"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if that mind cannot be known as either existent or non-existent, and it can neither be apprehended nor acquired;
yet, because there are causes and conditions, there is this expression: 'this mind exists,' or 'there is a mind,' or 'there is no mind.'"
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "How is this, Subhūti?
Is this a state of no-mind?"
He replied, "To have nothing created and nothing conceptualized— this is called all dharmas being without mind and without thought.
Śāriputra then said to Subhūti:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is it that one who has generated the mind [of awakening] has nothing created and nothing conceptualized?
If form is created yet there is no conceptualization, then feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so."
If there is nothing created and nothing conceptualized, then from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to those of bodhisattvas, all are without mind and without thought.
He replied: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
Such a mind does nothing and has no thoughts; therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise, doing nothing and having no thoughts."
Śāriputra praised the venerable Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”

Truly, as you are a son of the World-Honored One, born from the Dharma-gate and always acting in accordance with the Dharma, you have been transformed by the Dharma; you do not seek honor or profit because of the Dharma, but naturally, through causes and conditions, have ascended to the Dharma-body. Thus, you are foremost among those who practice emptiness.
The World-Honored One praised the benevolent one, saying, "Your realization of emptiness is supreme; it is difficult to equal, truly difficult to equal. It is thus, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the prajñāpāramitā should accord with this."
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be regarded as one who is irreversible (avaivartika).
Those who wish to study the stage of a śrāvaka should study the Prajñāpāramitā; they should hear it, receive it, uphold it, recite it, and constantly contemplate it.
Those who wish to study the stage of a pratyekabuddha should study the Prajñāpāramitā; they should constantly hear it, receive and uphold it, recite it, and always keep it in mind.
Those who wish to study the Bodhisattva stages should study the Prajñāpāramitā; they should hear it, receive and uphold it, recite it, and constantly contemplate it. Why is this so?

This Prajñāpāramitā is vast and universal, fully endowed with that which leads to the three vehicles—namely, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. Bodhisattvas study it all, attaining complete understanding without any obstruction.
Chapter 8: On Designations. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Eight: On Designations. Thereupon, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”
Regarding what the Noble One has said concerning a bodhisattva mahāsattva, I neither see nor can I find such a practitioner.
Since I neither see nor find a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how can I speak of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom?
How does one instruct a practitioner?
If I were to say that all dharmas can be attained, I would be creating a designation for the name "Bodhisattva";
if one were to do so, they would fall into doubt.
Furthermore, when one examines its name, it is neither anything at all nor does it abide anywhere. Why is this?
Because this name arises from ignorance; such being the nature of the name, it has no location and no abode.
Furthermore, there is no location and no abiding where form can be apprehended as "mine"; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended as "mine."
Why is this? Because they are merely provisional names.
For this reason, their causal conditions and their designated appellations neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because these names arise from the mind of ignorance; that which is so named neither abides nor does it not abide.
Indeed, World-Honored One!
I observe the eye and can never find what is called "mine"; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Upon examining the mind as well, I cannot find what is called "mine. Since I observe the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind and can never find their root or origin—anything that could be called "mine"—by virtue of what basis could one establish the name "Bodhisattva"?
Furthermore, observe that the eye is empty, non-existent, and elusive; its name neither abides nor does it not abide.

Why is this so? Because it is established as a provisional designation arising from ignorance. When one examines such a name, even that which is provisionally designated neither abides nor does it not abide.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
When I seek the beginning, end, and locus of form as being 'mine,' I am utterly unable to find them;
the same applies to the six sense-faculties. When I seek their names and titles, their origins and ends, or claim they arise from a locus that is 'mine,' I never find them."
It is the same for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; if one seeks their origin and end to find what is called "mine," it can never be found.

Likewise, regarding eye-and-form-consciousness, ear-and-sound-consciousness, nose-and-odor-consciousness, tongue-and-flavor-consciousness, body-and-tactile-consciousness, and mind-and-dharma-consciousness, if one examines their origin and end to find what is called "mine," it is entirely unfindable.

Suppose one examines the eye and its objects from beginning to end and finds that "this is mine" cannot be apprehended; the same applies to the six sense faculties and their objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—making eighteen categories in total.
Furthermore, for what reason is the designation "Bodhisattva" established?

Regarding the eighteen categories—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are reckoned to have no name; they neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this so? Because it is due to ignorance that names and forms exist. Furthermore, when one examines these names and forms, they neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide; the same is true for the contact experienced by the eye, and the contact experienced by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

From the eye conditioned by contact up to the mental formations—namely, form, sensation, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—one experiences suffering through the conditioning of these contacts. When one examines their beginning and end, the notion of "mine" can never be found.

Regarding the six sense bases—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena—as well as form, sensation, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, along with the eighteen elements: when one examines their beginning and end, the notion of "this is mine" can never be found. Furthermore, they possess no names; even those provisional designations neither abide nor do not abide.
Arising from ignorance, this is brought forth; yet that which is "mine" is entirely unattainable.

Examining the beginning and end of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, sickness, death, and suffering—none of these can be called "mine. They neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, and suffering. When one contemplates their beginning and end, this "mine" that has ceased cannot be found at all.
Lust, jealousy, anger, and delusion—when examining their origin and their end, the notion of "mine" is entirely unfindable; it arises and is established merely because of names.
When one calculates these names, they neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.

When form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the eighteen elements—form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena—have all been extinguished and eliminated, one examines their origin and end and finds that the notion of "mine" can never be apprehended.
It arises from names and designations; yet these names and designations neither abide nor do they not abide.

Regarding the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*, if one examines their beginning and end, the notion that "this is mine" can never be found; it arises solely from names and designations.

Furthermore, when we examine ourselves and investigate their beginning and end, we say, "This is mine. This arises from following designations; yet that which is a mere designation is entirely unobtainable—it neither abides nor does it not abide.

It is the same for the person, the life-span, and all that is created, observed, or perceived: when one examines their beginning and end and says, "This is mine," it can never be found. These arise and are brought forth by following designations; moreover, those designations themselves neither abide nor do they not abide.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path—when one examines their origin and end, saying "this is mine," they can never be found. It is through these designations that [the notion of self] arises; yet these provisional names neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one examines their beginning and end and finds that what is called "mine" is entirely unobtainable; it arises from names and designations, yet these provisional names neither abide nor do they not abide.

Regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the meditative attainments of the four formless samādhis, if one examines their beginning and end to find that which can be called "mine," nothing at all can be found. These arise solely from names and designations; furthermore, these provisional designations neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.

One contemplates the Buddha, the Dharma, the Noble Sangha, consciousness, giving, and extensive learning; one contemplates the guarding of the mind regarding inhalation and exhalation, and one contemplates old age, sickness, and death. One examines their root and their end, finding that nothing which can be called "mine" can be obtained, nor can it be seen. It arises from names and designations, yet these provisional names neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Regarding the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—if one examines their origin and end, that which is called "mine" is entirely unfindable; they arise from following mere designations, and yet these provisional names neither abide nor do they not abide.

Not perceiving beginning or end, there is no location and it cannot be apprehended; how then can one establish a name for a bodhisattva and speak of them as a "bodhisattva"? Although there is such a name, it neither abides nor does it not abide;

it arises from ignorance and thus results in a name. Furthermore, that name neither abides nor does it not abide. Calculating that the name results in the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), one examines its beginning and end and finds it cannot be apprehended; it arises from the name and thus comes into being, yet that name also neither abides nor does it not abide.

Examine form, sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these eighteen constituents and the twelve links of dependent origination are like an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, the moon in water, a phantom, and a transformation. Examine the five aggregates and the five clinging aggregates in this same way: when one investigates their origin and end, even the notion that "this is mine" cannot be found at all. They arise from names and designations, yet these names and designations themselves neither abide nor do they not abide; they are empty, void, and insubstantial.

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, signless, and wishless. When one examines their beginning and end, claiming them to be "mine," they are entirely unattainable; they arise only from their designations. Yet even those designations neither abide nor do they not abide. They are like an echo, a reflection, a mirage, a plantain tree, the moon in water, an illusion, or a magical transformation. When one examines their beginning and end, they are entirely unattainable—neither arising nor ceasing. Like a reflection in water, they are without defilement and without resentment.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these eighteen constituents; the twelve links of dependent origination; the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), the destination of all phenomena, and the quiescent dharma; the names of all dharmas such as good and evil, calamity and fortune; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; that which has an object and that which is non-existent; the outflowing and the non-outflowing—when one examines their beginning and end, the source from which these phenomena arise cannot be apprehended at all. They neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide, being like shadows, echoes, the moon in water, a mirage, a plantain tree, an illusion, and a magical transformation.

Regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present, when one examines their beginning and end, they cannot be apprehended; they neither abide nor do they not abide. Since the origin of the phenomena of the past, future, and present cannot be perceived, what is meant by "phenomena that are non-existent"?
That which is called the "dharma of non-existence" has no past, future, or present; seeking this unconditioned dharma, one examines its beginning and end, yet it is entirely invisible.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

When I examine the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and scrutinize their origins and endings, I can never perceive them. Furthermore, when I examine the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, and the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and scrutinize their origins and endings, I see nothing at all.

In the southern, western, northern, southeastern, southwestern, northwestern, northeastern, upward, and downward directions—in these nine directions—I examine the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, and the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and scrutinize their origins and endings; I see nothing at all.”
What is this Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva?
For what reason should the title "bodhisattva" be spoken?
Furthermore, that name also neither abides anywhere, nor does it not abide.

Why is this so? Because the various classes of sentient beings proceed from a mind devoid of wisdom through the provisional application of names and designations. It is likewise with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, sickness, death, and suffering (*jarāmaraṇaduḥkha*): these also exist only as provisional designations. The root of these designations abides nowhere at all, nor does it not abide.
Why is this? Indeed, World-Honored One,
it is because all dharmas are entirely without origin.
For this reason, when seeking its origin and its end, it is utterly unattainable; by what causes and conditions, then, could one establish a name for a bodhisattva?
Furthermore, O God among Gods!
That which is without basis has no name and no dwelling, nor does it not dwell.

Why is this? Sentient beings, through ignorance, derive these characters from the ignorant mind; yet these names themselves have no place of dwelling, nor do they not dwell. Through the convergence of causes and conditions, there is a provisional designation called "Bodhisattva."

That is beyond verbal expression; it is devoid of the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, ignorance, the eighteen constituents, the twelve links of dependent origination, and all the Buddha-dharmas—all these are merely provisional designations based on conditions.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

To borrow metaphors, such as a reflection, an echo, a mirage, a plantain tree, an illusion, or a conjuration—these exist only as provisional designations; they are like the emptiness of letters, being empty and without name.”
For example, although there are the names earth, water, fire, wind, and space, earth, water, fire, wind, and space do not themselves possess these names.
Likewise, the matters of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat—these are merely designations.
It is the same for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas: they possess only provisional names.
That which is called a "bodhisattva" and the word "bodhisattva" are merely provisional designations;
that which is named "Buddha" and the dharmas of all Buddhas likewise have no real characters and are but provisional designations.

Good and evil, calamity and fortune; permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure; self and non-self; tranquility and serenity; existence and non-existence, merit and demerit; permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure—I contemplate these meanings and see that they all arise from causes and conditions.
If one were to establish a name for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there would be doubt regarding all dharmas; yet, when examining their beginning and end, they cannot be found.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
There is its name, yet there is no dharma-realm, nor is there any place of abiding. Why is this so?
The various classes of sentient beings derive these names from the mind of ignorance; furthermore, those names neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide, and they have no location.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such descriptions of the auspicious signs associated with the Prajñāpāramitā, is neither terrified nor frightened, neither alarmed nor daunted, and does not harbor any anxiety in his heart, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that he dwells in the fruit of *avaivartika*, dwelling in non-dwelling and practicing in non-practice.”
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in form; he should not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he should not abide in the eye, nor should he abide in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; he should not abide in forms..."

Regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, one should not dwell upon eye-consciousness of forms, ear-consciousness of sounds, nose-consciousness of odors, tongue-consciousness of tastes, body-consciousness of tangibles, or mind-consciousness of phenomena;

one should not dwell upon the contact experienced by the eye, nor should one dwell upon the contact experienced by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; one should not dwell upon the cause of the eye.
Conditioned by the practice of feeling through the causes and conditions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one should not dwell upon the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind;
one should not dwell upon the element of space; one should not dwell upon the elements of the various consciousnesses;
and one should not dwell upon ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, or craving.
feeling, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, and death. Why is this so?
O God among Gods!
Form is emptiness; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also empty.
That which is called "emptiness" means that form is empty; it is not that the name is different from emptiness. Form itself is empty, and emptiness is provisionally designated as form.
