If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to seek the practice of prajñāpāramitā through the conceptualization of their own conditions, they should abide in form; they should abide in sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they should abide in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; in the eighteen elements; and in the twelve links of dependent origination.

Why is this so? Because form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, and the twelve links of dependent origination are also empty. The emptiness of the source of birth and death within the twelve links of dependent origination is no different from [other] emptiness; it has no different abiding place.

That which constitutes old age, sickness, and death within the twelve links of dependent origination is itself empty; the twelve links of dependent origination, including birth, old age, sickness, and death, are naturally empty, being fundamentally and spontaneously empty.
For this reason, O God among Gods!

One should not abide in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; nor in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; nor in the eighteen elements or the origins of the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not abide in the four applications of mindfulness. Why is this so?

One contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness as empty; yet it is not that the four foundations of mindfulness are different from emptiness, nor is it that they are empty through something else; rather, the four foundations of mindfulness are naturally empty.

Furthermore, one should not dwell upon the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Why is this? Because the bases of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path by which they proceed—namely, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are likewise empty.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are naturally empty, being no different from emptiness; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are by their very nature empty, being no different from emptiness.
Why is this? Because even the reckoning of the Buddha-dharma is itself empty; it is because it is empty that it is called the Buddha-dharma.
O World-Honored One among Gods!

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself empty.
If the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty, then that emptiness is not something other than the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? There is no difference between the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the *prajñāpāramitā* itself being empty.

Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is naturally empty, it is merely designated by way of conventional names consisting of syllables; yet those syllables are themselves empty—this is precisely what constitutes the *prajñāpāramitā*.

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not dwell upon the prajñāpāramitā itself. The five aggregates, the six sense-bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are all empty; a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should not dwell within them.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he should not dwell upon syllables, nor should he dwell upon the teaching of syllables; he should not dwell upon one meal or two meals, nor upon three, four, or even morsel-food (*kavadīkāra-āhāra*), mind-food (*manah-āhāra*), or consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*)."
Why is this so? It is because letters are empty; emptiness is no different from letters.
Letters are naturally empty, and that which is empty possesses no letters.
Words are fundamentally empty; that which is empty has no name.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they should not abide in the supernormal powers."

Why is this so? Because these supernormal powers (abhijñā) are empty by their very nature; the supernormal powers are fundamentally empty, and there is no distinct "emptiness" apart from the supernormal powers.
Since the supernormal powers are empty and there is no emptiness other than them, and because the supernormal powers themselves are empty of self-nature, they are called "supernormal powers."
For this reason, O World-Honored One among Gods!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should not abide in the supernormal powers.
Furthermore, O World-Honored One among Gods!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on the perception of form, nor should they dwell on the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this so? That which is impermanent is empty of impermanence; that which is impermanent is naturally empty. Thus, there is no impermanence, nor is there anything other than impermanence that is empty. There is no emptiness from another source; impermanence is empty of itself. As for that which is empty, it possesses no impermanence.

For this reason, O God among Gods! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should not dwell on the emptiness of form; he should not dwell on the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. He should not dwell on the impermanence of form; he should not dwell on the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. He should not dwell on the impermanence of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; he should not dwell on the impermanence of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. He should not dwell on the impermanence of the eighteen elements or the beginningless and endless cycle of the twelve links of dependent origination.
One should not dwell in suffering, nor should one dwell in pleasure.
One should not dwell on form as "mine" or "not mine," nor should one dwell therein on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as "mine" or "not mine";
nor should one dwell therein on the emptiness of form, nor on the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One should not dwell in the emptiness of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
one should not dwell in the emptiness of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
one should not dwell in the emptiness of the eighteen constituents, the twelve links of dependent origination, or the suffering of birth and death.
One should not abide in the conditioned or the unconditioned;
one should not abide in the dharma of the ultimate limit (*koṭi*);
one should not abide in the tranquility of form, nor should one abide in the tranquility of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One should not dwell on the emptiness and non-substantiality of form; one should not dwell on the emptiness and non-substantiality of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is likewise for the six sense bases, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not abide in the absence of a basis. Why is this? "

That which is without foundation is entirely non-existent and is likewise empty; being without foundation and being without difference are one and the same. That which is without foundation is emptiness, and there is no emptiness other than this; that which is no emptiness other than this is what is meant by "being without foundation."
The absence of a fundamental basis is naturally empty; emptiness is thus the absence of a fundamental basis.

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell in the absence of a fundamental basis. They do not dwell in the absence of a fundamental basis regarding form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This extends to all phenomena, the realm of all phenomena, and all quiescent dharmas, even up to the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), wherein there is likewise no dwelling.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not abide in any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor do they abide in any of the doors of samādhi."
Why is this so? It is because the so-called gate of dhāraṇī is itself empty;
the so-called gate of samādhi is likewise empty.
The gateways of samādhi and the gateways of dhāraṇī are naturally empty; they are not different from emptiness. That which is naturally empty has no other emptiness.
The gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi are fundamentally pure; this fundamental purity is the natural emptiness of all phenomena.
For example, O World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* lacks *upāyakauśalya*, such that they conceive of a self and what belongs to a self, and by thinking in this way dwell upon form (*rūpa*), performing the actions of birth and death within form; or dwelling upon sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), performing actions and engaging in practice therein—failing to eliminate the causes for the formation of birth and death, yet instead receiving the *prajñāpāramitā* while refusing to apply oneself diligently to it—then they will not be endowed with the matters arising from the *prajñāpāramitā* up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
For example, O World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), and their mind gives rise to the thought of "I" and "mine," they will be unable to practice the gates of *dhāraṇī* regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor suffering, pleasure, good, and evil; they will likewise be unable to accord with the gates of *samādhi*, nor cultivate the practice of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). Even if they receive the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be unable to apply themselves diligently to it. Because they are not fully endowed with the *prajñāpāramitā*, they cannot achieve the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*).

Why is this? It is because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), they should not grasp at form, nor grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Yet that bodhisattva conversely further undergoes form; form is fundamentally pure, and when fully realized, it is empty.

Speaking from this perspective, if one undergoes sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then verbal teachings are fundamentally pure and likewise empty, such that one does not grasp at the various doors of dhāraṇī or the various doors of samādhi.

If one does not accept the gateways of samādhi or the gateways of dhāraṇī, then one can establish that fundamental purity is emptiness; likewise, one does not accept the prajñāpāramitā, because of knowing through conditions that fundamental purity is emptiness.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they observe that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and empty. They should abide in this contemplation and not give rise to the thought of "mine" regarding the phenomena they practice; this is what it means for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to be without anything to receive, which is called the samādhi of non-reception.
The site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is fully perfected, vast and universal, without limit and without measure, such that it cannot be reached by any *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*.

Furthermore, it does not grasp at omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); rather, it observes that the internal is empty and the external is likewise empty. There is the emptiness of both internal and external; the emptiness of seeking is itself empty, which constitutes the great emptiness and the ultimate emptiness. There is the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of ultimate exhaustion, the emptiness of vast distance, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of primordial purity, the emptiness of natural characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-possession, the emptiness of spontaneity, and the emptiness of the spontaneous arising from causes.
Why is this so? Because one immediately proceeds toward transformation, and that which is transformed is precisely the afflictions (*kleśa*).
What is meant by "transformation"?

What is meant by perception (*saṃjñā*)? Form (*rūpa*) is a transformation; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these are what constitute perception. The eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the gateways of dhāraṇī, and the gateways of samādhi—these are called the perceptions of worldly affliction (*kleśa*). One should receive and practice them without relying on anything and without nurturing anything; these are not what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas believe in or delight in, for they do not possess *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
What is meant by "faithful joy"?
It is to have faith in this Prajñāpāramitā, to be steadfastly joyful and free from doubt, to contemplate and discern it, and to observe its essential meaning such that there is no conceptualization.

In practice there is also no perception; therefore, one does not grasp at perception. With single-minded reliance, one joyfully practices with profound faith. When its fundamental nature is empty and pure, one then attains liberation, no longer grasping at form, nor grasping at sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because its characteristic is naturally the present emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); that which is received as empty is likewise unobtainable. Why is this?

Regarding that samādhi-concentration, when it cannot be apprehended internally, this is the wisdom of the [right] time; nor can it be apprehended externally, nor both internally and externally. This wisdom of the time likewise has nothing to be seen; internal and external are entirely empty, except for their causal conditions. It is like what is studied and believed by non-Buddhists: having delighted in this, they are governed by firm faith. Therefore, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Because one harbors resentment toward all phenomena and reckons that all dharmas are ultimately unobtainable as to their point of origin, once such faith is established, there is no one who receives the dharma; one no longer conceives of anything that exists, nor can one apprehend any infinite number of dharmas.

When that which is received is given up, and one neither receives nor even thinks about it, and when one dwells and practices such that there is no conceptualization regarding any phenomena—this is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is likewise without coming or going.

He delivers those who are not to be delivered and yet wanders everywhere; the reason for this is that he does not grasp at form, nor does he grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and he likewise has no grasping toward any phenomena whatsoever.

Furthermore, they do not receive any of the gates of dhāraṇī, nor do they receive any of the gates of samādhi; regarding all phenomena, they give rise to no reception, nor do they enter parinirvāṇa in the interim. They are fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of supernormal power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

Why is this so? Because the four foundations of mindfulness abide in non-abiding; the same is true for the four right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the eightfold path.

That which is severed is severed as having nothing to be severed. The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—awakening to these dharmas as having nothing to be awakened to; yet even the reckoning of those dharmas is not a dharma. This is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: it does not grasp at form, nor does it grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This extends to the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of all samādhis, which are all equal and without distinction.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate in this way:
'What is this perfection of wisdom?'"
For what reason is this called the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Who is it that performs this *prajñāpāramitā*? How does this *prajñāpāramitā* exist?
By means of this prajñāpāramitā, there is neither anything obtained, nor anything seen, nor anything not seen; therefore, it is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they should reflect in this way:
'That which is a non-existent dharma cannot be apprehended, nor does the prajñāpāramitā exist.'"
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "Venerable sir!
What dharma is it that you say is non-existent and unobtainable?"
He replied: "The dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither existent nor obtainable.
The same is true for the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Thus, even non-existence cannot be apprehended; it is empty internally, empty externally, and empty both internally and externally.

That emptiness leads to great emptiness, reaching the emptiness of true reality and the emptiness of non-existence. Because of that emptiness, one reaches the emptiness of non-emptiness; permanence is empty, agitation is empty, conditioned phenomena are empty, primordial purity is empty, natural characteristics are empty, all dharmas are empty, the emptiness of non-existence is empty, spontaneity is empty, and even the spontaneity of existence is empty.
For this reason, form is non-existent and cannot be apprehended; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
As for its internal emptiness, it is non-existent and cannot be apprehended;
its emptiness of existence, emptiness of non-existence, and natural emptiness are all non-existent and cannot be apprehended;

its four foundations of mindfulness are all non-existent and cannot be apprehended; and its four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eightfold path are all non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all non-existent and unattainable;
the six supernormal knowledges are all non-existent and unattainable;
and that which is without origin is entirely non-existent and unattainable.

That which is called "Dharma" abides in the Dharma; yet whether it be the quiescent Dharma or the investigation of the ultimate limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), all are utterly non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
That which is called "Buddha" is likewise utterly non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is entirely non-existent and unattainable.
All-encompassing wisdom is entirely non-existent and unattainable.
Its interior is empty; its exterior is reckoned as empty; both interior and exterior are empty; all that exists is empty; and even nature itself is empty.
"Indeed, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they engage in such reflection.
Having observed in this way and having engaged in such reflection, the mind cannot be perceived."

When the mind is without attachment and without defilement, and is neither terrified nor fearful, neither apprehensive nor daunted, and harbors no anxiety, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know that he is not separated from the prajñāpāramitā?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"What is called 'detachment from form' is because of the intrinsic nature of form;
what is called 'detachment from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness' is because of the intrinsic nature of consciousness."
This refers to being detached from the dāna-pāramitā, because the dāna-pāramitā is of the nature of spontaneity;
it refers to being detached from the śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā, because these six pāramitās are of the nature of spontaneity.

This refers to the fact that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the eightfold path—are by their very nature spontaneous.

That which is called being detached from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is because the dharmas of all Buddhas are spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
This means being detached from all doors of dhāraṇī, all doors of samādhi, and detached from the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), for the original limit is spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "What is meant by the spontaneity of form (*rūpa*)?"
What is meant by the naturalness of sensation, perception, volition, formations, and consciousness?
What is meant by the naturalness of the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
Subhūti replied: "Because there is nothing that exists, it is called 'self-so' (svabhāva).
Form does not exist; therefore, form is said to be self-so."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent; therefore, it is said that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are *svabhāva* (self-so).
That which is non-existent reaches the ultimate limit (*koṭi*); therefore, it is called *svabhāva*.

Śāriputra! For this reason, one who practices this contemplation knows that which is detached from form (*rūpa*) is the natural state of form; they know that which is detached from sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the natural state of these. Thus, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*), the ten powers (*daśa-balāni*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharmāḥ*)—all the way up to their fundamental purity—are entirely non-existent. Therefore, it is called "fundamental purity as the natural state."

That which is called the detachment from form is the fundamental characteristic of form; that which is called the detachment from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the fundamental characteristic of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is because all phenomena and the Buddha-dharmas are the characteristic of the ultimate limit (koṭi) for those who have detached from the ultimate limit.
"Because form is by its very nature the nature of phenomena, it is said that one attains detachment through the naturalness of these characteristics. Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who study this Dharma, will they all inevitably attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!
O worthy one!”
Those who study this will ultimately attain *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Why is this?
Because all phenomena neither arise nor cease.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "For what reason, Subhūti,
are all dharmas neither arising nor ceasing?"
He replied: "Śāriputra, that which is called 'form'— that form is empty."
For this reason, neither arising nor ceasing can be apprehended.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; for this reason, they neither arise nor cease.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena—these eighteen constituents; the twelve links of dependent origination; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all the gateways of dhāraṇī and all samādhis—up to the ultimate limit (bhūtakoṭi), these are neither arising nor ceasing, and they cannot be apprehended.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā is able to act in this way, they draw near to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

If one can draw near to sarvajñatā, then their body, speech, and mind become naturally pure; all marks are naturally and fully endowed with purity. Because their body, speech, and mind are thus purified and they have attained the purity of all marks, the Bodhisattva shall no longer give rise to thoughts of lust, anger, or delusion.
When the minds of lust, anger, and delusion have been purified, one will then be free from pride, malice, and greed, and will no longer give rise to the sixty-two views.

When all such heterodox doubts and the minds of greed and anger no longer arise, one is able to eliminate the sixty-two views and all skeptical intentions. In whatever place one is born, one does not create the view of permanence; in whatever Buddha-lands one is born, one travels from one Buddha-land to another, teaching and transforming sentient beings and adorning and purifying the Buddha-fields. Always maintaining single-minded devotion without departing from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, until one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieves the state of an Arhat (A-vai-san-bou).
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
*The Sūtra of Radiant Praise*, Scroll Three.
*The Sūtra of Radiant Praise*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: Practice. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Nine: Practice.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā without upāyakauśalya, if he practices with regard to form (*rūpa*), then he practices with conceptualization (*saṃjñā*);
if he practices with regard to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), then he [practices with conceptualization].”
To practice perceptions: if one practices the perception that form is permanent, that is practicing perceptions;

if one practices the perception that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, that is practicing perceptions; if one practices the perception that form is impermanent, that is practicing perceptions;

if one practices the perception that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, that is practicing perceptions; if one practices the perception that form is suffering... [is practicing perceptions].

Regarding the perception of formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra*): if one practices with the thought that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are suffering, that is the practice of perception;

if one practices with the thought that form (*rūpa*) is pleasure, that is the practice of perception; if one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are pleasure, that is the practice of perception;

if one practices with the thought that form is "mine," that is the practice of perception; [and] if one practices with feeling, perception... [volitional formations... and consciousness... [as "mine," that is the practice of perception].
To practice the notion that consciousness is "mine" is to practice conceptualization; to practice the notion that form is "not mine" is to practice conceptualization;
to practice the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are "not mine" is to practice conceptualization;

to practice the notion that form is empty and non-existent is to practice conceptualization; and to practice [the notion that] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness... [is to practice conceptualization].
One who perceives consciousness as empty or non-existent thus forms a conceptualization.
Furthermore, O God among Gods!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom perceives the stillness of form, he forms a conceptualization; if he perceives the stillness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he forms a conceptualization.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), then practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) constitutes a conceptualization; practicing the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) likewise constitutes a conceptualization."
If one practices the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, that constitutes practicing with conceptualization.
O World-Honored One! O God among Gods!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should think to himself,
"I am practicing the prajñāpāramitā," this constitutes a conceptualization on the part of that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should think to themselves:
"One who practices in this way is practicing the prajñāpāramitā," they are still practicing with conceptualization.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the perfection of wisdom without *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
Śāriputra asked: "Subhūti!"
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom and attain the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "Suppose, worthy one!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not place faith in or understand the ideation of form; for if one establishes oneself in form, one is not liberated from ideation and thus practices the ideation of birth and death.

If one practices with the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), one cannot escape ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and thus lacks skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

If one abides in the perception of the eye, one does not believe in liberation; likewise, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, they do not believe in liberation.

If one establishes perceptions based on eye-and-form-consciousness, ear-and-sound-consciousness, nose-and-odor-consciousness, tongue-and-flavor-consciousness, body-and-tactile-consciousness, and mind-and-phenomena-consciousness, then one will not have faith in liberation.
If one establishes various perceptions based on the contact cultivated by the eye, or the contact cultivated by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, then one does not believe in liberation.

Even if one establishes the perceptions of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path, one still does not believe in liberation.

Those who form conceptions regarding the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha will not have faith or liberation; rather, they will harbor attachments and conceptualizations toward the thoughts and practices of the Buddha-dharma.
One who dwells on perceptions of mental formations does not believe in liberation from the afflictions of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not even aspire to the realization of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, much less attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a fully enlightened buddha.
It is beyond their reach.
Thus it is, Śāriputra:
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without skillful means (upāyakauśalya), [it is so].
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā possess upāyakauśalya?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice form, nor does he practice feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
he does not practice the notion of form, nor does he practice the notions of feeling, perception, or mental formations.”

Regarding the consciousness-perception of birth and death, one does not practice the notion that form is permanent, nor does one practice the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent;
one does not practice the notion that form is impermanent, nor does one practice the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent;

one does not practice the notion that form is suffering, nor does one practice the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering; one does not practice the notion that form is pleasure...

One does not practice the pleasure of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not practice the notion that form is "mine," nor that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "mine";
one does not practice the notion that form is "not mine," nor that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "not mine";
one does not practice the notion that form is empty and non-existent, nor [that feeling, perception, or mental formations are so].

One contemplates that the consciousness of birth-and-death is empty and non-existent; one does not practice the emptiness of form, nor the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one does not practice the signlessness of form, nor the signlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one does not practice the wishlessness of form, nor the wishlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. One does not...
One does not practice the stillness of form, nor does one practice the stillness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
one does not practice the non-conceptualization of form, nor does one practice the non-conceptualization of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this so? Form is emptiness; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is form. Form is naturally empty.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; thus there is no consciousness, and consciousness is not different from emptiness—consciousness is emptiness, and emptiness is consciousness.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path are empty; there is no emptiness other than these.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are reckoned as empty; there is no separate emptiness apart from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment themselves are emptiness, and emptiness itself is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise empty; there is no separate emptiness apart from them.
The Buddha-dharma is emptiness; there is no other emptiness distinct from it. Emptiness is the dharma, and the dharma is emptiness.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to accomplish skillful means (upāyakauśalya), and when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in such a manner, they shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Having practiced the perfection of wisdom, there is nothing received and nothing practiced; no receiving and no practicing, no practicing and no receiving; there is neither anything practiced nor is there non-practicing. Therefore, there is nothing received, nor is there anything that is received.
The venerable Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having practiced the perfection of wisdom, have nothing to apprehend?"
Subhūti replied: "The reason why a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā is that it is naturally unobtainable.
For this reason, the prajñāpāramitā is non-existent; thus, it is natural."

For this reason, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, there is nothing received and nothing practiced; there is no receiving and no practicing, no practicing and no receiving; there is neither anything practiced nor anything not non-practiced. Therefore, there is nothing received, nor is there anything that is received.
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are non-existent, they are said to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, there is no destination and no transgression; this is called the samādhi-concentration of "non-acceptance of all things."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is vast, universal, profound, and remote, beyond all measure, such that no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can reach him.
By means of this samādhi, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the supreme perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from this samādhi and swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
are there any other samādhis besides it?"
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are other samādhis by which one quickly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled perfect enlightenment."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"What other practices of samādhi enable a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the Śūraṅgama Samādhi will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment!”
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Jewel Seal; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Lion’s Delight;
furthermore, there is a samādhi named Moon Radiance; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Moon Banner Essence."
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "All Seals" (Sarvamudrā); furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Incapable of Seeing the Crown of the Head" (Anavalokitamūrdha);
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Comprehending the Dharma Realm" (Dharmadhātuprativedha); furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Discerning the Banner-Flower" (Vijñaptidhvajaketu);
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Metaphor of the Vajra" (Vajropama); furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Entering the Dharma" (Dharmapraveśa).
There is a seal, and furthermore, there is a samādhi named King of Established Concentration; furthermore, there is a samādhi named King of Seals;
furthermore, there is a samādhi named Vigorous Power; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Transcending Equality;
furthermore, there is a samādhi named Entry into Accordant Discernment; furthermore, there is a samādhi named...
Entering and discerning the realms of the ten directions,

there is further a samādhi named "Upholding All Intent," a samādhi named "Transcending the Unconditioned," a samādhi named "Equally Governing the Ocean-Seal of All Dharmas," a samādhi named "Pervasively Encompassing Space," and a samādhi named "Vajra Bodhimanda."
Furthermore, there is a samādhi called Holding the Victorious Banner; furthermore, there is a samādhi called Sovereign Brilliance Like a Door Threshold;
furthermore, there is a samādhi called Arising from the Source; furthermore, there is a samādhi called Lion’s Roar;
furthermore, there is a samādhi called Established in Diligence; furthermore, there is a samādhi called Supreme Jewel.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Illumination; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Unblinking;
furthermore, there is a samādhi named Not Abiding in the Lower; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Decisive Comprehension;
furthermore, there is a samādhi named Lamp-Light Widely Pervasive; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Immeasurable Practice.

Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Light-Creation," another samādhi named "That Which Illuminates," another samādhi named "Pure Adornment," another samādhi named "Stainless Light," another samādhi named "The Joy of Creation," and another samādhi named "Lightning-Lamp Radiance."

Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Exhaustive Search," another samādhi named "Trace of Majestic Power," another samādhi named "Detached from Exhaustive Search," another samādhi named "Invincible," another samādhi named "Opening and Penetration," another samādhi named "Lamp-Light," and yet another...
There is a samādhi named "Free from the Defilement of Lamps"; furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Adorned and Pure Eloquence";
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Possessing Radiance"; furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Accomplishing Deeds";
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Essence of Wisdom"; furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Abiding in Reflection. Furthermore...
There is a samādhi called Universal Radiance; furthermore, there is a samādhi called Well-Established;
furthermore, there is a samādhi called Jewel Accumulation; furthermore, there is a samādhi called Seal that Transcends All Dharmas;
furthermore, there is a samādhi called Universal Dharma; furthermore, there is a samādhi called Supreme Delight; furthermore, there is a samādhi called...

Having crossed over the summit of the Dharma, there is further a samādhi called "That Which Destroys," another samādhi called "All-Illuminating Phrases," another samādhi called "The Accomplishment of Equal Syllables," another samādhi called "Proceeding to Syllables," and another samādhi called "Severing Causes and Conditions. Furthermore, there is a samādhi...

There is a samādhi called "The Nameless," another samādhi called "The Wall-less," another samādhi called "Decisive Entry into the Designation," another samādhi called "The Practice of No Humility," another samādhi called "Dispelling Darkness," another samādhi called "Traces of Cultivation," and another samādhi called...
Immovable; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Vast Realm, another samādhi named Resolving All Virtues,
another samādhi named Abiding in Mindlessness, another samādhi named Purifying Adornment,
another samādhi named Transcending the Factors of Enlightenment, and another samādhi named...
There is the Samādhi of Immeasurable Lamp-Light; furthermore, there is a Samādhi named Equal and Unequal;
furthermore, there is a Samādhi named Delivering All; furthermore, there is a Samādhi named Severing All Affairs;
furthermore, there is a Samādhi named Detachment from Thought and Thorough Elimination; furthermore, there is a Samādhi named Freedom from Establishment; furthermore, there is a Samādhi...

The name of the first is "Single Victory. Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Performing All Deeds," another samādhi named "Single Deed," another samādhi named "Eliminating Hostile Deeds," another samādhi named "Extinguishing All That Is Improper," and another samādhi named "Entering According to the Sound of Conditions. Furthermore...
There is a samādhi named "Inexhaustible Utterance of the Trace of Sound"; furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Trace of Majestic Power";
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Blazing Radiance"; furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Pure Tree";
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Pure Realization and Tranquility"; furthermore, there is a samādhi named...

All-Victorious, there is furthermore a samādhi called "Not Delighting in Any Suffering or Pleasure," a samādhi called "Inexhaustible Matter," a samādhi called "Dhāraṇī Phrase," a samādhi called "Equal to the Lion Throne of the Right and the Wrong," and a samādhi called "Entering Resonance."
Beyond Resonance, there is further a samādhi named Attaining Resonance from Non-Resonance;
further, a samādhi named Stainless Radiance; further, a samādhi named Treading the Tracks;
further, a samādhi named Full Moon Stainless Light; further, a samādhi named Lightning Torch Light; further, a samādhi named...

It is called Great Purity; furthermore, there is a samādhi named Universally Illuminating the World, a samādhi named Universal Stabilization of the Mind, a samādhi named Responding Without Attachment and Free from Defilement, a samādhi named Governing All Equally in Space, and a samādhi named Without Blue... [not blue].

O Blue Jewel, furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Establishing the Mindfulness of the Rootless," another samādhi called "The Foremost in the Timing of the Body," another samādhi called "Eliminating Empty Thoughts at the Time of Speech," and another samādhi called "Liberation from the Obstructions of Space and the Protection of Extinction."
Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice these samādhis, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, regarding the other incalculable and limitless gates of samādhi and gates of dhāraṇī that a bodhisattva mahāsattva ought to study, they shall swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled perfect enlightenment!
Thereupon, Subhūti, receiving the holy intent of the Buddha, uttered this eulogy: "Śāriputra!

If you wish to know, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have already conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; and all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions have likewise already conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."
One who practices this samādhi does not perceive the samādhi, nor does he think of the samādhi, nor is there anything for him to settle in as samādhi, nor does he conceive the thought:
"I shall enter samādhi."
"Am I in samādhi? nor does he think,
"I am in the emptiness samādhi."
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is without conceptualization. Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi;"
"Have you received the prediction of enlightenment from a Tathāgata of the past? He replied, "No."
Śāriputra! Why is this? Indeed, Śāriputra!
The Prajñāpāramitā samādhi is not different [from it], nor is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva different from it.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the samādhi, and the samādhi is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"As you have stated, 'The prajñāpāramitā and the various samādhis of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are not distinct; the bodhisattva is the samādhi, and the samādhi is the bodhisattva.'"
"Since all dharmas are equal, one does not know this samādhi. For this reason, Śāriputra,
in this samādhi, a son of good family neither knows nor understands it.
Śāriputra asked again,
"For what reason is there neither knowledge nor understanding?
[The Buddha replied,] "Because they employ ignorance as their samādhi, for this reason, the bodhisattva neither knows nor understands."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the venerable Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
As I have praised you for practicing emptiness as foremost and extolled you as most venerable,

so too should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the *prajñāpāramitā*, and likewise in the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*; in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),

the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold path (*mārga*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, is he training in the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
"It is so! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they are training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet there is nothing to be apprehended in that which is trained in.
It is likewise for the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*."

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are spontaneously and fully possessed; though there is that which is attained, there is also nothing attained.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, by training thus,
does he train in the *prajñāpāramitā*, and does he attain the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha said:
"To train in this way is to train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which results in non-attainment.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
"How does one attain that which is non-attainment?
The World-Honored One replied:
"One does not attain a self, nor does one attain a person, a life-span, nor does one attain anything seen."
The five aggregates (*skandha*), from their ultimate beginning to their end, are entirely pure, yet they cannot be perceived.

The elements (*dhātu*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), from their ultimate beginning to their end, are likewise entirely pure and cannot be apprehended. Ignorance (*avidyā*), from its ultimate beginning to its end, is entirely pure; and so too are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, sickness, death, and suffering—from their ultimate beginning to their end, all are entirely pure.

Suffering is unattainable; from its beginning to its end, it is ultimately and entirely pure. The path to the exhaustion of habitual tendencies is likewise unattainable; from its beginning to its end, it is ultimately and entirely pure.
The desire realm is also unattainable; from its beginning to its end, it is ultimately and entirely pure.
The form realm and the formless realm are also unattainable; from their beginning to their end, they are ultimately and entirely pure.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise unattainable; from beginning to end, they are ultimately and entirely pure.
The six pāramitās are also unattainable; from beginning to end, they are ultimately and entirely pure.
The srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and [the Buddha] are also unattainable; from beginning to end, they are ultimately and entirely pure.
The bodhisattva, too, cannot be apprehended; from beginning to end, it is ultimately and entirely pure.
The Buddha, too, cannot be apprehended; from beginning to end, he is ultimately and entirely pure.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is it that is pure,
World-Honored One?”
He replied: "That which is without arising and without birth, without attainment and without activity, is purity. Śāriputra said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, what dharma is he training in?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are training in the dharma of non-training.
Why is that? Śāriputra!”
"These dharmas are reckoned as having existence, and are that upon which foolish commoners rely.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
"Who brings about this Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"As there is nothing to be attained, it is for this reason that one who attains in such a manner is said to have 'nothing attained'."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
Who is it that has nothing to attain, yet attains something?"
The Buddha said:
“Form is unapprehendable; its interior is empty, its exterior is likewise empty, and both its interior and exterior are empty.
That which is called ‘existence’ is naturally non-existent and is entirely empty.”
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither internal nor external, nor are they both internal and external; they are spontaneously non-existent and entirely empty.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise neither internal nor external, nor are they both internal and external; they are spontaneously non-existent and entirely empty.

Those foolish worldlings, instructed by ignorance, rely upon and cling to craving while harboring conceptual notions; thus, being as if both blind due to their reliance on ignorance and delusion, they neither know nor see.
Having neither known nor seen, they conceive of dharmas as unattainable; yet they rely upon name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and further depend upon and cling to the Buddha-dharmas.
Because they have already established such dependencies while wishing to understand the dharma of non-existence, they do not know and do not see.
What is meant by not knowing and not seeing?

One does not know and does not see form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; nor does one know and see the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. For this reason, such a person is called ignorant.
He does not relinquish giving.
What does he not relinquish?
He does not relinquish the desire realm, he does not relinquish the form realm, he does not relinquish the formless realm; he does not relinquish the stages of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha.
Then one will lack firm faith.
What would one not believe?

One would not believe that form is empty; one would not believe that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. One would not believe that the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty.

Being unable to establish them, they do not establish the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, or prajñā-pāramitā; they do not abide in the stage of avaivartika, nor do they establish the dharmas of all Buddhas.
For these reasons, they are called "fools."

There is that which relies upon and clings to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; that which relies upon and clings to the various elements (*dhātu*), aggregates (*skandha*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*); that which relies upon and seeks after lust, anger, and delusion; that which relies upon and yearns for various doubts and false views; and that which relies upon and yearns for the Buddha-way.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is he not training in the prajñāpāramitā?
Will he not give rise to sarvajñatā?”
The Buddha said,
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner in the prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend sarvajñatā.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, will they not attain sarvajñatā?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner without *upāyakauśalya*, yet conceives thoughts and relies upon the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*; and furthermore, conversely, conceives thoughts and seeks to rely upon the six *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and further conceives thoughts and seeks the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), having already sought omniscience and then relying upon it."
"Therefore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not study the prajñāpāramitā, they will not attain the wisdom of sarvajñatā.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way in the prajñāpāramitā, is he not training in the prajñāpāramitā?
Is he not practicing the wisdom of sarvajñatā?"
The Buddha said, “It is so,
Śāriputra! To train in the *prajñāpāramitā* in such a manner is to not attain *sarvajñatā*.”
Śāriputra asked: "O World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva study the prajñāpāramitā?"
"And how does one train in accordance with this to attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñā*)?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom."

In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and studies the perfection of wisdom in order to attain the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna), attaining that which is non-attainment.
There is no attainment and no non-attainment; furthermore, one does not attain the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, or prajñā-pāramitā;
nor does one attain the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, or buddha;
nor, moreover, does one attain sarvajñatā.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; they are training in the perfection of wisdom to attain sarvajñatā, attaining that which is non-attainment.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'non-attainment'?
The World-Honored One replied:
"It is empty internally, empty externally, and empty both internally and externally; all dharmas are empty.
Chapter Ten: The Chapter on Illusion (*Māyā*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
Suppose someone were to ask:
"This illusory person studies the Prajñāpāramitā, desiring to attain sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
If one is asked in this manner, how should one respond?

"Furthermore, this illusory person studies the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, and the *dhyānapāramitā*, desiring thereby to attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*);

they study the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path, desiring thereby to attain the wisdom of omniscience;
and they further study the wisdom of omniscience itself, desiring thereby to attain omniscience."
“If someone were to come and ask about this meaning, how would you answer them?
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
“I shall therefore question you.”
"What do you think, Subhūti? Answer me according to your understanding.
What do you think, Subhūti? Is form different [from the Tathāgata]?"
"Is illusion different from [the aggregates], or are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhūti replied:
"No, O God among Gods! What do you think, Subhūti? Is the illusion something other [than the mind]?"
Is the eye different?
Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind different?
Is illusion different?

Are the eye-consciousness of forms, ear-consciousness of sounds, nose-consciousness of odors, tongue-consciousness of tastes, body-consciousness of tangibles, and mind-consciousness of mental objects different from one another?
And is the illusion different from them?
"Is the pleasure of sensation arising from the causes and conditions one has practiced different [from that],
and is it further different from an illusion? He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! What do you think, Subhūti? Are the four foundations of mindfulness distinct from one another?"
Is illusion different?
Are the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path different from it?
Is illusion, moreover, different?
"Are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness different from one another?
And is illusion different from them? He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! What do you think, Subhūti? Is the illusion something other [than the dharmas]?"
"Are the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha something different [from the Suchness of all dharmas]?
He replied, "No, O God among Gods!"
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is illusion one thing and the Path another?”
He replied: "No, O God among Gods!
Illusion is not different, nor is form different."
Form is illusion, and illusion is form. O World-Honored One!

Illusion is not different from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; nor are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from illusion. Consciousness is illusion, and illusion is consciousness.
"Indeed, O Heaven among Heavens!
Illusion is not different from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; nor are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind different from illusion. Illusion is the eye, and the eye is illusion."
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—consciousness is illusion, and illusion is consciousness.
The pleasure derived from the sensations of causes and conditions that one has practiced is not something different; sensation and pleasure are illusion, and illusion is sensation and pleasure.
Indeed, O God among Gods!
Illusion is not different, and the four foundations of mindfulness are also not different; the four foundations of mindfulness are illusion, and illusion is the four foundations of mindfulness.

The right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the paths of practice are like an illusion; an illusion, moreover, consists of the paths of practice.
Indeed, O God among Gods!
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these dharmas are illusion, and illusion is these dharmas.
“What do you think, Subhūti? Does that which is called an illusion have any defilements or malice? He replied:
“No, O World-Honored One! Subhūti, what do you think?
Does that which is called an illusion arise or cease?”
He replied: "No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked: "What do you think, Subhūti?"

Regarding that which neither arises nor ceases: having studied the *prajñāpāramitā*, will they attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) and achieve all-encompassing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked: “What do you think, Subhūti?”

"Does one become a bodhisattva by giving rise to the conceptualization of 'that which is known' regarding these [aggregates], based on the causes of conventional teachings and the five aggregates of clinging? He replied, "It is so."
"Indeed, O God among Gods!

Subhūti, what do you think? If there is one who possesses cognition and thought, who speaks and teaches in accordance with worldly conventions, and who, by means of the five aggregates of clinging, undergoes arising and ceasing—could such a person still give rise to afflictions and resentment?"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! [The Buddha asked: “What do you think, Subhūti?”

If there is no thought, no habituation, no teaching, no establishment, no name, no body and no bodily affairs, no speech and no verbal affairs, no mind and no mental affairs; if there is neither arising nor ceasing, no defilement, and no resentment—and yet one studies the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of these things—will one thereby achieve *sarvajñatā*?
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! The Buddha said:
"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, the one who accomplishes *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is ultimately non-existent."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this manner in the prajñāpāramitā and train in anuttarasamyaksambodhi."
If one wishes to study, one should do so as if studying an illusion. Why is this?
Because, O World-Honored One!
"One should contemplate that the five aggregates are also like illusory beings. "What do you think, Subhūti?
Furthermore, by training in the Prajñāpāramitā, do these five aggregates achieve the wisdom of sarvajñatā?"
He replied: “No, O God among Gods! Why is this so? Because—”
"Those five aggregates are naturally non-existent;
that which is naturally non-existent is also unattainable.
He asked again:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is it by means of the analogy of spontaneity—that the five aggregates are like a dream—that one studies the Prajñāpāramitā and accomplishes sarvajñatā?"
He replied: “No, O God among Gods! Why is this so? Because—”
“Consider that what is dreamt is naturally non-existent;
that which is naturally non-existent cannot be apprehended.
“What do you think, Subhūti?”

The resonance of a shout is used as a metaphor for the five aggregates; furthermore, it is like the metaphors of a reflection in water, a mirage, and a magical creation. Is it by studying the Prajñāpāramitā that one attains the realization of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) regarding the five aggregates?
He replied: "No, O God among Gods! Why is this so?"
The resonance of a call, a reflection in water, a mirage, and that which is conjured are naturally non-existent.
That which is naturally non-existent cannot be apprehended.
Why is this so? O World-Honored One!
One discerns and understands that form is like an illusion;

likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the eighteen elements, the six sense bases, the five aggregates, and the five aggregates of clinging, are by nature like a dream.

"O World-Honored One! Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eighteen elements, the six sense bases, and the five aggregates of clinging are like a dream. They are empty within, utterly unobtainable; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty, utterly unobtainable."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now that this Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, will those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna and hear this teaching not experience fear, dread, or apprehension?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna does not understand upāyakauśalya (skillful means) regarding the prajñāpāramitā, and does not associate with virtuous friends, he may become afraid, terrified, or filled with dread."
Subhūti asked the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One! What is meant by a 'good spiritual friend' (kalyāṇamitra) for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"When practicing the Prajñāpāramitā with upāyakauśalya (skillful means), how is it that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is neither afraid, nor terrified, nor apprehensive?
The Buddha said:

"When this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā with a mind focused on single-minded diligence, he does not contemplate form as impermanent, for even form cannot be apprehended; he does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as impermanent, for even consciousness cannot be apprehended."
When one directs the mind toward observing sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), one does not perceive impermanence, nor is it to be apprehended.
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā with upāyakauśalya (skillful means).

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is intent upon the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), they do not contemplate form as suffering, nor do they apprehend form; they do not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as suffering, nor do they apprehend consciousness."
One does not regard form as "mine," nor does one apprehend "mine";
one does not regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as "mine," nor does one apprehend "mine."
One does not contemplate form as "not mine," nor does one apprehend it as "not mine";
one does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as "not mine," nor does one apprehend them as "not mine."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is dedicated to training for sarvajñatā contemplates that form is empty, yet does not apprehend emptiness;
he contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, yet does not apprehend emptiness."
One does not contemplate form as permanent, nor does one apprehend it as permanent;
one does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent, nor does one apprehend them as permanent.
One does not contemplate form as impermanent, nor does one apprehend it as impermanent.
One does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as impermanent, nor does one apprehend them as impermanent.
One contemplates form as quiescent, yet does not apprehend the quiescence of form;
one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as quiescent, yet does not apprehend the quiescence of consciousness.
One contemplates form as empty and void, yet does not apprehend even the emptiness and voidness of form;
one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty and void, yet does not apprehend even the emptiness and voidness of consciousness.
This is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate impermanence, nor do they apprehend anything; they do not contemplate suffering, emptiness, non-self, or non-body, nor do they apprehend anything; they do not contemplate impermanence, nor do they apprehend anything.
Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, stillness, and non-existence are likewise unattainable.
Regarding sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one does not contemplate them as impermanent, and they too are unattainable.

Regarding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena (*dharmas*), one does not contemplate them as impermanent, nor is there anything to be attained therein.

They are not permanent, suffering, empty, or non-self; they are not the body. They are empty, signless, wishless, tranquil, void, and non-existent. Contemplating these matters, one finds that there is absolutely nothing to be attained.
He has this intention for the sake of sentient beings:
"I shall preach the Dharma of impermanence for all classes of sentient beings, so that those who practice inverted giving may not fall into delusion."
Furthermore, one discriminates phenomena as suffering, non-self, empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and void, so that those who are subject to perversion shall not be deluded.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with upāyakauśalya!

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, training in and practicing the wisdom of sarvajñatā, they contemplate its meaning; they do not perceive form as impermanent, nor do they fall into inversion, nor do they apprehend anything.
Not contemplating that sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, one does not fall into inversion and has nothing to be attained.

That there is no suffering and no self constitutes emptiness; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are tranquil and void. There is nothing that does not cause one to avoid inversion and have nothing to be attained.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached from the four marks of impermanence; they are empty, signless, wishless, tranquil, void, and non-existent.
Contemplating these phenomena, one does not allow for inversion, nor is there anything to be attained.

If, while abiding in the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), one maintains this mindfulness without abandoning it, this is the *vīryapāramitā* (perfection of vigor) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, their resolve does not contemplate the matters of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they listen to, encourage, or follow such inclinations; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *dhyānapāramitā* (perfection of meditation), being neither afraid, nor terrified, nor fearful!

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he should cultivate this contemplation: one does not take the emptiness of form as being empty; rather, form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not exclusively empty; form is emptiness, and consciousness is naturally consciousness, while emptiness is consciousness."
The eye is not exclusively empty; the eye is naturally empty. That which is the eye is emptiness, and that which is emptiness is the eye; it is not exclusively emptiness.

So too with the ear and its consciousness of sound, the nose and its consciousness of fragrance, the tongue and its consciousness of flavor, the body and its consciousness of tactile sensation, and the mind and its consciousness of phenomena: they are not exclusively empty; consciousness is naturally empty. That which is consciousness is emptiness, and that which is emptiness is consciousness.

The pleasure derived from the causes and conditions of habitual practice is empty; the pleasure derived from the causes and conditions of habitual practice is naturally empty; when one contemplates the pleasure derived from the causes and conditions of habitual practice, it is seen as empty; the mind itself is empty, and thus the pleasure derived from the causes and conditions of habitual practice is also empty.

The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are not exclusively empty; because the four foundations of mindfulness are empty, they are thereby empty, and these four foundations of mindfulness are naturally empty.

The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*)—these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣikā dharmāḥ*) are not exclusively empty. Rather, the thirty-seven factors are themselves emptiness, and the thirty-seven factors are themselves empty.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not intentionally made empty; they are naturally empty.

That which is emptiness is the Buddha; the Dharma is emptiness; that which is emptiness is the Dharma. This is why the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is neither terrified, nor frightened, nor fearful.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Who are the good spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? [The Buddha replied:
“They are those who preach the Prajñāpāramitā with full protection; upon hearing it, one is not terrified, not frightened, not alarmed, and not afraid.”
In this regard, Subhūti!

A good spiritual friend teaches the Dharma for the sake of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, explaining that form is neither permanent nor impermanent; yet form is ungraspable and there is no attachment to it.

By means of these roots of virtue, they do not encourage or assist others to establish themselves on the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but instead cause them to study only the wisdom of sarvajñatā; such is the good teacher of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one does not speak of them as impermanent; they are neither to be apprehended nor clung to.
