"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva again cultivates meditative contemplation, practicing the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and the formless samādhis, he abides in tranquility.

He perceives emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); having seen these, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s great armor (*mahā-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
It is said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor (mahā-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha).
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus clad in this saṃnāha (armour), then the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, throughout the Buddha-worlds of the eight directions, above, and below, shall proclaim their subtle and wondrous teachings and extol his merits with resonant voices, declaring: "In such-and-such a world, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, clad in the armour of great virtue, transforms sentient beings and purifies a buddha-field."
Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"What is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s three *vyavakīrṇa* (mixed) practices that are equal to the Great Vehicle? Pūrṇa replied:
"In this regard, worthy one!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he quiets and eliminates manifold desires and extinguishes all evil and unwholesome states. Following the practice of contemplation on existence, he dwells in tranquility and abides in peace, thereby being able to fully accomplish the first dhyāna."

Having already departed from desire and being free from all evils, having eliminated all conceptual thoughts and objects of recollection, and being tranquil and at peace, one is then able to fully accomplish the practice of the second dhyāna.

Having eliminated all perceptions, being without thought or ideation, the mind cultivates itself according to the teachings of the noble ones; not contradicting clear insight, one attains joy and tranquility, and thus fully realizes the third dhyāna.

Having removed tranquility and departed from suffering, and having transcended all previously experienced states—whether wholesome or unwholesome, agreeable or disagreeable—one dwells neither in pain nor in pleasure, but in equanimity and mindfulness, attaining joy and peace; thus, one becomes fully endowed with the fourth dhyāna.

Practicing the four immeasurable minds, their hearts are constantly compassionate; they are free from enmity, free from fetters, and free from delusion. Vast and boundless, they accord with the infinite good throughout all worlds, and in the movements of their minds, they never abandon this.
It is the same for the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Guarding the mind constantly, one remains free from enmity and resentment, as well as from delusion; vast and boundless, following immeasurable goodness throughout all worlds, the mind’s activity never abandons this.
This is the meditative contemplation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

By means of this meditative contemplation, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the four immeasurable minds; by means of these auspicious responses, they practice samādhi. Having practiced these, they all provide encouragement and assistance toward the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

This is the foundation of the dāna-pāramitā among the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā are each likewise so.
This is what is meant by the "great armor" (*saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva!

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*); it is vast, far-reaching, universal, non-dual, boundless, and free from fetters, yet it does not abide in any single location.
The first, second, third, and fourth stages of faith are likewise so.
Reaching down to the limitlessness below and up to the boundlessness above, there is nowhere throughout the eight directions, above and below, that it does not pervade.
To be fully endowed with the four dhyānas constitutes the samādhi of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Suppose a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, honoring his mind with the aspiration for sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), practices the first dhyāna while gathering and protecting all sentient beings, and exhorts them all toward the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms. That bodhisattva-mahāsattva, being fully endowed with sarvajñatā, gives rise to the mind of wisdom; yet, through skillful means, he elucidates the meaning and preaches the sūtras for others. This is the dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Furthermore, when the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), they contemplate and practice the attainment of the first dhyāna.

If they are able to abide in the first dhyāna, no longer believing in or delighting in the arousal of divergent thoughts, and not following the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—this is the śīlapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, which consists in not transgressing against others.
Suppose a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sets his mind and will upon the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), and while practicing and contemplating it, he gives rise to this thought:

"May the suffering and toil of all persons and classes of sentient beings be extinguished; for them, I shall preach the Dharma, according to what their minds desire and delight in, observing their fundamental capacities to transform and enlighten them."
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a mind that cultivates the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñatā-jñāna), encourages and assists the root of all merits, yet perceives no destination for diligence within the various supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind that pursues and cultivates the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), practices from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, and furthermore contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as well as empty, signless, and wishless—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the dhyānapāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind that reveres and honors the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), contemplates all dharmas as being like illusions and transformations, perceiving no triple world, and expounds the sūtras for the sake of others—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
Worthy Śāriputra! This is the matter of the Mahāyāna for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is that which establishes all four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; furthermore, it establishes all [qualities], being fully endowed with the samādhi of emptiness, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi, as well as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—this is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not seek these two stages—the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha—nor does he inform others of such a desire; his mind delights solely in the wisdom of *sarvajñatā*. This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices vigilance as the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and thereby fulfills the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind devoted to cultivation, gives rise to all-embracing compassion and wisdom, such that their conduct is limitless and indestructible, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the *vīrya-pāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices meditative concentration while abiding in the four immeasurable minds, and does not lose anything of that meditative concentration or those four immeasurable minds, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the four immeasurable minds with heedfulness and upāyakauśalya (skillful means).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s samādhi of the mind of loving-kindness:
'I shall rescue and protect all sentient beings.'"
Then, by means of the samādhi of practicing compassion through reverence and honor, and by following this path of practicing pity through sympathetic sorrow;
and by means of the samādhi of practicing joy:
"I shall deliver and liberate all classes of sentient beings."

"Advancing further and further until reaching the samādhi of protection, extending it to all sentient beings until their outflows are exhausted—this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of the four immeasurables as the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) without negligence."

If one practices dhyāna-contemplation without negligence, cultivating the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni), and through these causal conditions and auspicious responses, does not employ them to encourage or assist those on the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but instead remains devoted to all-pervasive compassion and wisdom—this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of the four immeasurable minds that is irreproachable and fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is that which thoroughly understands internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and does not fall into inversion; it has nothing to seek and nothing to obtain. Suffering and pleasure, good and evil—all these are naturally empty of intrinsic existence. Within all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), there is likewise nothing to be obtained. There is neither internal nor external, and no middle can be apprehended. This is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which, regarding all dharmas, is neither distracted nor possesses the wisdom of samādhi; this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, he is constantly intent upon the Great Vehicle; his wisdom is autonomous. His wisdom does not abide in permanence, nor does it abide in impermanence; he does not calculate suffering or non-suffering, pleasure or non-pleasure. His wisdom does not depend on 'mine' or 'not mine. This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it is characterized by non-apprehension and does not fall into inversion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, its wisdom is autonomous; it does not abide in the past, does not abide in the future, and does not abide in the present. It does not abide in the three times—that which is a place where wisdom does not exist. This is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: it is eternally non-apprehending and does not fall into inversion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, their wisdom does not arise from attachment to the desire realm, nor does it abide in the form realm, nor does it abide in the formless realm; rather, their wisdom is sovereign."

To fully know the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, yet to attain mastery over them while having nothing to be attained, and not falling into inversion—this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the mastery of wisdom; it does not coincide with worldly wisdom, nor does it abide in the wisdom of the deceased. It does not abide in the conditioned, nor in the unconditioned; it does not abide in the out-flowing, nor in the non-out-flowing. Within this wisdom of dharmas, it attains freedom."
To fully know mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom, without falling short;

to fully know conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, without falling short, yet without anything to be attained and without falling into inversion—this is the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The Sutra of Radiant Praise, Scroll Five.
The Sutra of Radiant Praise, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 14: The Vehicle of the Mahāyāna. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Fourteen, "The Vehicle of the Mahāyāna," the Venerable Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva mount the Mahāyāna?"
Pūrṇa said to Śāriputra: "O worthy one!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices this prajñāpāramitā, they mount the dānapāramitā yet do not apprehend the dānapāramitā; there is no bodhisattva, nor is there a recipient from whom anything is obtained, nor is there anything acquired. To mount the dānapāramitā in this manner is what is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

The *dāna-pāramitā*, the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, the *vīrya-pāramitā*, the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and the *prajñā-pāramitā*: when one mounts the *prajñā-pāramitā*, one does not apprehend the *prajñā-pāramitā*, nor does one apprehend the bodhisattva; there is nothing to be obtained. This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to mount the *prajñā-pāramitā* while having no attainment whatsoever.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not lose or abandon the mind that pursues *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), but immediately practices the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). His thoughts are non-thought and his actions are non-action; even regarding these various meanings, he attains nothing. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Mahāyāna."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not lose or neglect the mind that pursues the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path—within these principles as well, there is nothing to be apprehended. This is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Mahāyāna."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not lose or abandon the mind that pursues *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), nor the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*), or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). Regarding these meanings, they attain nothing at all; this is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Mahāyāna."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva discerns this:
that which is called a 'bodhisattva' is a conventional designation according to worldly usage; if one seeks for it, it cannot be found, nor does it arise."
That which is called "form" is merely a provisional designation;
that which are called "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" are also merely provisional designations—they cannot be apprehended and have no arising.
What are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are merely provisional designations; they cannot be apprehended and have no arising.
What are called forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are merely provisional designations; they cannot be apprehended and have no arising.

What are called the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path are merely provisional designations; they cannot be apprehended, nor do they arise.

What are called the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are merely provisional designations; they cannot be apprehended, nor do they arise.
What are called internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness are merely provisional designations; they cannot be apprehended and do not arise.
What are called the emptiness of all things, natural emptiness, and the natural emptiness of all things are merely provisional designations.

Furthermore, what are called the dharmas of the Tathāgata, the dharma of no-origination, and the realm of all dharmas—these dharmas are quiescent and reach the ultimate limit (*koṭi*). This ultimate limit, moreover, cannot be apprehended and does not arise.
That which is called the Buddha-way is something that can be awakened to; yet this Buddha-way is likewise unattainable and does not arise.
This is the Mahāyāna in which the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva rides.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, from the first moment they resolve their minds, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully possess these bodhisattva supernormal powers to transform and guide sentient beings. They travel from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to and serving the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they diligently draw near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, listening to the Dharma and seeking the Bodhisattva Vehicle."

That person, practicing the bodhisattva path within that vehicle, travels from one buddha-field to another, purifying buddha-lands and transforming sentient beings; yet they do not become attached to those buddha-fields, nor do they dwell in the state of non-duality where there is no perception of a person. Nevertheless, by the power of their own body, they constantly lead and benefit the multitudes for the sake of sentient beings.
What is meant by "for the sake of oneself" taking up [the Dharma], such that the mind never departs from this vehicle until one attains the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
having attained the wisdom of *sarvajñā*, one then turns the wheel of Dharma;
and having turned the wheel of Dharma, one thereby brings benefit to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world.
Thereupon, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, all together praised and proclaimed his voice, saying:
"A certain Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in a certain world, has mounted the Mahāyāna and attained the wisdom of sarvajñatā; having attained the wisdom of sarvajñatā, he now turns the wheel of Dharma."
"Thus, Śāriputra, it is by this that a bodhisattva mahāsattva mounts the Mahāyāna. Chapter Fifteen:
On Being Unbound The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifteen: On Being Unbound Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddha' refers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva being armored with the armor of great virtue.
What is meant by the 'saṃnāhasaṃnaddha' of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of the virtue of the precepts and practices the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, they are said to have donned the great saṃnāha-saṃnaddha.”

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; having donned the armor of inner emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā-saṃnāha*), the armor of outer emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā-saṃnāha*), the armor of the natural emptiness of all that exists (*sarva-dharma-prakṛti-śūnyatā-saṃnāha*), and the armor of the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna-saṃnāha*), he then illuminates the trichiliocosm with his radiance, and likewise the eight directions, above and below.

That great radiance pervaded everywhere, and furthermore, it was able to shake the trichiliocosm, reaching as far as the Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; likewise in all eight directions and above and below, there was nothing that did not surge and tremble.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of this radiance, abides in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and dons the great armor of the Mahāyāna. He transforms the trichiliocosm so that it becomes entirely of deep-blue lapis lazuli;
having thus transformed the trichiliocosm into deep-blue lapis lazuli, he then further transforms it into the form of a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*).

Having manifested the majestic image of a wheel-turning sage king, he is able to bestow extensively: food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to those without clothes, and incense to those without incense; he provides flowers, mixed perfumes, powdered incenses, vehicles, elephants, horses, servants, and attendants. Granting whatever people seek—be it houses for dwelling, the means of livelihood, or whatever else others desire—he causes them all to obtain what they require.
Food and drink, clothing, incense and flowers, elephants and horses, houses, and whatever else they may require, he gives to all people.
Once each has obtained what they need, he then expounds the Dharma for sentient beings, proclaiming the teachings in their full detail, and practices the six *pāramitās*.

When these various classes of beings hear the Dharma that is preached, they immediately follow its traces and practice the pāramitās, until they finally attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the great armor-clad resolve (*saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) of the Mahāyāna for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas!
"Subhūti, it is like this: suppose a wise illusionist and his skilled disciple were to create at a major crossroads the various occupations by which people make their living."

Why is this? Because it is the very nature of the arts of illusionists that they employ such techniques as these, providing countless sentient beings with whatever they lack: food and drink, clothing, incense and flowers, various ornaments, elephants and horses, and dwellings.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that illusionist actually give anything to those who are in need?
He replied, "No, O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said: “So it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, and the emptiness of both internal and external, as well as the emptiness of all that exists by its own nature—donning the saṃnāha-kavaca (armour of resolve)—and when they don the saṃnāha-kavaca of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, as well as the saṃnāha-saṃnāha (armour of the armour) of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), they manifest as a buddha-image and don the armour of great virtue. Its light shines universally throughout the trichiliocosm and reaches the buddha-fields of the east, the eight directions, above and below, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, pervading them all without exception.”

In each of the ten directions, Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges trembled in six ways; abiding in the perfection of giving with a great light, he provided whatever was requested by people—food and drink, clothing, incense and flowers, various ornaments, elephants and horses, houses, and the means of livelihood—even though these were bestowed through transformation, in the end nothing was actually given.
The multitude each came to receive what they needed, taking up the requisites for their livelihood;
yet there was neither giver nor receiver.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
These dharmas are likewise like an illusion; the illusion does not exist apart from dharmas.
This is the great armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), desiring to rescue and protect all sentient beings who take birth, he manifests once again as being born into the lineage of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

Once established in the position of a Wheel-Turning King, he immediately inspires sentient beings with the ten wholesome paths of action, and extensively expounds the sūtras for all beings—namely, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—so that he never allows them to depart from these principles of the Way, enabling them to reach peace and security until they attain the Buddha-way; this is called *saṃnāha* (the armor of resolve).

For example, Subhūti, suppose a master illusionist or a wise disciple were to manifest at a great crossroads an incalculable and immeasurable multitude of beings, and for the sake of these manifested beings, preach the Dharma, establishing them in the ten wholesome paths of action, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

What do you think, Subhūti? Are there many people who abide in the ten wholesome paths of action, as well as in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
He replied, “No, O God among Gods! “So it is, Subhūti!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva transforms and enlightens sentient beings, causing them to abide in the ten wholesome paths of action, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; yet, he does not even conceive of himself as one who exhorts or establishes sentient beings in these states.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
These so-called dharmas are likewise like an illusion; the illusion does not exist apart from dharmas.
Thus it is, Subhūti! This is the great armor-clad setting forth (*mahāyāna-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they exhort and transform sentient beings, establishing them in the perfection of patience.
What is meant by a bodhisattva dwelling in the perfection of patience?
He transforms all classes of sentient beings, establishing them in the dharma of the infinite perfection of patience. Thereupon, Subhūti,
from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of virtue equally and makes this vow:
"Even if all classes of sentient beings were to inflict blades and staves upon me, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not give rise to thoughts of anger or resentment for even a single moment;
furthermore, he should teach and transform all sentient beings so that they may establish themselves in this patience."
“Subhūti, it is as if, for example,
a skilled illusionist and his wise apprentice were to conjure up at a great crossroads countless, incalculable people, and then immediately beat them with clubs or strike and kill them with knives.”
"Would he then be subject to being struck or cut,
or suffer harm? He replied, "No, O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said, “So it is,
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), if anyone should inflict blades or staves upon his body, he endures them all.”
Furthermore, they transform sentient beings, causing them to establish themselves in this patience; yet there is neither one who strikes nor one who endures.
Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s donning of the great armor of the Mahāyāna in the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), exhorts and transforms all classes of sentient beings, causing them all to establish themselves in the perfection of vigor."
The Buddha said:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva establish sentient beings in the perfection of vigor?
In this regard, Subhūti!"

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a mind that reverently cultivates the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; yet he is without conceptualization of marks and without [discursive] exertion, while exhorting and inspiring sentient beings to practice that conduct.

For example, Subhūti! Suppose a master illusionist, or a wise disciple, were to manifest at a great crossroads countless and incalculable people, causing them to practice diligence and guard their body, speech, and mind; yet there would be no such people, no body, speech, or mind, and nothing that was practiced.

Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in the *vīrya-pāramitā*, they exhort and transform all beings to practice diligence; yet there is no mark of diligence and nothing practiced, nor do they establish the various classes of sentient beings in diligence through such exhortation. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s great vehicle armor (*mahāyāna-saṃnāha*) within the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
dwelling in the dhyānapāramitā, exhorts and transforms all classes of sentient beings through the dhyānapāramitā."
"What do you think, Subhūti?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the dhyānapāramitā, how does he dwell equally in all dharmas, such that all dharmas are undisturbed, and he does not perceive any confusion among dharmas?"

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to abide in this, they dwell in the groundless state regarding the dhyāna-pāramitā and other perfections, exhorting and assisting sentient beings in the Dharma of equality.

Those whom they transform and teach never deviate from or distance themselves from the teachings of all Buddhas, until they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet even upon attaining that Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is no one who has "arrived" at that Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

For example, suppose a skillful illusionist or a wise disciple were to manifest countless, incalculable people at a great crossroads and cause them all to practice dhyāna, such that their minds are concentrated and focused, yet there is neither concentration nor distraction.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva exhorts and transforms sentient beings, causing them to practice the equal Dharma, he does not perceive any dharma that possesses a concentrated mind or a distracted mind. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s Mahāyāna armor-clad vow of the dhyānapāramitā.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they develop and awaken all classes of beings and cause them all to dwell in the ultimate perfection of wisdom."
How does one abide in the prajñāpāramitā oneself and exhort and transform sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom?
It is thus, Subhūti: for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no dharma whatsoever, nor is there anything to be protected in that which is practiced.

Once this bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom, they likewise use this Dharma to transform and guide all beings, enabling them to cross over and attain liberation without any obstruction.

For example, it is like a skillful illusionist or a wise disciple who conjures up countless, incalculable people; though their wisdom and eloquence may distinguish many things, there is no wisdom therein, nor is there anything spoken.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is there anything that is spoken, or anything that is heard? He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! The Buddha said,
"This is the great armor-clad penetration (*saṃnāhasaṃnaddha*) of the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva dons the armor of the Mahāyāna,

he abides in the naturally occurring Dharma and transforms all sentient beings throughout as many Ganges-river sands as there are in the eastern direction, causing them all to practice the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā, while preaching the Dharma for them."
If sentient beings should hear these six pāramitās, they will never again be separated from the six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā) and from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it is thus for all throughout the ten directions.
Just as it is with the Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, so it is in all ten directions, entirely equal and without distinction. For example, Subhūti!

A skillful illusionist or a wise disciple might, at a great crossroads, conjure up countless and incalculable people who practice giving, morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; yet, in reality, there is no giving, no morality, no patience, no diligence, no single-mindedness, and no wisdom.
Thus it is, Subhūti! This is the great armor-clad resolve (*mahāyāna-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having attained the third stage (tribhūmi), reveres his own mind; regarding omniscience (sarvajñatā), he never gives rise to any divergent thoughts toward others, nor does he have anything to believe in or receive through hearing, yet he may transform people by establishing them in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);
or he may transform people by establishing them in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā); or he may transform people by establishing them in the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
In some cases, he transforms people by establishing them in the *vīrya-pāramitā*;
in some cases, he transforms people by establishing them in the *dhyāna-pāramitā*;
in some cases, he transforms people by establishing them in the *prajñā-pāramitā*; yet in transforming these people, he ultimately abides in non-abiding.
Among those who were not yet transformed, he transformed some individuals and established them in the four foundations of mindfulness;
he transformed some individuals and established them in the four right efforts;
he transformed some individuals and established them in the four bases of supernatural power.
He transforms some people, establishing them in the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
he transforms some people, establishing them in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or there are those whom he does not transform.
Some he transforms and establishes in the fruit of srotāpanna;
some he transforms and establishes in the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin;
some he transforms and establishes in the fruit of anāgāmin.
Some he transforms and establishes in the fruit of arhatship;
some he transforms and establishes in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood;
and some individuals cannot be transformed.
He establishes some persons in the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*), while others he does not yet convert.

There are immeasurable and incalculable classes of sentient beings whom he shall convert and establish in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), as well as the perfections of morality (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), vigor (*vīrya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);

in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold path (*mārgāṅga*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). He converts these immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings and establishes them in the wisdom of omniscience.
What do you think, Subhūti?
If one were to convert and transform countless people, each having their own destination, each having their own motivation, and each attaining liberation—[would that be much?]
"Would there be anything that arises or passes away?
He replied, "No, O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:

“In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the six pāramitās, brings about the transformation of others through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all the Buddha-dharmas, yet there is no destination and no one to be delivered—neither for those of the four paths nor for pratyekabuddhas—this is what is called the great armor-clad vow (saṃnāha-saṃnaddha) of the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, O God among Gods!
If I were to hear the Dharma and examine its meaning, I would regard the bodhisattva mahāsattva as no longer undertaking the *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha* (the donning of the armor)."
Why is this so? Because all natural marks arise from emptiness.
For this reason, O God among Gods!
All forms are empty of form; all sensations, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses are empty.
One observes that the eye is empty of the eye; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the mind.

One observes that the eighteen elements—the eye, forms, and visual consciousness; the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness; the nose, odors, and olfactory consciousness; the tongue, flavors, and gustatory consciousness; the body, tangibles, and tactile consciousness; and the mind, mental phenomena, and mental consciousness—are likewise all empty.

That which is practiced by the eye, and that which is practiced by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these practices of the six sense faculties are likewise all empty practices; everything is entirely empty, for the dharmas practiced are empty.
"O World-Honored One!
The *dānapāramitā* is also empty; the *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā* are likewise all entirely empty."
Examine that the internal is empty, and that internal emptiness itself is empty; it is non-existent.
Naturalness is also empty, and that emptiness itself is empty.

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty, and the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path are also empty.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also empty.
That which is called a bodhisattva is also empty, and the saṃnāha-saṃnāha (the armor of the great vow) is also empty.
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
For this reason, one should regard the bodhisattva mahāsattva as being without *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha* (armored with the great resolve).
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti, it is exactly as you have said."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is conditioned and uncreated, yet it is not uncreated, nor does it exist as a thing;
all sentient beings likewise are uncreated and do not exist as things."
For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dons the great armor of saṃnāha; yet there is nothing done, nor is there anything not done, nor is there anything that exists.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
For what reason is the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) neither something that acts, nor something that does not act, nor something that exists?”
Are these classes of sentient beings likewise without action, not without action, and non-existent?
And is it also thus with the saṃnāha-saṃnaddha (donning of the armor) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Where there is something to be done and something to be attained, there is something that arises.
Yet, sarvajñā (all-knowledge) neither has anything to be done, nor is it not without action, nor does it possess anything at all.”
These sentient beings likewise have no agent of action, nor do they lack action;
they possess nothing at all.
Why is this? Form has no creator, nor does it lack a creator.
There is neither any activity nor any doing.
Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is no creator; there is neither non-creation, nor any activity, nor any doing.
The eye neither creates nor does not create; it has no activity and no agency.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind likewise neither create nor do not create; they have no activity and no agency.
Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are neither created nor uncreated, neither active nor acting.

The eighteen elements and the six sense faculties, which through their habitual practice give rise to sensations of pain and pleasure, are likewise neither created nor uncreated, neither active nor acting.
Subhūti, the self likewise neither creates nor does not create; it has no activity and performs no action.
Furthermore, whatever is known or seen likewise neither creates nor does not create; it has no activity and performs no action.
For this reason, from beginning to end, there is no root or source to be found.
Sentient beings and dreams likewise have neither creation nor non-creation, neither activity nor action.
Why is this so? Because from beginning to end, there is no root or source, nor can any be found.
Like an echo, a reflection, the moon in water, a magical illusion, or a mirage, they neither create nor do not create; there is nothing produced and nothing enacted.
Why is this? Because from beginning to end, it has no root or source, nor can it be apprehended.
As for its inner emptiness, Subhūti!
There is neither creation nor non-creation, neither activity nor action;
the same is true for external emptiness.
That which exists, as well as natural emptiness, likewise has neither creation nor non-creation, neither activity nor action.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise neither created nor uncreated, neither practiced nor performed.
Why is this? Because, from beginning to end, there is no root source, nor can one be found.
That which has no origin, Subhūti!
There is neither creating nor non-creating, neither practicing nor performing;
there is no fundamental basis, and likewise no other distinct phenomena.
As for the seeds of phenomena, they abide within the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), wherein all phenomena are quiescent.
As for their fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), there is neither creation nor non-creation, neither activity nor action.
Why is this? Because from beginning to end, there is no root or source, nor can any be found.
That bodhisattva neither acts nor does not act; there is nothing they practice, nor anything they produce.
The wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and the wisdom of universal compassion are neither created nor uncreated; they have no activity and nothing that is performed. Why is this so?
Ultimately, from beginning to end, there is no root or source, nor can anything be apprehended.
That bodhisattva neither creates nor does not create; there is nothing they practice, nor is there anything they do.
The wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and the wisdom of universal compassion are neither created nor uncreated;
they have no activity and no agent. Why is this so?
Ultimately, from beginning to end, there is no root or source,
nor can any be found. For this reason, Subhūti,
there is nothing to be done.
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) neither performs any action nor does it not perform any action.
Sentient beings are likewise: they neither perform any action nor do they not perform any action.
It is for this reason, Subhūti, that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dons the great armor (*saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, Subhūti...
"One should observe that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is likewise no *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha* (donning of the armor) of the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
I shall explain the meaning of this analysis: in my analysis of the meaning, form is neither attached, nor bound, nor liberated;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither attached, nor bound, nor liberated.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Subhūti: "Is form unattached, unbound, and unliberated?
Are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness unattached, unbound, and unliberated?"
Subhūti said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "In this way, worthy one,
form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Purna further asked Subhuti:
"In what way is form without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation?"
“In what way are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness unattached,
unbound, and unliberated? Subhūti replied,
“Form is by its very nature unattached, unbound, and unliberated;”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are naturally without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is like an echo—without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an echo—without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is like a mirage; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like a mirage; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is like an illusion; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is like an illusion; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Past form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Future form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
future feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Present form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is without reality; it is neither attached to, nor bound, nor liberated.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without reality; they are neither attached to, nor bound, nor liberated.
Form is serene, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are serene, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is unarisen; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Punna! Form is wholesome, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wholesome, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is unwholesome; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unwholesome; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is indeterminate, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are indeterminate, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Form is not differentiated; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not differentiated; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Punna! Worldly form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
worldly feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Transcending worldly form, there is neither attachment, nor bondage, nor liberation;
transcending worldly sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is neither attachment, nor bondage, nor liberation.
Tainted and untainted form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
tainted and untainted feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Emptiness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The indistinct is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
All phenomena are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Non-existence is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Quiescence is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The *dānapāramitā* is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.

The perfection of giving, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Reaching the ultimate reality, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Reaching profound stillness, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Inner emptiness, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
External emptiness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
That which exists as natural emptiness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The four foundations of mindfulness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.

The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical eloquences, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Arising from emptiness, it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The Buddha-way is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
In training in the bodhisattva path, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Arising from emptiness, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Being quiescent and unarisen, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
That which is without basis is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Furthermore, that which is without basis is equal and without distinction, abiding in accordance with the Dharma, without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
That dharma of tranquil concentration is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
That which is its original limit reaches the unconditioned, being without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
That which arises without reality has no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
That which arises from emptiness and stillness has no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Thus it is, worthy Śāradvatīputra!
This is the perfection of non-attachment, non-bondage, and non-liberation of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge), the wisdom of non-origination, and the wisdom of universal compassion—all these superior practices are likewise without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Progressing further upward, one cultivates generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom.
Advancing further upward, there is neither attachment, nor bondage, nor liberation.
Advancing further upward until one abides in the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and the wisdom of universal compassion, there is neither attachment, nor bondage, nor liberation.
To transform and guide sentient beings, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
To adorn and purify Buddha-fields, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
To serve and attend upon the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Listening to and examining the sūtras, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Never being separated from the Buddhas, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Never losing the supernormal powers, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Not departing from the five faculties, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Not relinquishing dhāraṇī, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Not abandoning samādhi, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
In the Path, one gives rise to compassion; it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
The wheel of Dharma that is turned is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
"To transform and guide sentient beings so that they abide in the Three Vehicles, yet remain without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Subhūti said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"This is the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation."
To realize that all the dharmas of perfect enlightenment arise from emptiness, being quiescent, tranquil, and born from the non-arising— this, Pūrṇa,
is the Mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddha (the Great Armor) of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Chapter 16: On Samādhi. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Sixteen, "On Samādhi," the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One! O God among Gods!"
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s great vehicle armor (mahāyāna-saṃnāha)?
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s great vehicle?
For one who trains in the Great Vehicle, what is the vow and resolve regarding that vehicle?
"In what does the *yāna* abide, and from what is it produced?
Within the *yāna*, who is it that accomplishes the *yāna*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As Subhūti has asked: 'What is the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
The six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) constitute the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
What are the six?

They are the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
What is called the *dānapāramitā*?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva reveres and upholds the aspiration for the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and practices giving; he does not begrudge anything internal or external that he possesses, bestowing it upon sentient beings. Taking this as a firm foundation, he does not harbor enmity toward adversaries, and thus encourages and assists them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the *dānapāramitā* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
What is the *śīlapāramitā* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

In this regard, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva reveres and upholds the aspiration for *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), personally practicing the ten wholesome deeds, and further encourages others with these ten wholesome deeds so that they do not fall into perversity, yet without apprehending anything.
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), suffers no loss, does not fall into inversion, and has nothing to be attained.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, O God among Gods!"
"What is meant by the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill patience within his own person, teaches others to establish themselves in patience, does not fall into perversions, and likewise has nothing to be apprehended."
"This is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, O God among Gods!"
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s mind reveres and honors the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). He does not distance himself from the five *pāramitās*, and he teaches and transforms sentient beings through these five *pāramitās* without falling into inverted views, nor does he grasp at anything as obtainable."
"This is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti then asked the World-Honored One:
"Indeed, O God among Gods!"
"What is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s dhyānapāramitā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattva reveres and upholds the arousal of the mind directed toward the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). He himself constantly practices the dhyāna-samādhi through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), yet he does not follow after or give rise to [attachment to] that samādhi. Furthermore, he teaches others to study meditative concentration so that they do not fall into inversion and have nothing to be attained."
"This is the dhyānapāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Yes, O Devātideva!"
“What is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The bodhisattva mahāsattva reveres and pursues the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) that has been generated; they have no dependence upon any dharma, they contemplate all dharmas as fundamentally pure from the beginning, they do not fall into inversion, and they have nothing to be attained.”

By being unattached to all phenomena and by contemplating that all phenomena are fundamentally pure from the beginning, one uses these dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings; thus one does not fall into inversion, nor is there anything to be attained.
This is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; this is the mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva consists of:

inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of the great, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the pure, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of natural characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of the absence of emptiness itself, and the emptiness of that which is seen as non-existent.
What is meant by internal emptiness?
Internal phenomena refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
That which is called the "eye," and that which is seen by the eye, is also empty; it cannot be injured, nor can it be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
The ear and that which is heard by the ear are likewise empty; they cannot be injured, nor can they be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
The nose and that which is smelled by the nose are likewise empty; they cannot be injured, nor can they be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
That tongue, as well as the flavors tasted by that tongue, are likewise empty; they cannot be injured, nor can they be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
The body and that which is experienced by the body are likewise empty; they cannot be injured, nor can they be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
That which is the mind and its mental objects is likewise empty; it cannot be injured, nor can it be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
This is called internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
What is meant by external emptiness?
It refers to the dharmas spoken of as external: form, sound, fragrance, flavor, tangibility, and mental objects.
As for form, form itself is likewise empty; it cannot be injured, nor can it be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally pure.
These forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty; they cannot be harmed or destroyed, nor can they be produced through destruction.
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally pure.
What is meant by the emptiness of internal and external phenomena (*adhyātmabahirdhā-dharma-śūnyatā*)?
The six internal bases and the six external bases constitute the emptiness of internal and external phenomena (*adhyātmabahirdhā-dharma-śūnyatā*).
What is meant by the emptiness of external phenomena?
They cannot be injured, nor can they be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally pure.
Since these internal and external phenomena are entirely empty, they cannot be injured, nor can they be destroyed or brought into being.
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally pure.
This is what is meant by the emptiness of internal and external phenomena.
What is meant by the emptiness of emptiness?

It refers to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of that very emptiness; this is called the emptiness of emptiness.
What is meant by the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*)?

That which is called the east is empty; the south, west, north, southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, the zenith, and the nadir are all likewise entirely empty—incapable of being injured and incapable of being destroyed.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
What is meant by "truly wondrous emptiness"?
It is said to be that which is non-active (*wuwei*).
That which is non-active is empty even in its non-activity; it cannot be injured, nor can it be destroyed or brought into being. Why is this so?
Because it is fundamentally pure.
This is called the "wondrous emptiness of reality.
What is meant by the "emptiness of that which exists"?
All that is empty refers to the emptiness of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, which cannot be injured or destroyed. Why is this so?
This is because it is fundamentally pure.
What is meant by the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?

That which is called the emptiness of the unconditioned does not arise and does not cease; it is neither autonomous nor abiding anywhere, yet it exists as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is the emptiness of the unconditioned.
That which is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): this emptiness of the unconditioned cannot be injured nor can it be destroyed.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*).
What is meant by ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
Ultimate emptiness refers to that which has no discernible limit. Why is this so?
Because it is fundamentally pure.
This is called ultimate emptiness.
What is meant by vast and remote emptiness?
This means that one does not see anything coming, nor is there anything to be obtained. Why is this?
Because it is fundamentally pure.
This is called the vast and distant emptiness.
What is meant by non-discriminative emptiness?
Therein, there is no dharma that can be abandoned, nor is there anything in which to abide.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
This is what is meant by non-discriminative emptiness.
What is meant by "emptiness of primordial purity"?
It is the thorough understanding that all phenomena are primordially pure—whether conditioned or unconditioned—and that they are not created by śrāvakas nor created by pratyekabuddhas.
This is called the emptiness of original purity.
What is meant by the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

"All phenomena" refers to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; and the sensations of pleasure and pain arising from the contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with their respective objects.
Conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena—this is called the emptiness of all phenomena.
All phenomena are empty of their own nature; they cannot be harmed, nor can they be destroyed or produced.
Why is this so? Because they are fundamentally pure.
This is called the emptiness of all dharmas.
What is meant by the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

It is because the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is such that form has no characteristic of its own; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which cognizes birth and death—are likewise without characteristics. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; as well as all other eighteen kinds of conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena—these all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature.
What is meant by the emptiness of the unobtainable and non-existence?
It is that all phenomena are likewise unobtainable; they cannot be destroyed or harmed, nor can they be produced through destruction.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally pure.
This is called the emptiness of the unobtainable and non-existent.
What is meant by the emptiness of non-existence?
To search for any form or characteristic and find it unobtainable—
this is called the emptiness of non-existence.
What is meant by the emptiness of the unconditioned (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?
That which is without conjunction or combination is the unconditioned;
this is the emptiness of the unconditioned.
What is meant by the "emptiness of non-existence and spontaneity"?
That which is spontaneous has no conjunction.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence and spontaneity.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! That which exists is empty of existence.
That which does not exist is empty of non-existence."
That which is intrinsic is intrinsically empty.
That which exists for the sake of another is also empty because it exists for the sake of another.
What is meant by "the existent being empty of the existent"?
This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As for those five aggregates, whatever exists is empty of that very thing.
This is called "emptiness of whatever exists" (*yad-yad-asti-tat-tac-chūnyatā*).
What is meant by the emptiness of non-existence (abhāva-śūnyatā)?
It refers to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
That which is unconditioned is empty because it is unconditioned.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence within non-existence.
What is meant by the emptiness of nature within nature?
That which is empty has no marks, no activity, and nothing that can be perceived.
This is called emptiness by nature! What is meant by emptiness for the sake of another?

Even if a Tathāgata appears in the world, or if a Tathāgata does not appear, that Dharma remains eternally constant; because that Dharma-realm is also quiescent, it is without origin. That which is without origin is the ultimate limit (*koṭi*). This, with respect to that, is emptiness for the sake of another; this is what is meant by emptiness for the sake of another.
This, Subhūti, is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti:
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi!
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Real Seal (Sārāmudrā); furthermore, there is a samādhi named Lion’s Play (Siṃhavikrīḍita);
there is a samādhi named Good Moon (Bhadramāsa); there is a samādhi named Moon Banner Essence (Candradhvaja-koṭi); there is a samādhi named All... [omitted].
Beyond the Dharma, there is a samādhi named Contemplating the Summit; a samādhi named Discerning All Dharmas;
a samādhi named Banner of Realization; a samādhi named Vajra-like; a samādhi named Entering the Seal of the Dharma;
according to the Dan edition, there is a samādhi named King of Good Abiding, and a samādhi named Emitting...
There is a samādhi called Unassailable Light; there is a samādhi named King of Concentrated Mind;
there is a samādhi named Well-Abiding; there is a samādhi named Emitting Light; there is a samādhi named Power of Diligence; there is a samādhi named Equal Transcendence;
there is a samādhi named Discerning Accordance; there is a samādhi named Entering All Languages; and so forth.
There is a samādhi named Illuminating All Directions; there is a samādhi named Seal of Total Retention (Dhāraṇī-mudrā);
there is a samādhi named Unassailable; there is a samādhi named Equal Mastery over the Ocean-Seal of All Dharmas;
there is a samādhi named Pervading Space; there is a samādhi named Vajra Maṇḍala; and there is a samādhi named Surpassing All Jewels.
There is a samādhi named Illumination; there is a samādhi named Unblinking; there is a samādhi named Abiding in the Non-Ultimate;
there is a samādhi named Decisive Comprehension; there is a samādhi named Lamp of Stainless Radiance;
there is a samādhi named Immeasurable Light; there is a samādhi named Creation of Light; and there is a samādhi named Universal...
Oṣadhī, there is a samādhi named Pure Sovereignty (Vimalavikrāmin), a samādhi named Stainless Radiance (Vimalaprabha),
a samādhi named For the Sake of Enjoyment (Ratipratilabdha), a samādhi named Lamp of Wisdom (Prajñāpradīpa), a samādhi named Inexhaustible (Akṣaya),
a samādhi named Endowed with Majestic Power (Vaiśāradyasamanvāgata), a samādhi named Exhaustion and Elimination (Kṣayavyantībhāva), and a samādhi named...
There is no distinction; there is a samādhi named Opening and Penetration, a samādhi named Sun-Lamp Radiance,
a samādhi named Moon Free from Defilement, a samādhi named Pure Illumination, a samādhi named Shining Upon All,
a samādhi named Performing What Must Be Done, and a samādhi named Essence of Wisdom.
There is a samādhi named "Like a Vajra"; there is a samādhi named "Well-Established Resolve"; there is a samādhi named "Jewel Accumulation";
there is a samādhi named "Transcending the Dharma Seal"; there is a samādhi named "Dharma Pervasiveness";
there is a samādhi named "Supreme Delight"; there is a samādhi named "Crowning the Dharma"; and there is a samādhi named "That Which Breaks Through."

There is a samādhi called "Destruction," a samādhi called "Discernment of All Phrases," a samādhi called "Equal Formation of Syllables," a samādhi called "Detachment from Words," a samādhi called "Elimination of Conditions," a samādhi called "Detachment from Activity," a samādhi called "Non-activity," and a samādhi called "Practice Without Exhaustion."
There is a samādhi named Dispelling Darkness; there is a samādhi named Path of Practice; there is a samādhi named Immovability;
there is a samādhi named Transcending Realms; there is a samādhi named Resolving All Virtues;
there is a samādhi named Resolving the Abode; there is a samādhi named Pure Adorned Flower; and there is a samādhi named Awakening.
In the *manas-pada*, there is a samādhi named Immeasurable Lamp-Light; there is a samādhi named Equal to the Unequaled;
there is a samādhi named Transcending All Dharmas; there is a samādhi named Because of Severance;
there is a samādhi named Free from Action; there is a samādhi named Free from Abiding; and there is a samādhi named Single Adornment and Purity.

There is a samādhi named "Controlling Activities," a samādhi named "Single Purpose," a samādhi named "Restraining All Affairs," a samādhi named "Eliminating Weariness with All Deeds," a samādhi named "Entering the Convergence of Conditions,
Images, and Sounds," and a samādhi named "Liberation from Sound, Teaching, Text, and Speech."
There is a samādhi named Blazing Radiance; there is a samādhi named Adorned Purity of Marks;
there is a samādhi named Signlessness; there is a samādhi named Creating All Utensils; there is a samādhi named Indifference to All Suffering and Pleasure;
there is a samādhi named Inexhaustibility; and there is a samādhi named Dhāraṇī-Phrase.

There is a samādhi named "Protecting All That Is Right and Wrong," a samādhi named "Entering All Form and Formless Realms," a samādhi named "Silence and Severing Sound," a samādhi named "Stainless Radiance," a samādhi named "Riding the Firm Essence," a samādhi named "Stainless Full Moon," and a samādhi named "Great."
He is pure and adorned; he possesses a samādhi named Illumination of All Worlds,
a samādhi named Universal Radiance, a samādhi named Soaring Through Space, a samādhi named Equal Soaring,
a samādhi named Ultimate Absence of Blue and Absence of Delight, and a samādhi named Ultimate Abiding in the Rootless.
There is a samādhi called "serene when naming the body," a samādhi called "removing thoughts of space when speaking with the mouth," and a samādhi called "liberation from emptiness and formlessness.
These are the one hundred and ten concentrations of non-attachment!
"What is meant by the so-called Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
As for the state of concentration therein, it enters into all practices of all samādhis; this is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."
What is called the *bhūtakoṭīmudrā-samādhi*?
At that time, by means of this concentration, one seals all samādhis; this is called the *bhūtakoṭīmudrā-samādhi*.
What is called the *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one finds delight in all states of meditative concentration; this is called the Lion’s Delight Samādhi.
What is meant by the Good Moon Samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things are equal and non-existent; this is called the Samādhi of the Good Moon.
What is meant by the Samādhi of the Moon Banner’s Pinnacle?
Abiding in this concentration of the mental state of samādhi, one universally upholds the banners of all samādhis by means of this concentration; this is called the Moon-Banner-Essence Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi that Transcends All Dharmas?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things reach the state of equality; this is called the Samādhi of Transcending All Dharmas.
What is called the Samādhi of Contemplating the Summit?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one then beholds the summits of all samādhis and states of meditative concentration; this is called the Samādhi of Beholding the Summit (Kūṭadṛśa-samādhi).
What is meant by the Samādhi of Discerning the Dharma-realm (Dharmadhātu-vibhaṅga-samādhi)?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one is able to discern all realms of existence; this is called the Samādhi of Discerning the Dharma-realm.
What is called the Samādhi of the Banner of Resolute Understanding?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all states of concentration reach their ultimate culmination and uphold the banner; this is called the Samādhi of the Banner of Resolute Understanding.
What is meant by the Vajra Samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things are equal and nothing can destroy them; this is called the Vajra Samādhi.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Entering the Seal of the Dharma?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one immediately attains entry into the seal of all phenomena;
this is called the *dharmamudrā-samādhi*. What is called the *susthitārāja-samādhi*?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all dharmas are established by the King Samādhi; this is called the "Well-Established King Samādhi.
What is meant by the "Radiating Light Samādhi"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis radiate light; this is called the "Radiating Light Samādhi.
What is called the "Power of Diligence Samādhi"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, it is initiated by the power of diligence within all samādhis; this is called the *vīryabala-samādhi*.
What is the so-called *samatānugata-samādhi*?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis reach a state of equality; this is called the Samādhi of Equal Passage.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Accordant Entry into Instruction?
When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one universally enters into and accords with all sounds of intention; this is called the Samādhi of Accordance with Verbal Instruction.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Entering All Verbal Instructions?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, everything proceeds from the verbal instructions of samādhi; this is called the "Entrance into Verbal Instructions" samādhi.
What is meant by the "Illumination of All Directions" samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one illuminates all directions and states of meditative concentration; this is called the Samādhi of Illuminating All Directions.
What is meant by the Samādhi of the Seal of Total Retention (Dhāraṇī-mudrā)?
When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one holds the seals of all samādhis; this is called the *dhāraṇīmudrā-samādhi*.
What is meant by the *asaṃhārya-samādhi* (the samādhi that cannot be taken away)?
When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one immediately does not forget any state of meditative concentration; this is called the "Unassailable Samādhi" (Anācchedya-samādhi).
What is meant by the "Ocean-Seal Samādhi that Equally Governs All Dharmas" (Sarvadharmasamavasaraṇa-sāgaramudrā-samādhi)?

When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one performs impartial deeds and contemplates the gathering and equal governance [of all things]; this is called the Ocean Seal Samādhi of Equal Governance.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Pervading Space?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis pervade space without anything remaining uncovered; this is called the "Samādhi of Pervading Space.
What is meant by the "Vajra-Assembly Ground Samādhi"?
When abiding in this samādhi of mental concentration, one universally maintains all the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) for mental concentration;
