this is called the Vajra-bodhimaṇḍa Samādhi. What is called the Sarvaratnavijaya Samādhi?
When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one eliminates all dust and defilements; no desires can cause blemish. This is called the Samādhi of Surpassing All Jewels.
What is called the Samādhi of Illumination?

When one dwells in this concentration of the samādhi of abiding, one attains equality toward all things; thus, there is nothing that shines upon the various paths. This is called the Illumination Samādhi.
What is meant by the Unblinking Samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not seek after any phenomena within all the samādhis; this is called the *animiṣa* (unblinking) samādhi.
What is meant by the *anavasthita* (non-abiding) samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any phenomena as abiding within the three realms; this is called the Samādhi of Non-ultimate Abiding.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Decisive Comprehension?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, there is no mind and no thought regarding the destination of phenomena; this is called the Samādhi of Decisive Comprehension.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Stainless Radiance?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis mutually illuminate one another; this is called the "Stainless Radiance Samādhi" (vimalaprabhā-samādhi).
What is meant by the "Immeasurable Light Samādhi" (apramāṇābhā-samādhi)?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, its radiance illuminates everything without exception; this is called the Immeasurable Light Samādhi.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Creating the Light of One's Purpose?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, if one attains samādhi such that all states of meditative concentration emit light, this is called the "Light-Maker Samādhi.
What is the so-called "Universal Illumination Samādhi"?
When one attains this samādhi, all gates of samādhi spontaneously radiate light; this is called the Samādhi of Universal Illumination.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Governing All Purities?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one immediately attains the universal purity of all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi that Governs All Purities.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Stainless Radiance?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all defilements within the various samādhis are removed and completely reduced to ashes; this is called the "Stainless Radiance Samādhi" (Vimalaprabhā-samādhi).
What is meant by the "Delightful Samādhi" (Rati-samādhi)?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one then finds delight in all samādhis; this is called the "Samādhi of Delight.
What is meant by the "Samādhi of the Bright Lamp of Wisdom"?
When abiding in this state of meditative concentration, one illuminates all samādhis; this is called the Wisdom-Lamp Illumination Samādhi.
What is called the Inexhaustible Samādhi?

When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one finds that among all samādhis there is neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion, and furthermore, one does not perceive exhaustion or non-exhaustion; this is called the "Inexhaustible Samādhi."
What is called the "Samādhi of the Sentence of Majestic Power"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things are equalized, and a majestic, towering radiance shines forth afar; this is called the Samādhi of the Sentence of Majestic Power.
What is called the "Samādhi that Eliminates All Exhaustion"?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one sees that all samādhis are entirely inexhaustible; yet, seeing them as having no fundamental basis, there is nothing to be seen. This is called the Samādhi that Eliminates All Exhaustion.
What is called the *asamihita-samādhi*?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things are equal; there is no attachment and no recollection, no suffering or affliction, and no causal conditions. This is called the *asamihita-samādhi*.
What is called the Samādhi of Opening and Penetration?

When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any phenomena as being penetrated, nor does one perceive any inversion; this is called the Samādhi of Opening and Penetration.
What is called the *sūryapradīpa* (Sun-Lamp) Samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, all gates of samādhi are opened and radiant light is emitted; this is called the *sūryapradīpa* Samādhi.
What is called the *candrarocavimala* samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, one dispels darkness among all samādhis with light; this is called the *candrarocavimala* samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Pure Lamp-Light?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, it universally protects all four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) within all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of the Pure Lamp-Light.
What is called the samādhi of illuminating?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all gateways of samādhi are fully illuminated; this is called the samādhi of illuminating.
What is called the *kṛtavi* samādhi?

When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one proceeds toward the accomplishment of all that is to be done in all samādhis; furthermore, when the *kṛtavi* samādhi is established, one universally perceives the excellence of the wisdom of all samādhis. This is called the *kṛtavi* samādhi.
What is called the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*)?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are extinguished and eliminated, and one no longer perceives any suffering, affliction, or calamity; this is called the diamond-like samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Abiding Mind?
When one dwells in this concentrated state of mind, the mind does not waver, nor does it open or close; it does not illuminate, nor does it perceive anything arising;
nor does it think, "There is this mind."
This is called the Samādhi of the Abiding Mind.
What is called the Universal World Samādhi?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one universally perceives all samādhis and concentrations, such that there is nothing they do not illuminate; this is called the Universal World Samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of dwelling in good intention?
When one dwells in this state of mind, all samādhis are universally established.
What is called the jewel-accumulation (ratnakūṭa) samādhi?

When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one universally perceives all samādhis as being entirely composed of accumulated jewels; this is called the Jewel Accumulation Samādhi (*ratnakoṭi-samādhi*).
What is called the Supreme Dharma Seal Samādhi (*dharmamudrā-viśeṣa-samādhi*)?

When dwelling in this state of meditative concentration, one equalizes the seals of all phenomena; those who have not yet encountered the seal perceive them all as being sealed, and are able to bring them all to ultimate completion. This is called the Samādhi of the Supreme Dharma Seal.
What is called the Samādhi of the Equality of Dharmas?
When one abides in this state of concentration, one perceives neither the equality nor the ruggedness of all dharmas; this is called the Samādhi of the Equality of Dharmas.
What is called the Samādhi of Supreme Delight?
When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, one subdues all dharmas of worldly pleasure; this is called the Samādhi of Supreme Delight.
What is called the Samādhi of Surpassing the Pinnacle of All Dharmas?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one brings all dharmas to a state of perfect harmony and stability at their very pinnacle, and furthermore transcends all other samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Surpassing the Pinnacle of All Dharmas.
What is called the "Destruction-Removal Samādhi"?
When one abides in this state of mental concentration, it removes all samādhis and destroys all dharmas; this is called the Destruction-Removal Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of Discerning All Dharmas?
When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, one is able to discern all samādhis and clearly understand the phrases of all dharmas; this is called the Samādhi of Discerning All Dharmas.
What is called the Samādhi of Equal Formation of Syllables?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one discerns and clearly understands that the attainment of samādhi results in equal syllables; this is called the Samādhi of Equal Formation of Syllables.
What is called the samādhi of eliminating all words and letters?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, not a single word or letter is found within any of the samādhis; this is called the samādhi of eliminating all words and letters.
What is called the samādhi of severing causal conditions?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one severs all conditions for the various samādhis and is free from all disturbances; this is called the samādhi of severing causal conditions.
What is called the "non-action samādhi"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any dharma as having something to do, nor is there anything created; this is called the non-action samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of detachment from activity?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any phenomena as being produced through causes and conditions; this is called the samādhi of detachment from activity.
What is called the samādhi of non-finality in practice?
When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one does not attain the ultimate limit of the practice of any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of non-finality in practice.
What is called the "Samādhi that Eliminates All Darkness"?

When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis eliminate every form of darkness; it extinguishes all disturbances and brings about purity. This is called the Samādhi that Eliminates All Darkness.
What is called the Samādhi of Practicing All Phrases?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, one universally perceives the practices of all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Practicing All Phrases.
What is called the "Immovable Samādhi"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any of the samādhis as being subject to agitation; this is called the Immovable Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of Crossing All Realms?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis cross over all perversions and are likewise free from error, conforming to their true meaning; this is called the Samādhi of Crossing All Realms.
What is called the Samādhi of Discerning All Virtues?
When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, one definitively discerns all dharmas and understands the samādhis of sentient beings; this is called the Samādhi of Discerning All Virtues.
What is called the samādhi of ultimate abiding?
When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one seeks the fundamental source of the mind within all concentrations but cannot find it; this is called the samādhi of ultimate abiding.
What is called the *Vimalapuṣpavyūha* Samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, one attains all pure adornments of various flowers for all samādhis; this is called the *Vimalapuṣpavyūha* Samādhi.
What is called the *bodhyaṅga-pada-samādhi*?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one swiftly attains awakening of mind (*bodhyabhisamaya*) regarding all samādhis; this is called the *bodhyaṅga-pada-samādhi*.
What is called the Samādhi of Immeasurable Eloquence?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one immediately attains immeasurable eloquence and the analytical discernment that follows it; this is called the Samādhi of Immeasurable Eloquence.
What is called the Samādhi of Equality with the Unequaled?

When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one attains the Samādhi of Equality with the Unequaled within all samādhis; it can cause all that is erroneous to reach a state of equality. This is called the Samādhi of Equality with the Unequaled.
What is called the Samādhi that Transcends All Dharmas?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one is able to transcend all three realms; this is called the Samādhi that Transcends All Dharmas.
What is called the samādhi of severing all activities?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, one perceives that all dharmas and all samādhis are entirely severed; this is called the samādhi of severing all activities.
What is called the "samādhi of no-mind and non-destruction"?

When one dwells in this state of concentration, having already attained all samādhis, one realizes that all dharmas ultimately lead to decay and destruction; this is called the samādhi of no-mind and non-destruction.
What is called the "Samādhi of Non-Abiding"?
When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one does not perceive any place where phenomena abide; this is called the Samādhi of Non-Abiding.
What is called the Samādhi of Single Purity?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any phenomena as having duality; this is called the Samādhi of Single Purity.
What is called the samādhi of "governing all activities"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any causal conditions or destinies among all phenomena; this is called the samādhi of governing all activities.
What is called the Samādhi of Surpassing All Things?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all samādhis do not perceive two things, nor is there anything seen; this is called the Samādhi of Surpassing All Things.
What is called the "Samādhi of Eradicating All Existence and Severing the Faculties"?

When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one eradicates all phenomena within all samādhis and attains wisdom; wherever one enters, there is nothing encountered. This is called the Samādhi of Eradicating All Existence and Severing the Faculties.
What is called the samādhi of entering in accordance with all sounds?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not follow after the various sounds of samādhis; this is called the samādhi of entering in accordance with all sounds.
What is called the samādhi of transcending all words, letters, and sounds?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one completely transcends and is liberated from all conditioned phenomena, letters, and matters; furthermore, there is nothing perceived. This is called the samādhi of transcending all words, letters, and sounds.
What is called the Samādhi of Blazing Radiance?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, the light that universally illuminates and subdues shines forth intensely; this is called the Samādhi of Blazing Radiance.
What is called the Samādhi of Adorned Purity of All Marks?
When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one adorns all marks with merit; this is called the Samādhi of Adorned Purity of All Marks.
What is called the signless samādhi?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one never perceives any signs within any samādhi; this is called the signless samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of Universal Fulfillment?
When one dwells in this state of concentration, everything sought is universally and completely fulfilled; this is called the Samādhi of Universal Fulfillment.
What is called the concentration on the non-delight in suffering and ease?

When one dwells in this state of meditative absorption, one does not perceive any suffering or ease within all concentrations; this is called the concentration on the non-delight in suffering and ease.
What is called the "Samādhi of the Exhaustless"?
When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, there is neither exhaustion nor any object of perception within all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of the Exhaustless.
What is called the dhāraṇī-pada samādhi?
When one abides in this state of mental concentration, one upholds all matters pertaining to every samādhi; this is called the dhāraṇī-pada samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of protecting all that is correct and erroneous?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one never perceives correctness or error within any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of protecting all that is correct and erroneous.
What is called the "samādhi of the elimination of all sounds and forms, being without sounds and forms"?

When one dwells in this state of concentration, within all samādhis one perceives no sounds or forms whatsoever; there is forever an absence of sounds and forms. This is called the "samādhi of the elimination of all sounds and forms, being without sounds and forms."
What is called the "Samādhi of the Cessation of Sound"?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one perceives that all phenomena are without sound and without resonance; this is called the Samādhi of the Absence of Sound.
What is called the "Stainless Radiance Samādhi"?
When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, one does not perceive any defilements within the radiance of all samādhis; this is called the Stainless Radiance Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of Essential Mastery?

When one dwells in this state of mental concentration, one does not perceive any samādhis as being either essential or non-essential, or as being mastered or unmastered; this is called the Samādhi of Essential Mastery.
What is called the *pūrṇacandra-vimalaprabhā-samādhi*?

When one abides in this state of meditative concentration, all merits and blessings are equally fulfilled and perfected, just like the moon at its fullness on the fifteenth day; this is called the *pūrṇacandra-vimalaprabhā-samādhi*.
What is called the Samādhi of Great Adornment and Purity?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things are entirely equal, infinitely pure, and universally complete with adornments; this is called the Samādhi of Great Adornment and Purity.
What is called the Samādhi of Universally Illuminating the World?
When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, all things are equalized and one is able to illuminate all dharmas; this is called the Samādhi of Universally Illuminating the World.
What is called the Samādhi of Universal Composure?
When one abides in this samādhi, all other states of concentration are neither disturbed nor attained as a single-pointed mind; this is called the Samādhi of Universal Composure.
What is called the Samādhi of Controlling Emptiness?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one equally controls all phenomena that are not conducive to joy and causes them to attain joy; this is called the Samādhi of Controlling Emptiness.
What is called the "Samādhi of the Equality of the Emptiness of Sarvajñatā"?

When one dwells in this state of concentration, regarding all matters of equality within the governance [of the mind], there is nothing further to be governed; this is called the Samādhi of the Equality of the Emptiness of Sarvajñatā.
What is called the "Samādhi of Ultimate Non-Blueness and Absence of Pleasure"?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one does not apprehend names or designations, nor is there anything to be attained; this is called the Samādhi of Ultimate Non-Blueness and Absence of Pleasure.
What is meant by dwelling in the samādhi of the rootless and mindless?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, one abides within all samādhis and universally enters the rootless, seeking nothing further; this is called dwelling in the samādhi of the rootless and mindless.
What is called the samādhi of composure at the time of the body?

When one dwells in this state of meditative concentration, within all samādhis there is ultimately nothing to be attained and no perception of a body; this is called the samādhi of composure at the time of the body.
What is called the "samādhi of the destruction and removal of the thought of space at the time of verbal expression"?

When one abides in this state of concentration, all samādhis cannot be reached through the destination of verbal expression; this is called the "samādhi of the destruction and removal of the thought of space at the time of verbal expression."
What is called the "liberation from emptiness and formlessness samādhi"?

When one abides in this state of concentration, one attains emptiness; all phenomena are unconditioned, innumerable, and quiescent. This is called the liberation from emptiness and formlessness samādhi.
"Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 17: The Chapter on Contemplation. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on Contemplation.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
Internally observing the body, one does not associate with the body, nor does one conceptualize it, nor does one apprehend the body."
Observing the external body, he does not identify with it; he neither conceptualizes it nor apprehends a body, and thus calmly and serenely masters his mind.
Observing the world’s ignorance, sorrow, and distress, he internally contemplates sensations and those mental phenomena, and thus calmly and serenely masters his mind.

Beholding the ignorance and sorrowful distress in the world, he contemplates external sensations; he does not dwell together with those sensations, nor does he give rise to thoughts of them, nor does he grasp at a body.
Contemplating internal mental formations, one does not associate with them; there is no perception of them, nor are they apprehended.
Contemplating external mental formations, one does not associate with them; there is no perception of them, nor are they apprehended.
Contemplating internal phenomena, one does not dwell together with them, nor is there any perception of phenomena, nor is any phenomenon apprehended.
Contemplating external phenomena, one does not dwell together with them, nor is there any recollection of phenomena, nor is any phenomenon apprehended.
Thereupon, he remains tranquil, disciplining his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance and sorrow.
What, Subhūti, is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing internal contemplation of the body?

Regarding this bodhisattva mahāsattva, he knows the movements of the mind—whether it is currently abiding or has already abided; he also knows whether it is currently seated or will sit; he likewise knows whether it is currently walking or lying down, or will walk or lie down. He knows all things exactly as they correspond to the body’s state of abiding, its intentions, and its inclinations.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body.
Therein, he calmly and skillfully governs his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, grief, and distress. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva moves to and fro with composure, observing and looking about without abruptness or violence; whether advancing or halting, bending or stretching, putting on robes or holding the alms bowl, eating, drinking, sleeping, or resting, he follows the conduct prescribed by the discipline in his coming and going, sitting, rising, lying down, or waking. In whatever he speaks, he always maintains a steady and deliberate manner; he delights in dwelling in seclusion, and his mind does not wander in pursuit of external things.
This, Subhūti, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates the internal body and finds it ungraspable. Furthermore, Subhūti:
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a single-minded focus, observes the inhalation and exhalation; he fully knows whether the breath is long or short;
he fully knows whether the mental breath is near or far;
and he fully knows whether the mental breath is slow or rapid.
He knows the mind’s breaths when they are abrupt and violent, as well as when they are gentle and mild.
It is, for example, like a wheel-turning sage king who knows the length, breadth, and extent of the land;
or like a potter making vessels who knows their size, depth, and shallowness.
Thus it is, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the inhalation and exhalation of the breath—its length and brevity, its slowness and speed, its rigidity and flexibility.
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates his internal body, knowing its composure and tranquility, and disciplines his mind so that it accords with the teaching of the Dharma.
This, Subhūti, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva internally contemplates the body and disciplines the mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow,
and distress. "Furthermore, Subhūti," [he said].
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates his own body as consisting of four elements: this present body possesses the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.

For example, it is like a butcher who, wielding a sharp knife, slaughters an ox or a beast and dissects it into four parts; once it has been divided into four parts, whether sitting or standing and examining it, there is no ox, for it was merely a synthesis of causes and conditions.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates this body of his, seeing that within this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe their own internal body, yet they do not perceive a body, nor do they apprehend anything. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva examines his own body from head to foot, seeing that it is filled with the physical form, hair, marrow, and brain—all thoroughly replete with foulness and impurity.

Those who possess this body have hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, sinews, veins, bones, joints, intestines, mesentery, abdomen, liver, lungs, heart, kidneys, the five viscera, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, mucus, saliva, filth, impurities, excrement, and urine.
For example, it is like a farmer who places various kinds of grain—sesame, rice, millet, beans, barley, wheat, and unhusked paddy—in a sack or vessel.

A person with clear vision would write them down, place them on the ground, and distinguish them, knowing: "This is sesame oil; this is non-glutinous rice; these are beans and millet; this is unhusked paddy."

In this way, Subhūti, this present body of a bodhisattva mahāsattva— from the feet to the head— consists of hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, sinews, veins, bones, joints, intestines, stomach, abdomen, liver, lungs, heart, kidneys, the five viscera, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, snot, saliva, filth, impurities, excrement, and urine.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva internally contemplates his own body and disciplines his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, grief, and distress, yet finds nothing therein to be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body as it encounters cold and heat, whether its life ends after one day, or three days, four days, or five days, the body becomes bloated, its color turns bluish, and it becomes putrid and rotten with pus and blood flowing out; considering such a body, one realizes that it cannot escape the nature of impermanence."
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates his own internal body!
He knows it to be tranquil and composed; he disciplines his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, grief, and distress, yet there is nothing obtained and nothing seen.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates how human life ends, encountering cold and heat, scorched by the sun, and buffeted by the wind; when death arrives on the first day, or the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, [the corpse] is devoured by crows and ravens, and by foxes, wolves, bears, brown bears, tigers, leopards, owls, hawks, and dogs; and countless worms emerge from its body and devour its flesh."
That person examines for themselves the places where their body wanders and observes that phenomena have no permanence; they are subject to dispersion and separation, and none can escape this.
Internally observing the body and disciplining the mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow, and distress, they likewise perceive nothing therein.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having perceived that the body is impermanent, sees it beset by cold and heat, scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, bloated, livid, and swollen, being devoured by birds and beasts, a foul-smelling and impure place.

Returning to observe one's own body, one should likewise do so: one should discipline the mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow, and distress, such that there is neither anything to be acquired nor anything to be seen.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body after death: it encounters cold and heat, being scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind; the bones and joints are linked together like an interlocking lattice, smeared with flesh and drenched in blood, bound by tendons, wrapped in skin, and covered by hide."
He observes his own body, harmonizing and stabilizing his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow, and distress;
therein, he neither attains anything nor perceives anything. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Suppose a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a person after their death, where only the white bones remain linked together by veins, skin, flesh, sinews, and marrow; he then observes them:
"The nature of this physical body is such that it must disperse and separate; this is not a permanent phenomenon, and there is no escaping it."

"In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body and composes his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, grief, and distress; yet he neither attains anything therein nor perceives anything."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the marrow, sinews, and bones—crushed, broken, scattered, and reduced to a state identical with the earth.
He contemplates it in this way:"
"This present body is of such a nature.
Thus he observes the body within himself, and regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow, and distress, he neither attains anything nor perceives anything therein.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose one were to see bones scattered upon the ground, with the bones of the feet in one place and those of the knees, shins, neck, spine, ribs, and skull each in a different location. One would then observe them, thinking:
'The nature of this body is such; its hands and feet are dispersed and separated. This is an impermanent phenomenon; there is no escape from it.'"
"Internally contemplating his own body, he composes and stabilizes his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow, and distress;
therein, he neither attains anything nor perceives anything. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva then contemplates the body: how, long after death has come, the bones are scattered upon the ground, having accumulated for years and for incalculable, immeasurable eons; how the blue bones are shattered and broken, mingled with dust and soil:
"Now this physical frame is of such a nature—dispersed and separated; this is a non-eternal dharma, from which there is no escape."

"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva internally contemplates his own body, regulating and stabilizing his mind regarding the matters of worldly ignorance, sorrow, and distress; therein, there is nothing to be apprehended and nothing to be perceived."
The same applies to the contemplation of sensation, perception, and mental formations.

For those who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], one employs the contemplation of impermanence to guide them forward; gradually entering into emptiness, they come to know that there is no fundamental basis.

For those whose resolve has reached maturity, one contemplates the internal and external body and finds no body; one contemplates internal and external perceptions and finds no perception; one contemplates internal and external phenomena and finds no phenomenon. There is neither object of contemplation nor thing seen. The Path does not depart from the mundane, and the mundane does not depart from the Path; both are empty, and there is nothing to be attained.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna, there are the four right efforts (*catur-samyakprahāṇa*).
What are the four right efforts?
Thereupon, when various evils and unwholesome dharmas have not yet arisen, or should they arise, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva restrains them so that they do not take birth;

with diligent vigor, he governs the root of his mind to sever all blemishes. As for all evil, unwholesome, and unrighteous matters, as soon as they arise, he immediately cuts them off; with diligent vigor, he self-governs his mind to bring about impartial severance.
If various roots of wholesome virtue should arise, and if he wishes to cultivate them, he diligently applies vigor to rescue and govern his mind, attaining impartial liberation.

Giving rise to wholesome dharmas within the heart, dwelling firmly without loss, contemplating them with fullness, and causing them to be extensively and universally prepared so that joy increases ever further; with earnest diligence, one rescues and gathers the mind, attaining impartial liberation.
There is something attained, yet there is nothing attained,
nor is there anything seen. Subhūti,
this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva!
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Mahāyāna, it refers to the five faculties:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom."
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, wherein there is both attainment and non-attainment, as well as nothing to be acquired.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to the five powers. What are the five powers?
They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of intention, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
These are the five powers of the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they involve both attainment and non-attainment, and likewise no acquisition whatsoever. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to the seven factors of enlightenment.
What are the seven factors of enlightenment? In this regard, Subhūti:

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva single-mindedly cultivates the mental application of reflection, relying upon tranquility, being free from desire, and having no basis for attachment; when he eliminates contention and relinquishes all dharmas—this is called the mental application of reflection.

There is the awakening factor of diligence which, being based on tranquility, is free from craving and has no dependence; it eliminates contention and relinquishes all phenomena—this is called the awakening factor of diligence.

Furthermore, practicing the awakening factor of joy, practicing the awakening factor of faith, practicing the awakening factor of tranquility, practicing the awakening factor of concentration, and practicing the awakening factor of discernment; relying upon stillness, being free from desire, having no basis for attachment, eliminating contention, and relinquishing all dharmas—this is called the Mahāyāna practice of the seven factors of awakening by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
There is neither attainment nor non-attainment,
nor is there anything acquired. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva refers to the eightfold noble path."
What are the eight?

Right view, right mindfulness, right speech, right livelihood, right action, right effort, right intention, and right concentration—these are the eight factors for practicing the Dharma of the noble ones.
To have nothing attained and yet no non-attainment, and likewise nothing acquired—this is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to the three types of samādhi.
What are these three?
They are the emptiness samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of emptiness?

Since the dharmas of characteristics are empty, emptiness is a gate of liberation; that which is signless is likewise a gate of liberation, for one who practices it has nothing to practice—this is the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
This, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Having attained this, there is neither anything obtained nor anything acquired.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva should be distinguished by one who understands what has been practiced, who decisively brings it to cessation and extinction, who perceives the path, who knows that which is exhausted, and who knows that which does not arise."
To thoroughly understand all phenomena and discern their selflessness;
to thoroughly understand the nature of gentleness and ultimate cessation; and to know one's own mind and the minds of others—this is called wisdom.
What is meant by "discernment"?
To know suffering as suffering, to know its non-origination, and its non-arising—this is called discerning suffering.
What is meant by "thoroughly understanding what has been practiced"?
It means to eliminate what has been practiced so that it does not arise again.
What is meant by "decisive eradication"?
It means that suffering has already ceased, such that its root is no longer present.
What is awakening through the path?
It refers to the Eightfold Path of the noble ones.
What is meant by knowing that which is to be exhausted?
It refers to the cessation of lust, anger, and delusion.
What is meant by "knowing that nothing arises"?
It refers to the wisdom that nothing arises from anywhere.
What is meant by "clearly understanding the wisdom of phenomena"?
It means that regarding the offenses and merits produced within the five aggregates, the severance [of attachment] constitutes wisdom.
What is meant by "discerning non-self"?
That is to say: form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not mine;
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are not mine.

Visual consciousness of forms, auditory consciousness of sounds, olfactory consciousness of fragrances, gustatory consciousness of flavors, tactile consciousness of tangibles, and mental consciousness of phenomena—these, too, do not belong to me.
What is meant by "clearly understanding the matter of gentleness at the time of death"?
There is much to be sighed over and much to be initiated.
What is meant by "knowing one's own mind"?
It means knowing the primordial source from antiquity.
What is meant by "knowing the minds of others"?
It is the ability to discern the thoughts and intentions within the minds of other sentient beings.
What is meant by "the mind according to wisdom"?
This refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna); this is called the mind that accords with wisdom as it is.
Having attained it, there is thus neither anything to be attained nor anything to be acquired.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have three faculties:
the faculty of distinct persons, the distinct faculty, and the separate faculty."
What is meant by "the faculties of other persons"?

It refers to those practitioners who have not yet attained the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of intention, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom in their state of equality.
What is meant by "distinct faculties"?

For a practitioner who possesses no distinct faith—the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of intention, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—this is called having distinct faculties.
What is meant by the distinct faculties?

It refers to those who, though not yet learned masters, have conceived the great resolve—namely, the pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas—and possess the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of intention, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom!
This is called the Mahāyāna of the distinct faculties of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
That which is attained is also non-attainment and there is nothing to be acquired. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to the samādhi of equality.
It comprises three aspects:
the samādhi with perception and with mental formation, the samādhi without perception but with mental formation, and the samādhi without perception and without mental formation.
What is called the concentration with perception and mental formation?

It is the liberation from all desires, the stilling and removal of all evil and unwholesome states; possessing perception and mental formation, one dwells in the foremost tranquility. This is called the concentration with perception and mental formation.
What is called the concentration of non-conceptualization with activity?

It refers to the state where within the mind there is no conceptualization yet there is activity; furthermore, there is no attachment up to the second stage of tranquility, nor is there anything internal or external. This is called the concentration of non-conceptualization with activity.
What is called the samādhi of non-perception and non-activity?

It transcends the second and third levels of tranquility; it passes beyond the concentration of immeasurable wisdom; it surpasses the suitability of immeasurable consciousness-wisdom; it exceeds the concentration of immeasurable non-perception-wisdom; and it transcends the concentration of immeasurable neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called non-perception and non-activity.
Subhūti, this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
as for the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, they should practice the ten recollections.
What are the ten recollections?

They are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Noble Sangha, recollection of the precepts, recollection of generosity, recollection of the devas, recollection of tranquility, recollection of non-arising, recollection of the contemplation of the body, and recollection of the inevitability of death; these are the ten recollections.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
there is both that which is attained and that which is not attained, and likewise nothing that is acquired. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva refers to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the four immeasurables, the eight gates of liberation, and the meditative concentrations on flavors never before attained; this, Subhūti, is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
That which is attained is also non-attainment and non-acquisition. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to the ten powers of the Tathāgata."
What are the ten powers? They are:
knowing the possible and the impossible regarding others and the various classes of sentient beings; knowing the finite and the infinite regarding their respective spheres;

and knowing with complete certainty the causes and conditions of the past, future, and present, as well as the spheres of conduct involving transgressions and merits, and the corresponding retributions thereof.
Just as he thoroughly knows that there are various kinds of people in the world whose natures differ;
and just as he thoroughly knows that other sentient beings have various kinds of minds, each with different preferences.
Just as one thoroughly knows the fundamental dispositions and destinies of others, how their roots and ends differ from one another;
so too does one thoroughly know the ultimate destinations of the beginnings and endings of all beings within the five realms of existence.

As he knows thoroughly and completely, he understands the minds of those who practice among the multitudes—their faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), one-pointedness of mind, doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), meditative absorptions (*samādhi-samāpatti*), as well as their fetters, enmities, and disputes—and is able to discern them with wisdom.
As he thoroughly and completely knows, it is immeasurable and tranquil.
He fully cognizes the events of countless billions of kalpas in the past.
He cognizes the locations of countless billions of kalpas in the past.
Wandering and dwelling among sentient beings, he observes where they ultimately go after their death;
with the eye of the Way, he penetrates and beholds all Buddha-fields in the ten directions—
the cycle of birth and death in the five realms, as well as good and evil, calamity and fortune, arising and ceasing, and beginning and end.

Having thoroughly and fully understood, his outflows are exhausted; he is free from defilement and has transcended conceptualization. Through wisdom, he is liberated from present formations; by means of his own supernormal powers, he realizes all conditioned phenomena. Birth and death have been severed; he proclaims the holy life accomplished and knows that those yet to cross over have been saved.
This, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
there is something attained, yet there is nothing attained, and there is nothing acquired.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four fearlessnesses.
What are the four fearlessnesses?

Now that I have already attained the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), should there be any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, humans, or even those of other heavens or other awakenings who come seeking to debate and find fault with the Buddha, claiming that I have not achieved Perfect Enlightenment and that no auspicious signs (prātihārya) are seen—should anyone dare to conceive such a thought regarding the Tathāgata!
He does not dare to give rise to a single thought; therefore, the Buddha’s conduct is peaceful and secure, free from difficulty and free from fear.

With courageous and heroic practice, he has attained non-attachment and utters the lion’s roar as a teacher for others, preaching and analyzing the pure Wheel of Dharma. Among śramaṇas, brahmins, the devas of the celestial palaces, Māra, and the Brahmās—throughout the heavens and the world—none can equal him in the meaning of the Path and its Dharma. All his outflows are exhausted; there is no beginning and no end.

Should any śramaṇa, brahmin, deity, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the heavens or the world seek to find fault with the Buddha, claiming that this is not so, it is because their outflows (āsravas) have not yet been exhausted.
Because he perceives no one at all who seeks to find fault with his resolve, the Buddha dwells in peace and security, free from fear, and thus roars the lion’s roar for the sake of the multitude.
He fully knows the internal dharmas; there is neither internal nor external, and he perceives no self.

Should śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone in the heavens or the world seek to find fault with the Buddha, claiming that it is not so, they do not understand the internal Dharma and falsely reckon that there is a self.
Since he never perceives anyone who has resolved to seek out his faults, the Buddha remains secure and free from fear, and thus he lets out the lion’s roar for the sake of all beings.

He expounds upon the noble ones so that those who do not understand may understand, those who have not attained may attain, and those who lack a vehicle may find one; through this equality, he universally eliminates suffering and affliction, such that no one can ever succeed in finding fault with the Buddha.

Because they uphold the Dharma, they do not violate the principles of the Way; with courage, fearlessness, and intrepidity, they expound the pure Wheel of Dharma for others and let out the lion’s roar.
Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
there is both attainment and non-attainment, and likewise nothing that is acquired.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four analytical eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*).
What are the four? They are:"
The first is the analysis of meaning; the second is the analysis of phenomena; the third is the analysis of the points of reliance; the fourth is the analysis of eloquence.
These, Subhūti, are called [the four analytical knowledges].

The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva involves both that which is apprehended and that which is not apprehended, and likewise that which is acquired and that which is not acquired. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
What are these eighteen?
First, the Tathāgata has no defects or shortcomings.
What he speaks is timely; his mind is free from deficiency, free from forgetfulness, free from manifold perceptions, free from lack of concentration, and free from lack of discernment.
In the discernment of what is observed, there is nothing to be delighted in;
diligence is severed yet not lost, and ultimately there is no loss of intent.
Wisdom is undiminished and liberation is without deficiency.
His transcendental knowledge and vision do not diminish.
There is no matter concerning the bodies of all beings that he does not penetrate;
there is no speech uttered by any mouth that he does not understand, causing each person to attain their proper place.
All that is conceived by the mind, he fully knows its source through his wisdom-mind.
Furthermore, he knows the events of past incalculable and infinite eons, seeing them all with his wisdom.
Furthermore, he knows the events of incalculable and infinite future eons, seeing them all with his wisdom.
He also knows the events of incalculable and infinite present eons, seeing them all with his wisdom.
This, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
there is something attained, yet there is nothing attained, and there is nothing acquired.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva refers to the gateways of dhāraṇī.
What are these so-called gateways of dhāraṇī?"
All letters and so forth are equal in what they express; they are the gateway of letters and that which enters through letters.
What is meant by the gateway of letters and the gateway of the causes and conditions for entering through letters?
All phenomena, being of the past, have likewise no arising.
That which acts as the gateway is the gateway of *ra*; that phenomena are free from all defilements is the gateway of *pa*; and the discernment of all meanings is the gateway of *ca*.
To attain the practice of all dharmas, yet to neither obtain anything nor perish, and to neither give rise to anything—this is that gate.
All dharmas are free from all names and words; reckoning their fundamental purity, they are unattainable—this is the gate of "La.
They completely transcend all worldly dharmas—affection, retribution, and causal conditions—this is the gate of "Da."
All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; the severance of existence and non-existence is the gate of *pa*.
Fully unraveling the knots by which all dharmas are bound is the gate of *ṭha*.
To burn away all phenomena and attain purity is the gateway of *sha*.
That all phenomena are without obstruction and that no things are grasped is the gateway of *huo*.
To sever all sounds, phrases, tracks, and destinations of all phenomena is the gateway of multiplicity.
That all phenomena are without origin and cannot be shaken is the gateway of calculation.
That all dharmas do not arise is the gateway of *ṭha*.
That all dharmas reach the ultimate is the gateway of *a*.
That all that is to be performed among all dharmas is fully attained is the gateway of *sa*.
That all dharmas have already been attained at their proper time and are universally unobstructed is the gateway of *ma*.
To understand that all dharmas arise from the self (*ātman*) is the gateway of *ka*.
That all dharmas attain protection is the gateway of *da*.
That all dharmas attain the locus of all dharmas is the gateway of *ja*.
That all dharmas do not arise is the gateway of *pa*.
That all dharmas do not arise is the gateway of *ta-ha*.
That all dharmas and all seeds do not arise in assembly is the gateway of *śa*.
That all dharmas are quiescent and do not arise is the gateway of *kha*.
That all dharmas are like empty space and are without production is the gateway of *kha*.
That all dharmas are utterly extinguished and unobtainable is the gate of *śīta*.
That all dharmas are firmly established in their place, immovable, and likewise unobtainable is the gate of *ṣṭhā*.
That the wisdom of all phenomena is unattainable is the gate of *ṭha-kha*.
That all phenomena are attained as that which is sustained is the gate of *phi-ha*.
That all dharmas have attained tranquility is the gate of *cha*.
That all dharmas have already been incinerated is the gate of *na*.
That all dharmas are without action is the gate of *śapa*.
To attain firm faith in all dharmas is the gateway of *ja*.
To bring all dharmas to complete cessation is the gateway of *kha*.
To reach the locus of the numerical cycle of all dharmas is the gateway of *ṭa*.
That all dharmas, having a place of abiding, attain non-abiding—this is the gate of Na.
That all dharmas neither come nor go, neither stand nor sit nor lie nor sleep, and are without response or non-response, without thought or non-thought—this is the gate of Pha.
That all dharmas cannot be proclaimed is the gateway of Śika.
That all dharmas do not obtain the five aggregates is the gateway of Ts’a.
That all dharmas do not obtain other thoughts is the gateway of It’a.
To relinquish all dharmas without anything to be attained is the gate of *i-ta*.
That all dharmas have no location where they may be found is the gate of *ṭha*.

All dharmas, having reached their ultimate limit and exhausted their locus, are without birth or death, without existence or non-existence, and without action; they strip away the discourse of words and sounds.
Why is this? Because one is weary of all obstructions;
it is without "that" and without name, without location and without what can be spoken of; it cannot be apprehended, it cannot be described, it cannot be exhausted, and it cannot be seen.
For example, Subhūti, just as space is empty and void, so too are all dharmas entirely like this.
This, Subhūti, is what it means.
The causes and conditions for entering into dhāraṇī consist of the analytical discernment of syllables.

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who understand all these causes and conditions and the skillful means of analyzing syllables, they will no longer be attached to sounds or verbal expressions, and they will be able to sequentially comprehend the ultimate destination of all phenomena.
18. Chapter on the Ten Abodes: The Eighteenth Chapter on the Ten Abodes of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "As you have said:
'What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being one who has set out in the Mahāyāna?'"
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās and enters the stages of the path (mārgabhūmi).
How does a bodhisattva enter the stages of the path?"
Entering into all dharmas, they neither come nor go; there is no departing and no destruction.
All dharmas have no place that can be known and are devoid of conceptualization; though they traverse the ten stages of the path, they do not perceive those stages as "stages of the path."
What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing the ten stages of the path?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the first dwelling, should perform ten things. What are these ten?
He cultivates his mental disposition so that it is not inverted;
he cultivates compassion so as to eliminate all conceptualizations;
and he maintains equanimity toward sentient beings while not perceiving them as sentient beings.
In performing acts of giving, there is no distinction between the giver and the recipient;
in honoring spiritual friends, there is no arrogance or contempt;
and in making the seeking of the Dharma one's vocation, there is nothing to be attained.
Diligently leaving home to study without any craving or longing;
seeking the Buddha-body without conceptualizing its marks and signs;
and expounding the Dharma-activities without harboring any expectations regarding sentient beings.
To cast aside arrogance so as to have no attachment to any phenomena,
and for whatever one speaks to be characterized by utmost sincerity—
these are the ten matters.
Subhūti! This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the first stage of the path. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the second stage, they should practice eight dharmas.
What are these eight?
Their precepts are pure and characterized by constancy;
They are able to recognize and repay kindness;
they abide in the power of patience;
and they constantly practice joy.
Not abandoning sentient beings, they exert themselves in great compassion;
they receive the instructions of their elders and superiors;
and regarding those who have left the household life, they regard them as the World-Honored One.
Practicing the perfections while aspiring for skillful means—
these are the eight matters. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the third stage, they practice five dharmas.
What are these five? They are:
inquiring extensively without weariness, and not being attached to words and letters;
To transform beings through the gift of Dharma without thoughts of clothing or food;
to purify Buddha-fields;
and to exhort others toward the roots of all virtues.
Furthermore, there is no expectation.
These are the five matters. "Moreover, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the fourth stage, they should practice ten dharmas and never abandon them.
What are these ten? They do not abandon secluded dwelling;
Their aspirations lie in seeking little;
they know contentment and sufficiency;
and they do not depart from tranquil sitting.
Not violating the prohibitions and precepts;
not being weary of receiving sensual desires;
and not ceasing at nirvana.
One gives all that one possesses without begrudging it;
one is not timid or weak;
and regarding all things, one has no longing.
These are the ten matters. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the fifth stage, he should abandon eight matters."
What are the eight?
Abandoning the household life;
staying away from bhikṣuṇīs;
Abandoning restlessness;
not craving merit;
relinquishing sleep and reclining.
They remain free from anger and contention;
they do not praise themselves,
nor do they disparage others.
These are the eight matters. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the sixth stage does so by being endowed with six dharmas."
What are these six? They are the six pāramitās; they do not constitute six dharmas.
They do not seek the state of a śrāvaka, harbor no thought of a pratyekabuddha, and do not dwell upon the Lesser Vehicle;
they look upon the poor and beggars with a serene and joyful countenance;
and when giving gifts, they do so without any sense of regret or distress.
The mind harbors no resentment;
this constitutes the sixth matter. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the seventh stage, they do so by being free from twenty things.
What are these twenty? They are:
having nothing to receive;
There is no self;
one does not reckon a person;
there is no life-principle.
Not dwelling on the notion of a life-span;
not dwelling on the notion of permanence;
and not clinging to annihilationism.
Free from all conceptual attachments;
detached from views concerning causes and conditions;
and not relying upon the aggregates.
Not longing for the various elements;
relinquishing the various elements;
relinquishing the various sense bases.
They have no perception of the three realms;
they do not cling to the Buddha;
they do not cling to the Dharma.
Not clinging to the assembly of noble ones;
guarding the prohibitions while relinquishing views;
not relying on the recollection of emptiness.
Abandoning all false views and remaining undefiled—this constitutes the twentieth matter.
One should further fulfill twenty other dharmic matters.
What are these twenty?
They clearly understand emptiness;
they do not realize signlessness;
their wisdom is free from aspiration.
Purifying the three spheres;
having compassion for sentient beings;
yet not perceiving sentient beings.
Free from contempt; viewing all phenomena with equanimity;
and realizing the meaning of the Dharma through direct experience.
Free from conceptual discrimination;
clearly understanding what is true and real;
and likewise free from attachment.
Attaining the patience of non-arising;
expounding a single chapter;
and eliminating all conceptualizations.
They cast off worldly toil;
they are tranquil and free from deviance;
their minds are harmonized and settled.
Not being separated from wisdom;
having no sudden outbursts of violence—
this is the twentieth.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the eighth stage does so by being fully endowed with four dharmas.
What are these four?
Entering the minds of sentient beings through the supernormal power of self-delight;
manifesting all Buddha-lands according to what is observed;
fully accomplishing one’s own land and prostrating before all Buddhas.
To contemplate the bodies of all Buddhas by means of ultimate truth—
this constitutes the four dharmas. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the ninth stage, they should further fulfill four dharmas. What are these four?
They are: thoroughly understanding the faculties [of sentient beings] and accomplishing Buddha-lands;
He diligently cultivates the Illusion-like Samādhi;
he transforms sentient beings in accordance with their needs, causing them to plant the roots of virtue and abide in purity and goodness;
for the sake of the multitude, he manifests a perfect body and expounds the meaning of the Path.
These are the four matters. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the tenth stage, they are fully endowed with twelve matters."
What are these twelve? They are:
establishing protection for immeasurable realms;
and causing each being to obtain what they require according to their respective wishes.
Whatever he proclaims with his voice, the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas each understand according to their own kind;
such is his eloquence.
Regarding the matters of the womb, noble lineage, place of birth, retinue, and kingdom, as well as his renunciation of country and home to proceed to the Bodhi tree, all are pure and complete.
All names and virtues are fully and completely possessed.
This is the twelfth. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
"The tenth bodhisattva-mahāsattva is precisely what is called a Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s cultivation of their resolute nature?"
The Buddha said:
"Regarding the roots of merit one has cultivated, the mind in all cases encourages and assists the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
What is meant by the 'equal mind' of a bodhisattva?"
All are resolved upon omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) because they practice the four immeasurable minds—compassion (*maitrī*), pity (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s activity of giving?
One practices giving to all beings because of being free from conceptualization.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s cultivation of spiritual friends?
It is to exhort and transform all beings to establish them in the Right Path, and to bow one's head, inquire after their well-being, and show reverence to elders and superiors.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the quest for the Dharma?
It is that regarding all dharmas sought, the mind constantly dwells upon the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), so as not to fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s earnest renunciation?

It is that in every place of birth, from lifetime to lifetime, he abandons his worldly occupations without causing them any ruin, following the teachings of the Tathāgata, because as one who has renounced the world, he cultivates the supreme practice.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s pursuit of the Buddha-body?
It is when, upon seeing the form of the Buddha, their mind never departs from the Buddha, even until they attain the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
What is meant by a bodhisattva elucidating all dharmas?

It is when a bodhisattva, whether seeing the Buddha in the present or after his parinirvāṇa, expounds the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; its initial words are good, its middle words are good, and its final words are good. Its meaning is complete, subtle, and fully endowed with pure conduct, as well as the twelve divisions of the sūtras—namely, the *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*. These are the twelve divisions of the sūtras of a bodhisattva, through which he elucidates all dharmas.
What is meant by a bodhisattva discarding the mind of arrogance?
It is never harboring self-importance, for they are never born into families of low standing.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s speech being ultimate sincerity?
"If there is anything spoken, it is because his words and deeds correspond.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"This is the first stage of practice for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, wherein one carries out ten matters!"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by the purity of the bodhisattva’s category of precepts?
The Buddha said:
"The mind does not harbor thoughts of seeking the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor does it disparage bodhisattvas.
If there are those who have violated the precepts, one exhorts and encourages them so that they do not fall into the ditch."
What is meant by a bodhisattva being one who returns kindness and knows how to repay gratitude?
When a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path, if they do not forget even a small gift received, how much less so a large one?
What is meant by a bodhisattva abiding in the power of patience?
It is because they are always free from a distracted mind toward sentient beings and do not harbor malice in their intent.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s mind and countenance being harmonious and joyful?
It is because mindfulness of transforming sentient beings does not contradict right practice.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning sentient beings?
It is being able to rescue, provide relief for, and protect all people.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being close to great compassion?
It is when, while practicing the path, the bodhisattva thinks to himself:

"For the sake of all people, even if I must remain in hell for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and even if I am subjected to torture and punishment, I shall never grow weary; I shall cause those people to achieve the Buddha-vehicle and thereby attain nirvana."
"In this way, one should apply this analogy to all sentient beings, encouraging their own minds with such subtle refinement.
What is meant by a bodhisattva receiving the instructions of elders?
If there is one who has left the household life, they should regard their teacher or preceptor as a Buddha."
What is meant by a bodhisattva seeking the pāramitās?
It is when a bodhisattva does not set their will upon other activities, does not dwell upon other dharmas, and is free from contempt, because they seek the ultimate.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s insatiable pursuit of extensive learning?

It is because they wholeheartedly receive, uphold, and preserve all that is spoken by the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, in this teaching, as well as all that is proclaimed from the mouths of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-giving being free from thoughts of clothing or food?
It is because, through this Dharma-giving, the mind maintains such a reflection that it does not conceive of the Buddha-way as a goal.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva purifying the Buddha-lands?
The roots of virtue they plant are all for the purpose of exhorting and assisting in the adornment and purification of Buddha-fields.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not wearying of birth and death?

It is because they constantly desire to fulfill all merits, accomplish the roots of goodness, and transform sentient beings; they purify the Buddha-fields without ever becoming indolent, until they have fully attained the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing a sense of shame and remorse?
It is because they never harbor the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning secluded dwelling?
Because they do not enter the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose resolve is set on few desires?
It means that while practicing the bodhisattva path, they have no greed or longing, for their resolve is fixed upon the Buddha-way.
What is meant by a bodhisattva knowing contentment?
It is for the sake of accomplishing sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning their moral restraints?
This means being able to discern and understand the profound Dharma.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning the training in the precepts?
It is because they maintain the prohibitive precepts without negligence.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not being weary of receiving desires?
It is because their mind has never given rise to craving.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s mind not entering parinirvāṇa?
Because they do not engage in any phenomena whatsoever.
What is meant by "all that belongs to a bodhisattva"?
It is that which they can fully protect through giving, because they have no craving for any internal or external phenomena.
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose will is not timid?
It is because the mind has never been stirred to give rise to dualistic consciousness.
What is meant by a bodhisattva observing all that exists without any craving?
Because they have no thoughts regarding any phenomena.
What is meant by a bodhisattva abandoning their kingdom and renouncing their home?
It means that from one buddha-field they travel to another buddha-field; wherever they are born, they shave off their hair and beard, don the *kāṣāya*, and manifest as a śramaṇa.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s relinquishing of bhikṣuṇīs?
It means not engaging in their affairs for even the duration of a finger-snap, because no mental activity arises toward those causes and conditions.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s relinquishing of caste?
A bodhisattva should reflect:
"I shall cause sentient beings to abide in peace and security through spontaneous tranquility.
This is because, should they see others so situated, they will never give rise to a mind of envy.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s relinquishing all greed as well as sleep and lying down?
If a bodhisattva is present in an assembly and someone there should give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva ought not to associate with or follow after them.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from ill-will?
It means not following a mind of resentment, anger, or harm; it is because they have no intent for strife or litigation and do not engage in contention.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not praising themselves?
One does not perceive internal phenomena, because there is nothing to be observed.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not disparaging others?
It is because one perceives nothing at all externally.
What is meant by a bodhisattva abandoning the ten unwholesome actions?
It means practicing the path of the noble ones as one's primary conduct, for the sake of purifying body, speech, and mind.
What is meant by a bodhisattva casting aside arrogance?
Such is their practice, for they do not perceive any phenomena and thus have no pride.
What is meant by a bodhisattva relinquishing self-importance?
It is because in their practice they do not perceive forms, appearances, or any possessions.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from inversion?
It is because, upon examining all that exists, nothing can be apprehended.
What is meant by a bodhisattva abandoning lust, anger, and delusion?
Because one never beholds the locus of the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion.
What are the six dharmas that a bodhisattva fulfills?
One who dwells in the sixth stage should fulfill these six dharmas.
What are these six? They are the six pāramitās that one should bring to fulfillment.
How does one fulfill the six pāramitās?
By abiding in the six pāramitās, one is able to transcend the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not giving rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha?
Such practices as these should not be taken as the Path; those who practice the Lesser Vehicle do not accord with the Buddha-way.
If they see a beggar, they harbor timidity and weakness.
A practitioner of the Bodhisattva-way should abandon such [reactions], their mind free from sorrow or distress.

Why is this? Because the practices of these individuals do not lead into the Way; from the moment they first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they have constantly practiced giving, never forgetting to relinquish it from their hearts.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not being greedy for his own body?
Why is this so? Because when one investigates from beginning to end, there is no self; the reckoning of persons and lifespans is likewise thus. Why is this so?
Because when one observes with discernment, the mind is found to be non-existent.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not falling into the view of annihilation?
It is because all phenomena have nothing in the mind that can be severed; from beginning to end they do not arise, for all phenomena are likewise without production.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not reckoning things as permanent?
It is because, if all phenomena are entirely without arising, then there is no permanence.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not forming attachments through conceptualization?
The reason for this is that when one calculates in this manner, there is no affliction (*kleśa*) and no perception based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The reason for this is that what is seen therein does not perceive any views.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not relying on name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?
It is because all that has been conditioned is non-existent.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not clinging to the aggregates (*skandha*)?
One does not rely on the aggregates (*skandha*) nor long for the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Why is this so? Because such practitioners are entirely self-resentful and possess nothing; for this reason, one should not rely upon or become attached to the aggregates, the elements, or the sense bases.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not relying on the three realms?
These three realms are naturally formless; although they exist within the three realms, there is nothing upon which to rely.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling in anything that exists?
One does not regard the fixed period as empty space, because all that exists is ultimately non-existent.
What is meant by a bodhisattva seeing the Buddha without attachment?
It is because one does not rely on visual perception to see the Buddhas.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not contending regarding emptiness?
All phenomena are entirely empty and non-existent; emptiness does not disturb emptiness, for there is nothing with which to contend.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with emptiness?
If the physical marks are like empty space, it is because the bodhisattva is fully endowed with emptiness.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not realizing the signless?
It is because they have no mental engagement with any signs whatsoever.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s wisdom of the vowless resolve?
It is because they do not engage in anything whatsoever within the three realms.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s purification of the three spheres?
This is because one is then able to fulfill the ten virtuous deeds.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s compassionate pity for all classes of sentient beings?
It is because one is then able to practice the virtue of infinite great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
What is meant by a bodhisattva not being arrogant toward sentient beings?
It is because they desire to fully perfect the Buddha-field.
What is meant by a bodhisattva viewing all phenomena with equanimity?
Because one examines all phenomena as being neither high nor low.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the stages of the path?
It is because one does not habituate oneself to any phenomenon and remains unmoved and unshakable.
What is called the bodhisattva’s patience regarding non-arising?
It is because all dharmas neither arise nor cease, and one is patient with their non-existence.
What is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom regarding the unproduced?
Regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), because wisdom does not arise therein.
What is meant by a bodhisattva teaching a single category?
Because they do not engage in two things.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling on any thoughts?
It is because they have no thoughts regarding any phenomena (*dharma*).
What is meant by a bodhisattva discarding all views?
Because they are able to relinquish and depart from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s eradication of afflictions?
It is the complete severance of the stains of desire within all places where the various outflows (āsrava) have been habitually cultivated.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s ground of serene detachment?
It refers to being able to attain and perfect the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
What is meant by the taming of the mind?
Because there is no affliction or hardship within the three realms.
What is meant by "tranquility of mind"?
It is the ability to govern the six sense faculties.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning wisdom?
It means being able to attain the clear eye.
