What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from sudden violence?
Because one contemplates the six sense bases as being free from defilement and attachment.
What is meant by "the bodhisattva’s mind having an entry"?
It is because with a single mind, they universally perceive the thoughts of all sentient beings.
What is meant by "the bodhisattva’s self-entertainment through supernormal powers"?
It is that he entertains himself by means of supernormal powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another, because wherever he wanders, he has no conception of it as a "buddha-field."
What is meant by a bodhisattva seeing all buddha-fields?
By abiding in this buddha-field, one sees the immeasurable buddha-fields of the ten directions, for one has no attachment to any of those buddha-fields.
What is meant by a bodhisattva observing things as they truly are?
It is seeing that all Buddha-lands are fully adorned and pure; wherever one travels within the trichiliocosm, one invariably becomes a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
What is meant by a bodhisattva prostrating before all Buddhas, making offerings, serving them, and recollecting them?
It is because they discern the meanings and purports of all sūtras and dharmas.
What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly and carefully contemplating the bodies of all Buddhas?
Because seeing the Buddhas with true insight constitutes the Dharma-body.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thorough understanding of the faculties?
If one can abide in the ten powers of the Tathāgata, then one can thoroughly understand the fundamental faculties of all sentient beings.
What is meant by the purification of a bodhisattva’s buddha-field?
It is called the purification of the buddha-field because the people therein are purified.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi?
When a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, they are able to manifest all things and enter everywhere, because the mind has no fixed dwelling place.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s samādhi of equality?
Because the Bodhisattva has no expectations regarding any samādhis.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva being able to teach sentient beings?

He brings them to spiritual maturity according to their respective practices, establishing the roots of virtue for each; thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva protects his own person with utmost sincerity and brings sentient beings to liberation according to their needs.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s utmost sincerity?
It is that they naturally give rise to exhortation and inspiration, desiring thereby to deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s ability to surely attain their vows and aspirations as they intend?
Because the Bodhisattva is always fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
What is meant by the sound produced by the Bodhisattva such that when devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas hear it, each understands it and is transformed accordingly?
This is because they employ great compassion and a universally equal voice.
What is meant by a Bodhisattva entering the womb?
It is because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, throughout all lifetimes in which he is born, is in truth not born at all.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being in a state of nobility?
It means that wherever a bodhisattva is born among various lineages, they are able to transform them.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being endowed with a noble birth?
If a bodhisattva is born into the caste of nobles, the caste of brahmins, or the caste of householders, it is because they are able to exhort and transform others.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being born into a noble lineage?
Because all past bodhisattvas are fundamentally without distinction in their essential nature,
what is meant by a bodhisattva’s perfection of retinue?
It refers to the fact that the various attendants and servants from whom a bodhisattva draws support are never lacking.
What is meant by the adornment and purification of a Bodhisattva’s land?
At the moment of birth, their radiance illuminates countless worlds; for all who receive this light attain peace and security.
What is meant by a bodhisattva abandoning his kingdom and renouncing his home?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva leaves his home to study the Path, he transforms countless hundreds of thousands of millions of people and causes them to follow him as his retinue, for he is able to establish sentient beings in the Three Vehicles.
What is meant by a bodhisattva approaching the Bodhi tree?

That tree has roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, all made of the seven treasures and the color of purple-polished gold, illuminating countless Buddha-lands in the ten directions with great brilliance; this is the bodhisattva’s approach to the Bodhi tree in its adorned purity.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with all names and virtues?
If a bodhisattva is pure, then the buddha-field is pure; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be fully endowed with names and virtues.
What is meant by a bodhisattva dwelling in the ten stages of the path and becoming a Tathāgata?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is fully endowed with the six pāramitās, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; when they attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*), severing all afflictions and being free from all obstructions—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva dwelling in the ten stages of the path and becoming a Tathāgata.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās with upāyakauśalya, they enter the eight stages of the lineage through the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the thirty-seven auxiliaries, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—remaining tranquil and free from views.

If there is a state wherein one abides in the stage of detachment from desire and the stage where what was to be done has been accomplished—being detached from the stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s entry into the ninth dwelling in the Buddha-stage; this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s tenth practice-dwelling; this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s tri-samādhi!
The Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasamādhisūtra (The Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Miracle of the Decisive Pacification), Scroll Seven; The Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasamādhisūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen: On the Source from which the Mahāyāna Emerges.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“Regarding what you have asked, from where does the Mahāyāna emerge?”
From where does one abide within the Great Vehicle?
Who is it that accomplishes the Great Vehicle?
Arising from the three realms, one abides in *sarvajñatā* (omniscience); there is the fundamental non-arising, and there is no such thing as having just arisen.

Why is this? Because in the Mahāyāna’s omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñājñāna*), regarding these two matters, dharmas neither conjoin nor disperse; they are without form, without visibility, and without anything to be grasped or abandoned. Thus, they constitute a single mark, which is to say they are markless.
Why is this so? Because the markless dharma has no place from which it arises.

If a dharma were to arise, it would be intended to cause the dharma-realm to arise; if the markless dharma were to have something produced, it would be intended to cause that which was originally non-existent to arise. Yet, the markless dharma has nothing produced.
To wish for the arising of that which arises is to wish for the arising of the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
To wish for the arising of the signless (*animitta*) is to wish for the production of the inconceivable *dharmadhātu*.
Whoever wishes to cause the dharma of signlessness to arise, they wish to cause it to be born through dedicated and ardent practice.
Whoever wishes to cause the dharma of signlessness to arise, they thereby wish to cause it to be born from the severance of the realms.
To state the essential point, Subhūti:
it would be as if one wished to cause birth within the realm of desire;
for anyone who wishes to cause the arising of signless dharmas, it would be as if they wished to cause birth within the realm of parinirvāṇa.
Subhūti! That is because they wish to bring forth that which is tranquil, empty, and non-existent.
Whoever wishes to cause the birth of the signless dharmas—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—is wishing to cause the birth of dharmas that possess signs.
Why is this? Form is emptiness; it arises from the three realms and abides in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no emptiness; they arise from the three realms, yet sarvajñatā has no place of abiding.

Why is this? If one understands form (*rūpa*), then form is empty; if one understands feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), then consciousness is empty; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise empty.
To wish for these to arise is equivalent to wishing for space to be produced.

Eye-consciousness of forms, ear-consciousness of sounds, nose-consciousness of odors, tongue-consciousness of flavors, body-consciousness of tangibles, and mind-consciousness of mental objects—these eighteen kinds of phenomena perceived through causes and conditions are empty and non-existent. To wish for them to arise is equivalent to wishing for the signless (*animitta*) dharma to be produced.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
That which is perceived by the eye is entirely empty; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise, for their habitual activities are all empty.
Subhūti! The three realms are empty; that which is seen by the eye is empty, arising from the three realms, and thus the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) has no place of abiding.
The six sense-faculties are also empty, arising because of the three realms, and thus the *sarvajñatā* has no place of abiding.
That which is received and practiced by the six sense-faculties is entirely empty and devoid of marks; to wish for its arising is to wish for the arising of that which is like a dream or an illusion.

Why is this so? Dreams, illusions, the moon reflected in water, plantain trees, mirages, and echoes in deep mountains are all spontaneously so; such spontaneous phenomena are the transformations of the Tathāgata.
The three realms are naturally such that nothing is produced; omniscience (sarvajñatā) likewise has no place of abiding.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Like a dream, which is spontaneous; that which is spontaneous has nothing at all. The affairs of illusion and transformation are also like this. Subhūti!

One who wishes to cause the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) to exist, or wish for the perfections of morality (śīlapāramitā), patience (kṣāntipāramitā), vigor (vīryapāramitā), meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to arise, is thereby wishing to cause the dharma of signlessness (animitta-dharma) to arise.
Why is this so? Subhūti, the six pāramitās are all naturally so, arising from the three realms; likewise, sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) has no place of abiding.
Why is this so? Subhūti, the six pāramitās are spontaneous; that which is spontaneous is therefore called empty.

Whoever wishes to cause the dharma of signlessness to arise, thereby wishes to cause internal emptiness, external emptiness, emptiness of existence, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of the near, emptiness of the far, and true emptiness to be produced.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Those seven emptinesses are of their own nature (*svabhāva*); because they are of their own nature, they arise from within the three realms, yet omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) has no place of abiding.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Because it is by virtue of the seven kinds of emptiness being spontaneous that it is called "empty"; thus, emptiness is emptiness.

Subhūti! Whoever wishes to cause the signless dharma to arise, they thereby wish to cause the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path to arise.
Why is this? Because all things are naturally empty, arising from the three realms; as for sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), it has no place of abiding. Subhūti!
Subhūti, whoever wishes to cause the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to arise, they wish to cause the signless dharma to arise.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are spontaneous and do not arise within the three realms; Sarvajña (all-knowledge) likewise has no place of abiding.
Why is this? The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are spontaneously empty; because they are empty, they are called "empty."

Subhūti! Should anyone wish to cause the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the four analytical eloquences to all be naturally empty—being empty, they are called "empty."

Whether it be a srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha, or even one who has become a tathāgata, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha, they do so because they wish to bring forth the dharma of signlessness.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Those of the three vehicles are likewise spontaneous and do not emerge from the triple world; as for sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), it has no place of abiding.
Why is this so? Subhūti, an arhat is of the nature of spontaneity; because it is spontaneous, it is empty, and thus it is called "empty."
The Pratyekabuddha is of the nature of spontaneity; because he is spontaneous, he is empty, and thus he is said to be empty.
The Tathāgata is of the nature of spontaneity; because he is spontaneous, he is empty, and thus he is said to be empty.
Subhūti! Whoever wishes to cause a name to arise, they wish to cause the dharma of signlessness to arise.
It is likewise with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
If one wishes to cause the arising of words regarding causes and conditions, that is to wish for the arising of the dharma of signlessness.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Its name and designation are empty; it does not arise within the three realms, and that which is sarvajña (all-knowing) has no place of abiding. Why is this?
Because names and designations are empty, and by virtue of the emptiness of names and designations, they are said to be empty.

All bases for causes, conditions, speech, and terminology are entirely empty; because all phenomena are empty in their basis, they are said to be empty. To wish for that which is unarisen to arise is to wish for the arising of signless phenomena.
Why is this so? Because the dharmas of signlessness are empty and entirely without location; since their location is empty, they are called "empty.

Should anyone wish to cause that which is signless, unceasing, non-conceptual, stainless, free from anger, and non-existent to arise, they would thereby be wishing to cause the dharmas of signlessness to arise.
Why is this so? These various phenomena are empty; because they are empty, they are called "empty.

This applies likewise to names, designations, causes and conditions, and the sphere of verbal expression, as well as to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the four analytical knowledges.
Therefore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna arises from the three realms, yet it is an arising of that which does not arise; the arising of sarvajñatā likewise does not arise, for there is no place of movement.
Furthermore, regarding Subhūti’s question as to where one dwells: the mind dwells nowhere, and the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) has no location. Why is this?
Because there is nothing in which to dwell, all dharmas likewise dwell nowhere.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
That which the Mahāyāna abides in abides in non-abiding.
That which is the dharma-realm likewise abides in non-abiding, dwelling in non-abiding.
The Great Vehicle is also like this: it abides in non-abiding.
Just as the aforementioned empty space has no basis from which it turns;
the Great Vehicle is also like this: it abides in non-abiding.
Furthermore, for example, as non-arising abides in non-abiding, so too does the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) abide in non-abiding.
For example, as non-ceasing, non-defilement, non-anger, and non-existence abide in non-abiding; so it is with the Great Vehicle.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it abides in non-abiding. Why is this?
Because the dharma-realm is spontaneous, abiding in non-abiding.

Why is this so? Because the dharma-realm is spontaneous; by virtue of being spontaneous, it is empty. Furthermore, the seven kinds of emptiness are all non-existent. Being spontaneous is itself emptiness, and since emptiness is non-existent, it is called "empty."
Therefore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) has no place of abiding; because it abides in non-abiding, it is without movement or change.
Regarding what you asked, Subhūti—how the Great Vehicle is established by means of abiding—the Great Vehicle is without arising.
Why is this so? Because there is nothing that has arisen from within, nor is there anything that is about to arise; all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely non-existent.
Since they are thus non-existent, all phenomena are likewise so; what phenomenon could possibly have an arising?
Why is this so? The self, the person, and the life-span are likewise thus: they possess no suchness, nothing is seen, and nothing is attained; they are pure from beginning to end.
Therefore, the self, the person, and the life-span—this dharma-realm—is entirely unattainable, for it is empty from beginning to end.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is entirely unattainable;
his original limit is likewise unattainable, for both beginning and end are utterly pure.
Thus, all realms are inconceivable and entirely unattainable, for both beginning and end are pure.
Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all unapprehendable, being pure in their beginning and end.
Because the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are unapprehendable, they are pure in their beginning and end;
likewise, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are all unapprehendable, being pure in their beginning and end.
Therefore, even the seven kinds of emptiness cannot be apprehended, for they are pure from beginning to end;

the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path—the thirty-seven auxiliaries to enlightenment—as well as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the four analytical knowledges, likewise cannot be apprehended, for they are pure from beginning to end;
from the stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, all cannot be apprehended, for they are pure from beginning to end.
Because the Dharma of the three vehicles and the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) cannot be apprehended, they are pure from beginning to end.

That which is non-existent and arises is entirely unapprehendable; it is pure from beginning to end—without cessation, without defilement, without anger, and without contention. All that is non-existent and all that exists are entirely unapprehendable; they are pure from beginning to end.

Those matters of the past, future, and present, as well as the coming and going, the abiding and dwelling, and the arising of things—all are entirely unapprehendable; they are pure from beginning to end.
That which is benefited and that which is harmed are both entirely unobtainable; from beginning to end, they are pure.
Who could attain that which is unattainable?
Even that dharma-realm cannot be attained, for there is no one who attains it.
Why is this? Because when one seeks to reach the dharma-realm, it cannot be apprehended.
If one seeks arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or tathāgatas, and desires to obtain them, none of these can be apprehended.

If there are those who wish to attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the four analytical knowledges, these likewise cannot be attained, for there is no one capable of reaching them.
If there is anyone who wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is entirely unattainable; the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is entirely empty and unattainable.
The six *pāramitās* and the seven kinds of emptiness are likewise thus, all being entirely unattainable.
That which is neither produced nor extinguished, free from dust, free from anger, and free from anything possessed—none of these can be apprehended. Why is this so?
When one contemplates them correctly and truly, they are entirely non-existent and entirely unobtainable.
Even that which seeks to attain the first stage is unobtainable;
even up to the tenth stage, they are unobtainable, for from beginning to end they are pure.
What is that which possesses the first dwelling? That which is the pure contemplation,
as well as the stages manifested by the lineage and the eightfold [path], all these stages— the stage of detachment from desire,

the stage of having accomplished what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva path, the stage of the samyaksambuddha, and even the first stage— are all unobtainable.
Regarding those seven emptinesses, they are all unattainable.
Calculating from internal emptiness up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), they are all unattainable; the seven emptinesses and the ten stages are entirely non-existent and all unattainable.
Why is this so? Subhūti, the first dwelling is merely a name; it is unobtainable, and the same applies up to the tenth dwelling.

Even if there were something obtained, it would be unobtainable; being pure from beginning to end, one preaches to sentient beings that internal emptiness is entirely unobtainable, and that all sentient beings are likewise unobtainable. Thus, for the sake of sentient beings, one explains the sevenfold matters of emptiness, wherein all that can be spoken is entirely unobtainable, pure from beginning to end.
Because of internal emptiness, the Buddha-lands are pure, and nothing at all can be apprehended.
The seven kinds of emptiness are spontaneous; because they are spontaneously empty, the Buddha-lands are pure, and nothing at all can be apprehended, being pure from beginning to end.
Therefore, both internal emptiness and the five eyes are entirely unobtainable;
they are all non-existent and spontaneous. Spontaneous emptiness constitutes these five eyes, which have no location whatsoever and are pure from beginning to end.
Therefore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended, he thereby attains the Mahāyāna and reaches the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Chapter 20: On the Absence of Coming and Going The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty: On the Absence of Coming and Going At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding what is called the ‘Mahāyāna,’ O Devātideva, as for the destination of the meaning of this Mahāyāna—”
Among the worlds of gods and humans, he is the most honored, and there is none who does not take refuge in him.
The Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness; it is like space, which contains and covers immeasurable asaṃkhyeya beings, all of whom revere and look up to it. O, God among Gods!
The Mahāyāna is also like this: the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva covers immeasurable asaṃkhyeya beings, all of whom attain deliverance through him.
As for the Mahāyāna, its time of coming is not seen, its time of going is not seen, and its place of abiding is not seen.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!

The Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present; it has no perception of an intermediate state, nor is there anything to be attained. Its name is equal throughout the three periods of time; therefore it is called "Yāna" (Vehicle), and thus it is the Mahāyāna.
Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! That which is called the Mahāyāna consists of the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
The perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom.
This, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti:
The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to all the gates of dhāraṇī, all the gates of samādhi, and the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

To state the essentials: the samādhis of emptiness and so forth, the samādhi of liberation, the samādhi of non-attachment, and the samādhi of quiescence—these are called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists in thoroughly understanding the seven kinds of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the four analytical knowledges; this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Furthermore, Subhūti! That which is called the Mahāyāna is the most supreme in the world above and below; there is none who does not look up to it in reverence.

For example, Subhūti, the desire realm is fundamentally non-existent, and this fundamental non-existence is equal and without difference, such that it cannot be distinguished. It is without inversion, truly real, and spontaneous; it is long-lasting and firm, a dharma without separation, without union, and without dispersal—never having existed as something [substantial]. This is the Mahāyāna, the most honored among gods and humans in the world above and below, to whom all look up in reverence.

"Suppose, Subhūti, that at the time when the kalpa is consumed by fire, [the Buddha] manifests it all in order to teach and transform all beings, so that they may know impermanence: that nothing endures, nothing is solid, and everything is utterly non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna is the most honored in the heavens above and the world below; there is none who does not look up to it with reverence."

Furthermore, Subhūti! The desire realm and such [realms] as these are without distinction; they are without inversion, truly real, and spontaneous. They are without origin, firm and stable, and possess no dharma of separation. They are without causes and conditions; that which is non-existent never becomes existent. This is the Mahāyāna, the most honored in the heavens above and the earth below.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if the perceptions of the desire realm—which are impermanent and inverted—manifest as subject to destruction; if all things are impermanent, lacking duration, and incapable of solidity; and if the nature of separation is such that nothing at all exists [independently].
Therefore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna is likewise so in the heavens above and the heavens below, and even so in the formless realm.
Suppose, Subhūti, it were the case that...

All forms are fundamentally non-existent and entirely devoid of anything; it is likewise with this equality, which is without distinction, manifold, or even a natural truth. Fundamentally, there is nothing solid and no phenomenon of separation. That which does not exist cannot be made to exist; this is the Mahāyāna, the most honored in the heavens above and the earth below.

"Suppose, Subhūti, that form has an object of thought which should be pure, yet it is inverted and entirely filled with [defilements]; all of it is impermanent, nothing endures for long, and it lacks solidity. It is a phenomenon of separation and is utterly non-existent; therefore, it is the Mahāyāna."
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so;
the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are equal and without distinction.

Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are equal and without distinction; all are non-existent and beyond any differentiation.
The ultimate truth of supreme sincerity is that those who calculate things to be permanent, long-lasting, and solid do not possess the Mahāyāna.

Because they practice the six matters with a mind full of conceptualizations, they are deluded by the conditions of their practice and seek much to satisfy themselves; yet all these dharmas are entirely impermanent, with nothing that endures forever or can remain stable for long.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna is the most honored in the heavens above and on earth below. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if all that exists within the dharma-realm were utterly non-existent, this would constitute the Mahāyāna as the most honored in the heavens above and on earth below.
It is firm and without anything arising.
Subhūti, it is like this:
all that exists within the dharma-realm is entirely non-existent; its activity is non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna is the most honored in the world above and below.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to manifest that which exists, it would all be non-existent; its true fundamental limit is inconceivable.
Whatever exists within those realms is entirely non-existent; this is why the Mahāyāna is the most honored in the heavens above and the earth below.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those realms are inconceivable, and whatever exists therein is entirely non-existent; for this reason, the Mahāyāna is the most honored in the heavens above and the earth below.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if all that exists within the six pāramitās is neither existent nor non-existent, this is called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
That which is internal emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent; it is naturally empty, being neither existent nor non-existent—this is the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, Subhūti, that which is internal emptiness is naturally non-existent; because there is neither existence nor non-existence regarding the emptiness of existence, it is called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,

the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the four analytical knowledges are neither existent nor non-existent, yet not non-existent either— this is the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, Subhūti! That dharma of the lineage is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is not non-existent; because this dharma of the lineage is neither existent nor non-existent, yet not non-existent, it is therefore called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti! These eightfold dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent;

the dharma of the srotāpanna, the dharma of the sakṛdāgāmin, the dharma of the anāgāmin, the dharma of the arhat, the dharma of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharmas of all Buddhas are neither existent nor non-existent. Because they are neither existent nor non-existent, and because they are also not the absence of non-existence, this is therefore called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti, these eightfold noble paths and the Buddha-dharma are neither existent nor non-existent, and yet they are not even non-non-existent; for this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti, as for their application:
those various dispositions are neither existent nor non-existent, yet they are not without non-existence;

the application of the eightfold equality is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is not without non-existence; from the stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, they are neither existent nor non-existent, yet they are not without non-existence. For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.

Subhūti! If you wish to know how all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not even non-non-existent, it is for this reason that it is called the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if the devas, humans, asuras,

and the world were neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not even non-non-existent— because all that belongs to the devas, humans, asuras, and the world is neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not non-non-existent— it is for this reason called the Mahāyāna.

Suppose, Subhūti, that from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until sitting at the site of awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, a bodhisattva generates the mind such that it is neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not even non-non-existent.
Subhūti, it is like this:

from the first generation of the mind of awakening until reaching the site of enlightenment, every thought that arises therein is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it even the absence of non-existence; for this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.

Suppose, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses a wisdom as supreme as a vajra—neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not even the absence of non-existence. This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to clearly understand and perceive all obstructions and the various afflictions, thereby attaining sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
For this reason, Subhūti,
because the bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all obstructions and all afflictions are entirely non-existent and attains sarvajñā (all-knowledge), it is therefore called the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, Subhūti! As for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, his thirty-two marks of a great man are neither existent nor non-existent, yet they are not even non-non-existent. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is the most honored in the heavens above and the world below; his majestic spiritual power and holy virtue are subtle and wondrous, illuminating all things without exception, and he has no equal.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s majestic and sublime spiritual power and the radiance of his holy virtue illuminate the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as all the heavens above and below, the devas, humans, and asuras. This light is universally pervasive; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not non-non-existent. For this reason, the light of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha illuminates the worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Tathāgata possesses eightfold sounds that are neither existent nor non-existent, yet not even non-non-existent. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, using these eightfold sounds of the Tathāgata—which are neither existent nor non-existent, yet not even non-non-existent—proclaims throughout the ten directions across asaṃkhyeya and immeasurable worlds. Thus, there are eight kinds of vocal sounds by which he proclaims throughout the inconceivable and immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata is neither existent nor non-existent, and yet it is not the case that there is no non-existence; this is what constitutes the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Tathāgata.

Shramanas, brahmins, and the hosts of Brahma-devas—none in the heavens above or the world below can withstand him—and he causes them all to obtain their respective places in accordance with the Dharma.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma, no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, human, or any being in the world above or below can withstand it.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

All sentient beings are neither existent nor non-existent, and yet they are not without non-existence. For this reason, the Tathāgata repeatedly turns the wheel of Dharma, so that all sentient beings do not reach a nirvāṇa realm without remainder.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

These sentient beings are neither existent nor non-existent, and yet not even non-non-existent; because they have fully realized this, the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma. Therefore, these sentient beings reach the realm of no-remainder and enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvāṇa.
Chapter 21: The Chapter on the Great Vehicle Being Equal to Emptiness. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Great Vehicle Being Equal to Emptiness. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"As you have said, that the Great Vehicle is equal to emptiness is a statement of ultimate truth."
So it is, so it is! The Mahāyāna is equal to space.

For example, just as one cannot calculate or know the number of *li* in the eastern direction, nor can one know [the distance] in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below; it is neither distant nor near, and it has no boundaries.

The wisdom of the Tathāgata is also like this: it cannot be exhausted or reached its limit throughout the eight directions, above and below; it has no boundaries and no distance, for this wisdom is inexhaustible.
For example, just as space is neither long nor short, has no cardinal directions, and neither increases nor decreases;
so too is the wisdom of the Tathāgata—neither long nor short, neither round nor square, and neither increasing nor decreasing. Furthermore, Subhūti!
For example, just as space has no five colors— blue, yellow, red, or white—
the Mahāyāna is likewise. Furthermore, Subhūti,
just as space has no past, future, or present;
The Great Vehicle is also like this, having no past, future, or present.
Furthermore, Subhūti, just as with empty space, there is nothing that can increase it and nothing that can decrease it;
the Great Vehicle is also like this.
It neither increases nor decreases;
therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is like space:
it has no afflictions, no anger or resentment, no one who is born, nor anything that is extinguished; it neither abides nor does it not abide, and it is without thought.
The Mahāyāna is also like this.
Therefore, it is said that the *vaipulya* is equal to emptiness. Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is like space: it has neither good nor evil, neither speech nor non-speech; it is like space: it is without seeing or hearing, without thought or cognition.
The *vaipulya* is also like this.
Therefore, it is said that the *vaipulya* is equal to emptiness.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
For example, just as space is neither different nor not different, neither something to be severed, nor something to be realized, nor something to be eliminated;
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, just as space has no phenomena of desire and is not separate from phenomena of desire; it has no phenomena of hatred and is not separate from hatred; it has no phenomena of delusion and is not separate from delusion—so too is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
For example, just as space does not merge with the desire realm, nor does it merge with the form realm or the formless realm, yet it is also not separate from the three realms;
so too is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Just as space has no initial generation of the mind nor progression from the first stage, so too is the Mahāyāna; it has no ten stages.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Just as space is neither clear nor turbid, is invisible, and has no location; it has no stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi), no stage of the eight persons (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi), and no stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi); it has no stage of "mine-ness" (mamakāra-bhūmi), no stage of desire (kāma-bhūmi), and no stage of action or non-action (kṛtākṛta-bhūmi);
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is like space, which has no fruit of the stream-enterer, no fruit of the once-returner, no fruit of the non-returner, and no fruit of the arhat.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Just as space contains no stage of the śrāvaka, no stage of the pratyekabuddha, and no stage of the samyaksaṃbuddha;
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, space has no form or image, nor does it lack form; it is neither visible, nor is it not visible; it is without grasping and without relinquishing; it is without conjunction and without dispersion.
The Mahāyāna is also like this.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
For example, just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither suffering nor happiness, and neither self nor non-self;
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Just as space is neither empty nor non-empty, neither different from emptiness nor characterized by different conceptions, neither having no conception nor having any aspiration or non-aspiration;
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, it is said that the *vaipulya* is equal to emptiness. Furthermore, Subhūti!
For example, as with space, there is neither tranquility nor non-tranquility; there is neither serenity nor non-serenity.
Furthermore, Subhūti! Just as space has neither radiance nor darkness,
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Just as space is neither attainable nor unattainable,
so too is the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is like space:
there is neither speech nor discourse, yet there is also no absence of speech.
The *vaipulya* is also like this.
Therefore, it is said that the *vaipulya* is equal to emptiness. For this reason, Subhūti!
As space is equal, so too is the Mahāyāna equal.
As Subhūti has said, for example, just as space is without limit and can shelter incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings,
so too is the Mahāyāna, which provides a resting place for incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings.
Thus it is, Subhūti! Just as space covers incalculable, asaṃkhyeya beings;
so too is the Mahāyāna, which protects incalculable, asaṃkhyeya beings by reckoning persons as being personless.
For example, space cannot be apprehended because it is empty by virtue of its non-existence;
the Mahāyāna is also like this. Therefore, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna protects and safeguards countless asaṃkhyeya beings. Why is this?
Because persons, space, and the Mahāyāna—all these dharmas—are ultimately unattainable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, beings are incalculable, emptiness is also incalculable, space is also incalculable, and the Mahāyāna is also incalculable; therefore, the Mahāyāna covers incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings."
Why is this so? Subhūti! Persons, space, and the Mahāyāna are all incalculable and all unattainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is incalculable;
therefore, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable asaṃkhyeya persons. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Since persons have no intrinsic existence, the dharma-realm likewise has no intrinsic existence, and all phenomena likewise have no intrinsic existence; therefore, it is said that even empty space has no intrinsic existence.

Sentient beings, space, and the Mahāyāna are all non-existent; incalculable numbers are non-existent, the immeasurable is non-existent, and the unfathomable is non-existent. Therefore, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable, asankhyeya beings.

Why is this so? Because the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the Mahāyāna—moreover, being incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), immeasurable, and without limit or bottom—are all ultimately ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Sentient beings do not exist;

the Tathāgata does not exist; space does not exist; the Mahāyāna does not exist; the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) does not exist; the immeasurable (*aprameya*) does not exist; the bottomless (*ananta*) does not exist; and all dharmas likewise do not exist."
Therefore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna provides protection for immeasurable, incalculable,
and boundless beings. Why is this?
The Tathāgata, empty space, sentient beings, and the Mahāyāna—these are all incalculable, immeasurable, and without limit or bottom; because they are entirely ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The self does not exist;

that which is known and that which is seen also do not exist. The limit of beginning (*pūrvakoṭi*) does not exist. One should understand in this way that the limit of beginning is non-existent, extending even to the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), which likewise do not exist."
Because there is nothing that exists, all dharmas likewise do not exist; therefore, the Mahāyāna is called the immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite protection for countless beings.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
All that is known and seen by all sentient beings, as well as their original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), up to the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the uncountable—all these are ultimately unobtainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The self and the person are both non-existent;

that which is known and that which is seen are also non-existent; the inconceivable realm is also non-existent; form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-existent; space is also non-existent; the Mahāyāna is also non-existent; the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is also non-existent; the uncountable (*agaṇeya*) is also non-existent; the infinite (*apramāṇa*) is also non-existent; and all dharmas are also non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna is the protection for incalculable, asaṃkhyeya persons."
Why is this? Because, Subhūti, as it is,
both the self and all phenomena are entirely unattainable!

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The self and the person are entirely empty; that which is known and that which is seen are likewise void and non-existent. The eye is also void and non-existent, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise void and non-existent. Because the non-existent is itself empty and non-existent, and emptiness is itself void and non-existent, the Mahāyāna is also void and non-existent. Because there is no duality in this voidness, the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the uncountable (*agaṇeya*) are also void and non-existent. Because the uncountable is itself void and non-existent, all dharmas are also void and non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna covers incalculable, immeasurable, and uncountable *asaṃkhyeya* beings."
Why is that? Subhūti! The self, the person, and all dharmas are entirely unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The self does not exist, and that which is known and seen also does not exist;
because that which is known and seen does not exist, the dānapāramitā does not exist, and the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā also do not exist."
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent, empty space is also non-existent, and the Mahāyāna is likewise non-existent;
therefore, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable, immeasurable, and asankhyeya numbers of people.
Why is this so? Subhūti, it is because the self,
the life-span, and all dharmas are entirely unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The self and the person do not exist.

That which is known in the world—internal emptiness, external emptiness, near emptiness, far emptiness, true emptiness, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of non-existence—also does not exist.

Since these seven kinds of emptiness do not exist, empty space also does not exist; the Mahāyāna also does not exist; incalculable, immeasurable, and asaṃkhyeya [numbers] also do not exist; and all dharmas also do not exist. For this reason, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable, immeasurable, and asaṃkhyeya persons."
Why is this so? Subhūti, it is because the self,
the person, the life-span, and all dharmas are entirely unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Self, person, knowledge, and vision are all non-existent;

the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—are also non-existent. The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also non-existent; even space and the Mahāyāna are non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna provides protection for immeasurable, infinite, and incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings."
Why is this? Because the self, the person, and all dharmas are entirely unapprehendable. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Self, person, knowledge, and vision are all non-existent; the various dharmas of the spiritual lineage are also non-existent; the ground of practice is non-existent by virtue of being non-existent; empty space is also non-existent; the Mahāyāna is also non-existent; and even the incalculable, asāṃkhyeya number of people and all dharmas are also non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable, boundless, and asāṃkhyeya numbers of people.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The self, persons, knowledge, and vision are non-existent;

the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha are also non-existent; and all dharmas are likewise non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable, limitless, and asaṃkhyeya numbers of people."
Why is this? Because the self, the person, and all dharmas are entirely unapprehendable. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even up to the Tathāgatas are non-existent; omniscience (sarvajñatā) is non-existent; and all dharmas are also non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna protects and shelters incalculable, infinite, and asaṃkhyeya numbers of people.
Why is this so? Subhūti, it is because the self,
persons, and all phenomena are entirely unapprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The realm of nirvāṇa protects and shelters incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings; the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is likewise. Therefore, the Great Vehicle is equal to emptiness, protecting and sheltering incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings.
As Subhūti has asked, that which is called the Mahāyāna is neither seen to come, nor seen to go, nor seen to abide;
the Mahāyāna is likewise thus.
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are immovable; therefore, there is no one who abides, no one who comes, and no place of abiding.
Why is this so? Subhūti, form,
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Subhūti! Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure; they come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no origin; they come from nowhere and go nowhere, nor do they abide anywhere.

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are *svabhāva* (natural); they come from nowhere and go nowhere, nor do they abide anywhere. The intrinsic nature (*svabhāvalakṣaṇa*) of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
Regarding the natural characteristics of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: they come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

As for these elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—they possess no purity, nor do they lack a fundamental basis. Regarding their natural state, there is no natural characteristic of the earth element that comes from anywhere, goes anywhere, or abides anywhere; the same is true for the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
The Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent by nature and lacks the marks of natural existence; he comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and likewise abides nowhere. Subhūti!
The primordial limit is pure; the primordial limit has no origin. The primordial source is spontaneous, and its primordial natural characteristic is beyond calculation or deliberation.
As for that which belongs to the pure realm, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and likewise abides nowhere.

It is inconceivable and without origin; it is the realm of non-conceptualization and spontaneity. This realm of inconceivability and the characteristic of spontaneity have no place from which they come, no place to which they go, and no place wherein they abide.
Subhūti! The six pāramitās are also pure; the prajñāpāramitā is neither without origin nor is it spontaneous. The characteristic of spontaneity comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these dharmas of the Buddhas are pure in virtue and conduct; the Buddha and his perfect awakening come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

That which is non-existent and without origin, that which is unconditioned, does not exist as something spontaneous; that which is unconditioned has no characteristic of spontaneity; it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and likewise abides nowhere.
As Subhūti has said:

"The Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended in the past, cannot be apprehended in the future, and cannot be apprehended in the intermediate [present]; the three periods of time are equal. The Mahāyāna is merely a name."
"In this way, Subhūti, that which is called the Mahāyāna has no past, future, or present; it is equal throughout the three periods of time.
The Mahāyāna is merely a name."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

The past is empty, the future is empty, and the present is empty; the three periods of time are equal, for the emptiness of the three periods of time is equal, and the Mahāyāna is likewise equal in its emptiness.

The bodhisattva is also empty; that which is empty is without one, two, three, or four, neither many nor few. Therefore, it is called the equality of the three periods of time, and this is the Mahāyāna.

The merit of a Bodhisattva is sublime and lofty; there is no peer to it, neither right nor wrong. It is neither desire nor the absence of desire; neither anger nor the absence of anger; neither delusion nor the absence of delusion. One does not attain pride, nor is one separated from pride; one does not attain greed, stinginess, or envy, nor is there anything from which one is separated. One does not attain wholesome or unwholesome dharmas; one does not attain permanence or impermanence; one does not attain suffering or pleasure; one does not attain self or non-self. The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm are likewise unobtainable; one does not transcend the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.
Why is this? Because they cannot be grasped as inherent; past form is empty, future form is empty, and present form is empty;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Form cannot be apprehended because form—past, future, and present—is empty; it cannot be apprehended because it is empty, and thus it is called "empty.
Since emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, how much less can one conceive of emptiness as having a past, future, or present?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Furthermore, Subhūti,
the six pāramitās cannot be apprehended in the past, cannot be apprehended in the future, and cannot be apprehended in the present.
Subhūti! The six pāramitās are also unattainable because the three periods of time are equal.
The six pāramitās are unattainable because that which is equal has no past, future, or present; it is by virtue of this equality.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise unattainable, because the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are equal."
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas are likewise unattainable; that which is equal has no past, future, or present.
Because the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas have no past, future, or present due to their equality, they are called "equality."

How much less could one possibly attain the equal thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which pertain to the three times of past, future, and present?
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) of the past, future, and present are likewise unapprehendable; because the three periods of time are equal, ordinary persons are thus equal."
Why is this so? Because when one seeks for a person, they can never be found;

likewise, a srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, or tathāgata cannot be found. This is also true for the future and the present, because the three periods of time are equal.
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas are likewise ungraspable, because when one investigates to the ultimate limit, the fundamental nature of persons is ungraspable.

Thus, Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this manner within the prajñāpāramitā, awakening to and comprehending the three periods of time, thereby becoming fully endowed with the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). This is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and this is the Mahāyāna equality of the three periods of time.
“Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this, they are the most honored in the world, both above and below; by means of this, they give birth to the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

"O World-Honored One! This Mahāyāna—those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who study this Mahāyāna, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past attained the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) because they studied it; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the future will also attain the wisdom of omniscience because they study it; and the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas currently in the incalculable, immeasurable, and asankhyeya worlds of the ten directions likewise study this Mahāyāna and attain the wisdom of omniscience."
"Therefore, O God among Gods!
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is indeed the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! In the past, future, and present, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have all studied this Dharma and attained the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna)."
The Sūtra of the Radiant Praise, Scroll Eight;
The Sūtra of the Radiant Praise, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 22: Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Chapter Twenty-two: Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
At that time, the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Subhūti, the Buddha has commissioned you to speak on the *Prajñāpāramitā*; why then do you speak of the matters of the Mahāyāna?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I say that my explanation of the Mahāyāna is without fault.
The Buddha said:
"It is so. What you have spoken regarding the Mahāyāna accords with the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Because..."

Subhūti, all wholesome dharmas whatsoever—the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment—all arise from the Prajñāpāramitā; they are fundamentally derived from its teaching.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, O God among Gods!

All wholesome dharmas—the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the Buddhas, and the dharmas of the bodhisattvas—all arise from the Prajñāpāramitā; do they all proceed from its teaching?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"The dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the four analytical knowledges; great loving-kindness, great compassion, the quality of non-forgetfulness, and the [four immeasurables] of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the thorough understanding of the dharmas practiced within the factors of enlightenment; and the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—all these dharmas are born from within the prajñā-pāramitā and all proceed from its teaching."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
This Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā and the five pāramitās, as well as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, [the body and tangibles, and the mind and phenomena]—these are all such.
Body-contact consciousness and mind-object consciousness; the conditions of contact and the conditions of habitual practice;

all types of objects of habitual practice that are either agreeable or disagreeable; the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

The gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; all wholesome dharmas—whether with outflows or without outflows, with something remaining or without anything remaining, conditioned or unconditioned; suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; and internal emptiness, external emptiness, and near emptiness.
The emptiness of the distant sky, the emptiness of true reality, the emptiness of all that exists, and the emptiness of non-existence are all equal;
as well as the various samādhis and dhāraṇī-doors, the Dharma realized by the Tathāgatas which he has personally attained and perfected,
the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas, the original limit of the Tathāgata, and the inconceivable realm— if...
Whether combined or dispersed, without combination or dispersion; with form or without form, visible or invisible;
with shape or without shape, with characteristics or without characteristics—all these dharmas are born from the Mahāyāna, in accordance with the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

The Mahāyāna and the Prajñāpāramitā are equal and without distinction; the six pāramitās likewise have no difference; even the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas have no difference. Therefore, the Mahāyāna and the dharmas of the Buddhas are without distinction, without duality, and without multiplicity.
"Therefore, Subhūti, that which is called the Mahāyāna is the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā. Chapter 23:
On the Equality of the Three Times The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Twenty-three: On the Equality of the Three Times Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The bodhisattva does not dwell upon the past, nor does he dwell upon the future, nor does he dwell upon the intermediate;
form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise boundless, and the bodhisattva is also boundless.”
Form and the bodhisattva are both non-existent and unapprehendable;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—consciousness and the bodhisattva—are both non-existent and unapprehendable.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!
Since all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are non-apprehendable,
how should one teach the *prajñāpāramitā* to a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
Since all that is sought by a bodhisattva is entirely unobtainable and invisible, how can one speak of the Prajñāpāramitā as teaching a bodhisattva?
That which is called a "bodhisattva" is merely a name.
It is like a person who says of themselves,
"I have a self," yet when sought from beginning to end, it is found to be entirely non-existent.
All dharmas are naturally so; what gives rise to form, and that which is produced by form?
What gives rise to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and that which is produced by consciousness?
"O World-Honored One! That which is unarisen has neither form nor consciousness.
What, then, could there be that is called 'the perfection of wisdom'?"
How then should one instruct a bodhisattva?
There is no other place, nor is there any arising; neither a bodhisattva can be apprehended, nor can one who practices the path be apprehended.
When a bodhisattva hears this, they are neither terrified nor frightened, and have no fear; such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is then practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"In what way are bodhisattvas of the past, the future, and the present unobtainable?"
Why is this? Form is without limit; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also without limit, and the bodhisattva is likewise without limit.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all non-existent and unobtainable; all bodhisattvas are likewise unobtainable.
How does one instruct a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
What is it that the Prajñāpāramitā teaches?
Since the self (*ātman*) is entirely invisible and the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended as a locus, how can one instruct a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the Prajñāpāramitā?
For what reason is it said:
"A bodhisattva-mahāsattva is merely a name; when one seeks for a self, there is neither beginning nor end.
All dharmas are of their own nature; from where does form arise?"
From what do sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise?
O World-Honored One! That which is unarisen has no form; that which is unarisen has no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Just now, Subhūti spoke these words:
"Since there is nothing that is produced, how should one teach the Prajñāpāramitā?
For what reason did he say this?
"Nor is there any other place.
Can one who has been born [in such a state] be found as a bodhisattva?
For what reason, Subhūti, does the practitioner of the path speak these words?
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this and their mind is not terrified, then they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
What does this mean? Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
Because persons do not exist, past bodhisattvas cannot be apprehended; since sentient beings are entirely empty, past bodhisattvas have nothing to be grasped.
Sentient beings are deluded; therefore, the bodhisattvas of the past had nothing to receive.
Form is non-existent; therefore, the bodhisattvas did not receive the past feelings, perceptions, mental formations, or consciousness.
Emptiness is non-existent; therefore, the bodhisattva does not receive past sensations.
Past form is empty, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also empty;
form is evanescent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also evanescent.
Form is naturally so; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are naturally so.
For this reason, the bodhisattva does not grasp the past.
The dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā are all non-existent; for this reason, the bodhisattva does not attain the past.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!

Because that which is empty cannot be apprehended as past, future, or intermediate; there is no emptiness distinct [from it], nor is there a bodhisattva. There is no past emptiness, no bodhisattva, and no past events; all are entirely non-dual and without differentiation.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not grasp at the past; the same applies to the future and the intermediate [present].

To state the essential point: the *dānapāramitā* is likewise illusory; the *dānapāramitā* is spontaneously so. The *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā* are all likewise empty. Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is also illusory, it lacks any inherent nature (*svabhāva*). For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not grasp at the past.

Therefore, Śāriputra! That which is empty has no past, no future, and no intermediate; emptiness and the bodhisattva, as well as that which has already passed, are neither two nor many. Therefore, Śāriputra!
The bodhisattva does not grasp the past.
Since even those seven emptinesses are non-existent, the bodhisattva therefore does not grasp the past.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path—these thirty-seven factors of awakening are likewise empty and likewise evanescent;
the seven kinds of emptiness are also like this. For this reason, the bodhisattva does not grasp at the past.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all empty and elusive; therefore, the bodhisattva does not accept the past.
The six perfections likewise do not exist, are also elusive, and lack intrinsic nature; therefore, the bodhisattva does not accept the past.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All samādhis are non-existent, and all dhāraṇī-doors are non-existent;
these gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī are likewise entirely empty and likewise ethereal."
All the gateways of samādhi and the gateways of dhāraṇī are non-existent;
all the gateways of samādhi and the gateways of dhāraṇī are likewise entirely empty and likewise elusive;
all the gateways of samādhi and the gateways of dhāraṇī are devoid of self-nature. For this reason, the bodhisattva does not grasp at the past.
The six *pāramitās* are also like this.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, even the *dharmadhātu* is non-existent;

the *dharmadhātu* is entirely empty, the *dharmadhātu* is ethereal, and the *dharmadhātu* is spontaneous. Within the *dharmadhātu*, there are also no seven kinds of emptiness; therefore, the bodhisattva does not grasp the past.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also non-existent and entirely without origin; that which is without origin is indeterminate, and that which is without origin is also empty. Since this absence of origin is itself without intrinsic nature, for this reason the Bodhisattva does not grasp the past."

That ultimate limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is likewise non-existent; the ultimate limit is entirely empty, the ultimate limit is indeterminate, and it is also without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). All realms are likewise inconceivable and without intrinsic nature. For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not grasp at the past.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas are likewise non-existent; the tathāgata is empty and elusive, and possesses no intrinsic nature. For this reason, the bodhisattva does not grasp at the past."

The Way is non-existent; it is empty and vague, and it has no inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is also empty and vague, and it has no inherent nature. For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not grasp at the past.
Why is this so? Śāriputra, emptiness, the state of vagueness, and that which lies between the past and the future are likewise unobtainable; the bodhisattva, too, is unobtainable.
Therefore, Śāriputra, emptiness and the indeterminate, as well as the past and the future, are neither two nor many; for this reason, the bodhisattva does not grasp at the past.
Furthermore, Śāriputra asked:
"For what reason is form (rūpa) boundless, sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) boundless, and why is the bodhisattva also boundless?"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like emptiness and empty.
They are like space, which has no boundaries, no middle, and no bottom; it is a void that exists only as a name.
Śāriputra! Form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are also like this: they have no limit, no middle, and no bottom or depth, because form is empty.
That which is empty has no boundaries, no intervals, and its bottom cannot be reached;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Therefore, Śāriputra!
Form is without limit; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without limit; the bodhisattva is likewise without limit—all are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, Śāriputra, form and the bodhisattva are both non-existent and unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the six pāramitās are empty, they are said to be empty;
internal emptiness is also empty, and external emptiness is also empty."

Because it is empty, it is empty: the near-empty, the far-empty, the true-empty, and the seven kinds of emptiness; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas are likewise entirely empty.

Because they are empty, they are empty: the primordial limit does not exist, and all inconceivable realms are likewise empty. Because they are empty, they are empty: the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī are likewise empty; that sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is likewise empty; and the understanding of the factors of the path and the wisdom of the path is likewise empty. Because they are empty, they are empty:
the three vehicles of the Dharma are likewise empty, and even the Tathāgata is likewise empty.
Therefore, Śāriputra, the emptiness of the Tathāgata does not exist, and form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended; form and the bodhisattva are both non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.
It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Śāriputra asked: "For what reason are all bodhisattvas entirely unapprehendable?
How does one teach the Prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva?"

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unobtainable. Form is unobtainable; sensation, perception, and mental formations are unobtainable; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unobtainable. Whatever is conceived by thought—that thought itself is non-existent;

that which is conceived as sensation is also non-existent; that which is conceived as birth-and-death is also non-existent; and that which is conceived as volitional formations and consciousness is also non-existent and unobtainable.

That which is cognized by consciousness is also non-existent and unobtainable; the form cognized, the sensation cognized, the perception cognized, and the birth-and-death cognized—all are non-existent and unobtainable.
Śāriputra! These six sense faculties likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The ear is entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended;
the ear and the eye are both entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended;
the ear and the nose are both entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The nose and the one who smells are both non-existent and unobtainable;
the nose and the eye are both non-existent and unobtainable;
the nose and the tongue are both non-existent and unobtainable.
As for that which is reckoned as the tongue, it is entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The tongue, eye, ear, and nose are all entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended;
their odors and the body are also entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The body and the body are both non-existent and unobtainable;
the mind and the mind are both non-existent and unobtainable.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all non-existent and unobtainable.

The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and fragrances, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, the mind and mental objects—the eighteen bases (āyatana) consisting of the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, and the six objects—all such phenomena are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
It is likewise with internal and external forms, as well as with feelings and all other dharmas.

The six pāramitās and the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the various dharmas of the Buddhas; the gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī; the dharmas of the spiritual lineages—the dharmas of the arhats, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the Tathāgatas, and the dharmas of the bodhisattvas; the dharmas of the ten stages, the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the wisdom of the paths—all these, up to and including the Tathāgatas and the bodhisattvas themselves, are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The bodhisattva and the prajñāpāramitā are both non-existent and unobtainable.
Furthermore, the prajñāpāramitā within the prajñāpāramitā is also entirely non-existent and unobtainable.
The *prajñāpāramitā* and the bodhisattva are both entirely non-existent and unobtainable.

Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is without speech, without discourse, without instruction, and without transformation—and because it is unobtainable—there is likewise no speech, no discourse, no instruction, and no transformation regarding the bodhisattva; it too is entirely non-existent and unobtainable.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise non-existent and unobtainable. Therefore,
Śāriputra, all dharmas are also non-existent and there is no one who attains them, because they are unobtainable.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise unapprehendable and there is nothing to be said about them, just as Śāriputra has stated. Why is this?
By what name is he designated, and from where does that name "bodhisattva" come?
As for this name, in what place does it exist such that one is called a bodhisattva? For this reason, one is named a "bodhisattva.
To speak of a "bodhisattva" is merely a designation; from where has it come?

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely names; they are merely words attached to speech, yet there is no form, and there is no sensation, perception, mental formation, or consciousness.

Why is this so? Names are empty, and names are naturally empty; it is not on account of these that one is called a bodhisattva, nor is there a name of one's own (according to the Dan edition), nor is emptiness itself designated as a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the six pāramitās are merely names; it is not by virtue of these names that they are the six pāramitās.
This which is called 'bodhisattva' is also merely a name."
Therefore, when one speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is merely by means of words; yet it is not because of these words that it is the *prajñāpāramitā*. The *prajñāpāramitā* has no words.
Why is this? Both the word and the Prajñāpāramitā are empty, for neither can be apprehended. Śāriputra!

What is called a "bodhisattva" is merely a provisional designation. What are called internal emptiness, external emptiness, proximate emptiness, remote emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of non-existence are merely words; as for these seven kinds of emptiness, they are not empty by means of words.
