Why is this? It is not because of words that they are empty; these various emptinesses are ungraspable. Therefore, Śāriputra!
What is called a "bodhisattva" is merely a provisional designation. Śāriputra! This name is but a provisional designation.

The applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path—the thirty-seven auxiliaries of enlightenment—as well as the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are all but provisional designations. It is not by virtue of these names that they constitute the dharmas of a Buddha; the dharmas of a Buddha are empty.
Therefore, Śāriputra, what is called a "bodhisattva" is merely a provisional designation.

All the gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, as well as the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and up to the Buddha—these too are merely provisional designations; they do not take words to be real words.

Regarding what is called "self" and "what belongs to self," if one traces them back to their origin and end, they are likewise non-existent and unestablished; since a self cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anything apprehended regarding the Way?
That which is known and that which is seen are likewise unattainable; how much less can one desire for anything to be accomplished? Śāriputra!

Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—both their beginning and their end are unattainable; how much less can one desire for consciousness to possess the accomplishment of an eye, or for the eye to further give rise to feeling through conditions?
The six sense organs—ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and that which enters through them are likewise unattainable;
the six pāramitās and the seven emptinesses, including the emptiness of the beginning and the end, are also unattainable, so how much more so could anything be brought to completion?

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses—the dharmas of all Buddhas—cannot be found even when one traces their beginning and end; how much less can one wish for them to be something that is accomplished?

As for the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī, if one investigates their beginning and end, they are entirely unobtainable; how much less could one wish for anything to be accomplished therein?
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas are all entirely unobtainable.
Therefore, Śāriputra, that which is called "self" is entirely non-existent; all dharmas are likewise non-existent, for they are all of the nature of spontaneity (svabhāva).
"Why is this? Because it is naturally without conjunction and without dispersion. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What is meant by 'spontaneously neither uniting nor dispersing'? He replied:
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—because they function spontaneously, they neither unite nor disperse."

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the objects received and produced by these six sense-faculties, and the sensations of pain and pleasure that arise from their conjunction—are all spontaneously so, being neither joined nor dispersed;
the six pāramitās likewise are neither joined nor dispersed, being entirely spontaneous. Therefore, Śāriputra, [it is thus].
All dharmas are entirely non-existent and are all of the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all dharmas are neither permanent nor do they go anywhere."
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "What is meant by 'all dharmas are impermanent and have no arrival'? Subhūti replied:
“Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise without permanence and have no destination. Why is this?
That which is impermanent is entirely non-existent and lacks even an eye; therefore, all dharmas are without permanence and have no destination.”
All phenomena are likewise thus: they are entirely without permanence and have no destination.
Whether they be all the outflows (*āsrava*) or even the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), there is nothing that can be spoken of, nor is there any dharma that is taught.
That which possesses permanence is, in fact, non-existent and lacks even the faculty of sight.
Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are entirely without permanence and have no destination to which they may resort.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all dharmas are neither accumulated nor destroyed.
He then asked Subhūti:
“What is meant by ‘all dharmas are neither accumulated nor destroyed’? He replied:
“Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither accumulated nor destroyed.”
Why is this? Because it is pure.
All dharmas—whether wholesome or unwholesome, existent or non-existent, with outflows or without outflows—are entirely without accumulation and without destruction.
Why is this? Because it is pure. Therefore, Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, all that exists is entirely non-existent.
As for what you have asked:
"From what is form produced?
Form is not produced from anything; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not produced from anything. Why is this so?

Śāriputra, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-existent. One who understands and practices this realizes that there is no form and nothing produced; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also not produced; and form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise non-existent.
Why is this so? Because one who understands practice is without eyes; the eye does not exist. Why is this so?
The practitioner who understands clearly perceives that all things are non-existent;
the six sense faculties are likewise so. "Furthermore, Śāriputra, all dharmas are entirely non-existent."
Why is this? Because one who understands through practice does not create anything whatsoever. Therefore, Śāriputra!
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unarisen.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which you ask about—
form being unarisen— is not form, nor is it sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Form (*rūpa*) is pure, empty, without arising or ceasing, without abiding, and without distinction.

Because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise pure, and because emptiness is pure, they are called "pure. They are without arising or ceasing, without abiding, and cannot be differentiated. All that exists is also pure; because emptiness is pure, it is called "pure. It has no arising, no ceasing, and no abiding, and cannot be known as distinct.
Therefore, Śāriputra, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unarisen.
As you have asked, Śāriputra:
"Why do you say that all these things are utterly unarisen?
From what source should one speak of the Prajñāpāramitā? Why is this so?"
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise without arising.
Since it is without arising, the Prajñāpāramitā is also without emergence; there are not two dharmas, nor are there any distinctions.
Therefore, this was said: from what source, then, should one speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Śāriputra asked:
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not arise from any other place to attain the practice of the Way."
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not follow after ordinary beings, nor do they perceive any difference between them.
Furthermore, the perfection of wisdom does not distinguish between different locations, seeing all things as equal; likewise, the practice of the bodhisattvas is without any arising.

Furthermore, for a bodhisattva, there are no two dharmas, nor are there any distinctions; nor does he perceive that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness arise from different locations.
Why is this? Because of non-arising, form is neither dual nor manifold; it does not arise from anything else, nor is form seen to arise from any other place.
Why is this so? Form has no place of arising, and consciousness has no name, nor does it possess any plurality.

As for the eighteen constituents, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the teachings of all Buddhas, as well as the seven emptinesses and the teachings of the three vehicles—none of these are seen to have arisen.
Why is this? Because there is nothing produced; there are no two dharmas, nor are there any multiplicity. Therefore, Śāriputra!
There is no Bodhisattva who attains the Way by being born in another place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
as to what you asked previously:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, is without alarm, without fear, and without dread, then they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Why is this so? Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as being entirely like a dream, like an illusion, a mirage, a plantain tree, a shadow, and an echo.
Therefore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this, they are not terrified,
not frightened, and do not feel fear; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “O God among Gods!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he contemplates phenomena in this manner and thus does not grasp at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He neither abandons anything, nor dwells anywhere, nor clings to the *prajñāpāramitā*. Thus, there is no form, feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness; he neither grasps, nor abandons, nor dwells, nor clings. There is no conceptual differentiation, nor does he grasp at the six sense bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he grasp at a self.”
Furthermore, one does not accept the dāna-pāramitā; there is nothing to be relinquished, nothing in which to abide, and nothing to which to cling, nor does one dwell in a sense of self.

Regarding the śīla-, kṣānti-, vīrya-, dhyāna-, and prajñā-pāramitās, as well as the seven emptinesses, one likewise does not accept them; there is nothing to be relinquished, nothing in which to abide, nothing to which to cling, nor does one dwell in a sense of self.
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!

For one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā, it is likewise with respect to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha: there is nothing received, nothing discarded, nothing in which to abide, and nothing to which to cling; one does not dwell in a self."
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!

A bodhisattva does not receive any of the gates of samādhi or the gates of dhāraṇī; there is nothing received, nothing relinquished, nothing abided in, and nothing clung to, nor does he dwell in a self."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness; they do not perceive the eighteen elements, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, or the seven emptinesses; nor do they perceive śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even Buddhas up to omniscience (sarvajñatā). They perceive nothing at all.

Why is this so? Because there is no form, sensation, perception, volition, or consciousness; nor is there any arising, nor is there any consciousness. The six sense-faculties do not arise, nor do they exist as six sense-faculties. The six pāramitās do not arise, nor do they exist as six pāramitās. The prajñāpāramitā also does not arise; it is neither dual nor manifold. Internal emptiness and external emptiness do not arise, and the same applies to near emptiness, distant emptiness, true emptiness, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of non-existence.
Why is this? Because those seven emptinesses do not arise, nor are they dual, nor are they manifold.
Therefore, O God among Gods!

Furthermore, the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha likewise do not arise; they are neither dual nor manifold.
Why is this so? O God among Gods! This is because there is nothing that arises;
therefore, it is neither two nor three, for there is no plurality. Thus, all the dharmas of the Buddhas are entirely without arising; whatever does arise is not the Buddha-dharma.
"Indeed, O God among Gods!
That which is without basis is likewise inconceivable; the realm of all phenomena likewise has no arising. This inconceivable realm is neither dual nor manifold."
"O World-Honored One!

From the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva, up to the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), all are without arising and without existence; therefore, sarvajñatā is without arising."
Why is this so? Because there is no diligence, there is neither two nor three, nor any plurality;

as for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, these are utterly extinguished and possess no form. Therefore, consciousness is also utterly extinguished, and thus there is neither two nor any plurality.

Why is this so? O Devātideva! That which is diligence is neither one, nor two, nor three, nor manifold; even the consciousness of that diligence has no consciousness. This is the *dānapāramitā*, which likewise does not arise and has no exertion of diligence; it is neither two, nor three, nor manifold. The same applies to the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitās*. Furthermore, it is the same for all the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He said, "O God among Gods! There is no exertion whatsoever;

within this practice, there is nothing that can be calculated. It is likewise for the five aggregates, the six sense-fields, the six perfections, and the teachings of the three vehicles, up to and including the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
Chapter 24: On Practice (*Caryā-prakaraṇa*) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-four: On Practice. At that time, Subhūti addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the prajñāpāramitā and contemplate all dharmas?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing the path for the sake of all people, such that it is said the bodhisattva fully understands all dharmas of the path and remains unattached to any dharma?
To thoroughly understand all phenomena is to thoroughly understand form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet to remain unattached even to the activity of consciousness.
To thoroughly understand the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses—the various dharmas of the Buddhas—is likewise to remain unattached.
"What is meant by 'the affairs of all dharmas'? Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"To contemplate the forms, images, and auspicious responses of all dharmas—the dharmas of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch; their internal and external dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, existent or non-existent—to realize that these forms, images, and auspicious responses are entirely without causes or conditions: this is the contemplation of dharmas."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
as to what you asked:
"What is meant by Prajñāpāramitā?"
"The exhaustion of all things without finding anything to delight in—this is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
What is meant by 'exhaustion' and 'not finding anything to delight in'? Śāriputra!"
Not delighting in the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*);

not delighting in the six perfections—namely, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), vigor (*vīrya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*); not delighting in the seven emptinesses; and not delighting in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—this is called the exhaustion of all that is not to be delighted in, and this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To have no attachment even toward omniscience (sarvajñatā) is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
This is called "exhaustively having nothing to delight in," and it is the perfection of wisdom.
Question: "What is meant by 'contemplation'? Answer:

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not contemplate form as permanent or impermanent; they do not contemplate form as suffering or pleasure; they do not contemplate form as having a self or being selfless; they do not contemplate form as empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, with wishes or wishless; they do not contemplate form as tranquil or untranquil; they do not contemplate form as elusive or non-elusive.
It is likewise with feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, the seven emptinesses, and the three gates of liberation.

One does not contemplate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—the dharmas of all Buddhas consisting of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path—nor does one contemplate suffering and pleasure, good and evil, self and non-self, permanence and impermanence, nor the various gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, or the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). One does not contemplate existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure, good and evil, self and non-self, emptiness and non-emptiness, or the three gates of liberation.
“Śāriputra! This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplative practice of the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"What is meant by saying that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not arise, and thus consciousness does not exist; that the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, the thirty-seven auxiliaries, the seven emptinesses, the four dharmas of impermanence, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) all do not arise, and thus omniscience itself is non-existent?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Regarding form as the sevenfold emptiness, that which is empty has no form; therefore, form is without arising, and thus there is no form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise."
The six pāramitās are empty; that which is already empty is not the prajñāpāramitā, for wisdom has no arising.
Therefore, Śāriputra, the prajñāpāramitā has no arising;

it is not the prajñāpāramitā, nor are the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the various dharmas of the Buddhas, the various gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, or the wisdom of sarvajñatā—of these, too, it is likewise so.

When form does not arise, it is then non-form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so, up to and including the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). That which does not arise is then non-wisdom.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "What is meant by saying that from form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), there is no duality?"
Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is!

That which is non-dual—form is non-dual; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all dharmas of cognition are without conjunction or dispersion, without form and without visibility, and without anything to be grasped or abandoned. Such a characteristic is precisely the absence of conceptualization."
It is likewise with the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four dharmas of impermanence, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
From the five aggregates and the six sense-fields up to omniscience, there is entirely no duality.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What is meant by form being non-dual and pure, having no coming, and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the wisdom of sarvajñatā?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "So it is, so it is!
Form is not different from that which is unarisen, nor is there a form that is different from that which is unarisen."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the wisdom of *sarvajñatā*, are likewise thus.
In this way, Śāriputra, form is non-dual;
the five aggregates and the six sense-bases, up to and including the wisdom of *sarvajñatā*, are also non-dual—entirely pure and coming from nowhere.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and contemplates all dharmas, he sees that all forms (rūpa) neither arise nor cease, being pure from beginning to end; feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are likewise so.
The self, knowledge, and vision are all without arising, being pure from beginning to end.”
The *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitā* are likewise thus: they are entirely without arising, pure from beginning to end;

as are the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas—none are seen to arise, being pure from beginning to end;
and when observing the various gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), none are seen to arise, being pure from beginning to end.
Observing the dharmas of ordinary beings and seeing the dharmas of ordinary beings, they are entirely without arising, pure from beginning to end;

observing the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattvas, seeing that all these dharmas are entirely without arising, pure from beginning to end; observing all Buddha-dharmas, seeing them as without arising, pure from beginning to end, and not seeing any arising at all.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: “Regarding what has just been said, how should it be understood?

If the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, the dharmas of the three vehicles, and even sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) are all without arising, then there would likewise be no five destinies, no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and no attainment of supernatural powers.”

Suppose, Subhūti, that all dharmas are entirely without arising. Why then is it said that one becomes a srotāpanna by severing the three fetters and practicing the path; that a sakṛdāgāmin likewise severs the three fetters and thins out lust, anger, and delusion while practicing the path; that an anāgāmin casts off the heavy burden and eliminates the various fetters while practicing the path; that an arhat eradicates the various fetters and the five hindrances, being free from birth and death while practicing the path; and that those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle awaken through causes and conditions while practicing the path?
For what reason does a bodhisattva diligently practice the path with such hardship for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings?
For what reason does he attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turn the wheel of Dharma?

Subhūti said: "I do not wish for dharmas that are unarisen to have any attainment; nor do I wish for dharmas that are unarisen to reach the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha—it is likewise so."
I do not cause bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice arduous austerities, nor do I require bodhisattvas to exert themselves in ascetic practices.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
It is not by means of distinct characteristics or through arduous toil that one delivers incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, those who practice the bodhisattva path should deliver incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings, regarding them as a mother, regarding them as a father, regarding them as a son, and regarding them as oneself; yet, in their practice, there is nothing that arises.
A bodhisattva should form this thought:
"When seeking for a self, it is entirely non-existent and cannot be found; one should understand internal and external phenomena in this way."
"Even if a perception arises, one does not dwell upon it with effort nor give rise to that perception. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are entirely without arising and cannot be apprehended."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

I do not wish for the Tathāgata to have nothing from which he arises, nor do I wish for him to lack anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; nor do I wish for him to turn the wheel of Dharma, nor do I wish for him to attain the dharma of non-arising.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "What do you mean by saying that one who intends to give rise [to something] attains the Dharma,
while one who does not give rise [to anything] does not attain any dharmas?"
Subhūti replied: "One does not attain all dharmas through non-arising, nor does one attain all dharmas through arising.
He was asked again: "Subhūti," [the interlocutor said].
"How does one attain all dharmas through the dharma of non-arising, yet without there being no arising? Subhūti replied,
"I do not wish for that which is unarisen to be produced so as to attain all dharmas, nor do I wish for there to be nothing attained."
Śāriputra said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is there no attainment and no realization of the Way? Subhūti replied:
“There is attainment and there is the Way, yet in reality there are no two.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, ‘attaining the realization of the Way’ is merely a worldly expression; the terms *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha* all exist only because of worldly teachings.”
"Tracing its beginning and end, there is nothing to be attained, no realization of the Way, and no Three Vehicles.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Is that which is attained and realized due to worldly conventions?"
"Thus, what is spoken of as the five paths by worldly convention—all such things are destroyed and do not constitute ultimate truth.
He replied: "What has been said thus relies upon worldly convention; it speaks of attaining something and thereby achieving the Way, and the same applies to the five paths."
When worldly conventions are entirely destroyed, they do not constitute the ultimate truth. Why is this so?

To realize the ultimate truth, there must be neither good nor evil, neither arising nor ceasing; it is only when all afflictions are absent and there is no resentment that one attains the ultimate truth.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Does that which is the dharma of non-arising ever arise?
Or does that which is an arisen dharma give rise to arising?"
Subhūti said: “Dharmas that are unarisen are not produced, and those dharmas that are produced are likewise not produced. Śāriputra said:
"How can one wish for that which is unarisen to be born?
Subhūti replied, "Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unarisen; they are by nature empty, and thus one does not wish for them to arise."
"From the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to the Buddha-way, all are without arising; they are naturally empty, and one does not wish for them to arise.
Śāriputra asked: "Does that which has arisen undergo further arising?"
“Does that which is unarisen arise? Subhūti replied,
“That which arises is also unarisen, and that which is unarisen is likewise unarisen.”

Why is this so? Śāriputra, these two dharmas—arising and non-arising—are neither joined nor dispersed; they are without form and without visibility, and there is nothing to be grasped or maintained within them. Thus, they constitute a single characteristic: the characteristic of non-existence.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, that which is produced is non-produced; that which is non-produced is likewise not produced. Śāriputra said:
"Who is able to endure the dharma of non-arising? Subhūti, it is thus:
that which is the dharma of non-arising is itself non-arising, and the dharma of non-arising is also non-arising."
Subhūti said: "That which is non-arising is the non-arising of dharmas; that which is capable of enduring the non-arising of dharmas is non-arising."
Why is this so? Because that which is the dharma of non-arising has nothing that arises, and eloquence likewise has nothing that arises;
all these dharmas are without conjunction or dispersion, without form or visibility, and cannot be grasped or maintained—they are thus of a single characteristic, the characteristic of non-existence.
Śāriputra said: “The eloquence of non-arising is itself unarisen; since even the dharmas of non-arising are themselves unarisen, for this reason one is capable. Subhūti said:
"So it is, so it is! Because there is nothing produced, there is the eloquence of non-production; and since even the dharma of non-production is itself unproduced, one is thereby capable."

Why is this? It is because form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unarisen; the six sense bases and the four great elements—namely, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are also unarisen; earth, water, fire, wind, space, and the various seeds of consciousness are also unarisen; the activities of body, speech, and mind are also unarisen; and even the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, up to and including the Buddhas, are also unarisen.

Therefore, Śāriputra, there is no non-arising eloquence, nor is there anything that is not non-arising; because all dharmas are non-arising, they are non-arising. Only one who practices in this way is able to bear the dharma of non-arising.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, the Dharma you have taught is the most supreme. Why is this so?"
"If there are those who ask questions, he explains according to what is asked, yet remains without attachment to any phenomena whatsoever. Śāriputra said:
"In what way does he remain without attachment to all phenomena?"
Subhūti said: "Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure and empty, without attachment, and without interior, exterior, or that which lies between them;
the six sense bases and the eighteen elements are likewise empty and pure, without attachment to the interior or exterior, and without that which lies between them."

The six pāramitās and the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise pure and empty; they do not adhere to the internal or the external, nor do they exist in between the two.
It is so, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six pāramitās has no attachment to any phenomena (dharmas), they are pure regarding form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; indeed, they are pure up to and including omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Śāriputra asked: "What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva purely practicing the six pāramitās to purify the bodhisattva path? Subhūti replied:

"Regarding that *dānapāramitā*, there is mundane giving which does not lead to transcendence of the world; likewise for *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*, there is both mundane wisdom and wisdom that transcends the world."
Śāriputra asked: "What is meant by mundane dānapāramitā and supramundane dānapāramitā? Subhūti replied:

"Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas bestow many gifts upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and beggars: they give food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty; they provide incense, flowers, music, dwellings, the seven treasures, the means of livelihood, and medical treatment for the sick and emaciated—each according to what the person desires. They do not cherish or begrudge even their sons, daughters, wives, heads, eyes, limbs, or bodies; whatever people covet, they give it away freely."
Śikhin said:
"I bestow this without stinginess or envy; acting as a donor, I relinquish everything and practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) according to the Buddha's teaching."

Having given such gifts while harboring expectations, and with a mind fixed upon perversion as their firm resolve regarding all sentient beings, they employ these to encourage and assist toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that by means of these gifts, all living beings may attain peace and security in the present life and eventually enter *parinirvāṇa* in the realm of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu*).
He practices giving by combining three things.
What are these three?
The perception of self, the perception of a personal identity, and the calculation that others will receive a reward for their gift—these are the three.
This is the dānapāramitā of the mundane world, not that which transcends the world.
Why is it called the mundane dānapāramitā? Because it does not transcend the world;
remaining within the mundane without shifting, one fails to attain liberation and reach the state of non-obstruction. This is what is called the mundane dānapāramitā.
One can purify three categories. What are these three?

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices giving, they do not grasp at a self, do not perceive a recipient, and do not conceive of anything taken or any reward; this is how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva purifies the three categories.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives to sentient beings, there is no person [as a recipient], yet he encourages them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Being without the notion of a multitude and seeing nothing at all—this is the transcendent perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*)."
The reason it is called the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving) is that, because it transcends the world, it does not cling to the world.

It is the same for the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitā*: where there is expectation or conceptualization, it is mundane knowledge; where there is no expectation or conceptualization, it is supramundane knowledge.
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva purely practices the six pāramitās to accomplish the bodhisattva path.
Śāriputra then asked Subhūti:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishing the bodhisattva path? Subhūti replied:

"The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as well as the seven emptinesses, all samādhis, the gates of dhāraṇī, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great compassion; these constitute the bodhisattva mahāsattva path."
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"Which pāramitā is able to accomplish valor, becoming the foremost and supreme so as to attain deliverance? Subhūti replied,
"It is through the grace of the valor of the prajñāpāramitā that one attains deliverance."

Why is this so? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all dharmas; it protects and delivers the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and causes them to achieve the state of a bodhisattva. Therefore, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.

The Prajñāpāramitā encompasses all three vehicles. All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions in the past, future, and present, have all attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieved the state of an Avyavartika Buddha by means of the Prajñāpāramitā.

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, does not harbor doubt or entertain hesitation, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is leading all sentient beings; for the sake of all, they have nothing they do not cherish, being able to give everything away without error. This is precisely not departing from the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"One who reflects in this way is practicing the contemplation of infinite great compassion.
Śāriputra said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates and delights in great compassion and great pity, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva has abandoned all sentient beings."
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings do not depart from thought. Subhūti said:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
I now praise what the worthy one has spoken; it is true and real.”
The person has no intrinsic existence, and that which they contemplate likewise has no intrinsic existence;
the person has no self-nature, and that which they contemplate likewise has no self-nature;
the person is an empty action, and their contemplation is also an empty action.
When the person is vague and indistinct, thought is also vague and indistinct;
when the person's body is empty and non-existent, thought is also empty and non-existent;
when the person has no perception, thought also has no perception.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-existent; that which is contemplated is also non-existent.
The seven emptinesses are also non-existent; form is empty and indistinct because it is non-existent, and there is nothing of form to be perceived, nor is there anything of thought to be perceived.

The eighteen elements—the realms of earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness; the perfections of *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñā*; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all other qualities of a Buddha; as well as all *samādhis*, *dhāraṇī* gates, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—one who understands that all these are non-existent, this is the Way.

What is contemplated is non-existent; there is nothing for a person to perceive, and what is contemplated is likewise beyond perception. One must understand this in order to achieve perfect enlightenment.
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice in this manner; it is by not departing from this mindfulness that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should speak of the prajñāpāramitā in this way.
As you have said, all is sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the prajñāpāramitā in this manner.

When the venerable Subhūti was preaching the Prajñāpāramitā, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; it quaked, trembled, and vibrated in the east, west, south, north, above, and below. At that time, the Buddha smiled.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, O God among Gods!
For what reason do you smile?"
"There must certainly be an underlying intention. The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Just as I am now teaching the Prajñāpāramitā here in this Sahā world-system, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions are likewise each teaching the Prajñāpāramitā."

When the Buddha spoke these words, twelve nayutas of devas and humans all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas; at that very moment, they all beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions, each of whom was preaching the Prajñāpāramitā.
When these words were spoken, incalculable, asankhyeya numbers of people all resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
*Prabhāsa-praśaṃsā Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
*Prabhāsa-praśaṃsā Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-five: The Chapter on Questions. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-five: The Chapter on Questions.

At that time, there were the Śakras of the Trichiliocosm, the Caturmahārājikas, the Suyāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Paranirmita-vaśavartins, the Brahmās, the Brahmakāyikas, and the Śuddhāvāsas, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of devas.

The various devas and humans possessed merit from past lives, and their radiance was so sublime that, compared to the light of the Tathāgata, it was a hundred billion, a thousand billion, ten million billion, or even a trillion times inferior; the Tathāgata’s light was supreme, foremost, peerless, and without equal, penetrating all things without exception.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

“Now the Four Heavenly Kings of this trichiliocosm, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and all the gods and humans have come to this great assembly, desiring to hear Subhūti preach the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom?
How should they practice?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“O sons of the gods, listen with joy; I shall speak.
Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power and receiving the Buddha’s grace, spoke the Prajñāpāramitā:
“Regarding the conduct in which all bodhisattvas should establish themselves, those sons of the gods who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should now all resolve to do so.”
Those who enter into right views are unable to give rise to the aspiration for the Great Way.
Why is this? Because they block the path of birth and death.
Even if such persons practice the bodhisattva path, I rejoice on their behalf and encourage them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for I shall never cease from cultivating merit.
"I wish to cause them to take up the central, upright, and honored Dharma; I truly wish to cause them to ascend to the Buddha’s unsurpassed Way.
Subhūti said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"Regarding what was asked just now:"
"How does a bodhisattva dwell within the *prajñāpāramitā*?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having generated the mind of *sarvajñatā*, does not reckon that form (*rūpa*) is permanent or impermanent, suffering or pleasure, self or non-self; nor does he reckon it as the affliction of disease, grief, or distress; nor as harmful or harmless, bound or unbound, or as something to be crossed over or not. He destroys fear and reaches the body that is empty and non-existent through the practice of realization. He is entirely without belief and without contention; furthermore, he has no mental constructions and is free from inversion.
It is the same for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Regarding the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and the various consciousnesses—none of these are seen to possess permanence or impermanence, self or non-self, suffering or pleasure, nor the afflictions of disease, sorrow, and distress.

Regarding all sounds and forms, there is no recollection or thought, nor is there any perversion. The five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the various seeds of consciousness are tranquil and ethereal; yet to conceive of any mental conceptions while examining the Buddha-dharma is entirely perversion.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accord with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) practices the dānapāramitā without attachment, and likewise practices śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, and dhyāna entirely without attachment."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he contemplates all dharmas and thoroughly understands all dharmas.
Having thoroughly understood that all dharmas are established through mutual dependence, he thereby attains the fulfillment of their mutual establishment."
He clearly understands all phenomena as being without self and without body.
The means by which a bodhisattva encourages and assists the mind of enlightenment—that mind of enlightenment itself is also non-existent.
Subhūti said to Kauśika:
"When one encourages the mind of the Way (bodhicitta) with the knowledge that it is non-existent, then by knowing the mind of the Way to be non-existent, it becomes ungraspable."
Even if one were to encourage and assist the aspiration for enlightenment, it would be unattainable;
this, Kausika, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas through the prajñāpāramitā, seeing no dharma whatsoever that can be attained.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"In what way does one encourage and assist the mind of enlightenment such that it is non-existent?
In what way does one encourage and assist the mind of enlightenment such that it is unattainable?"
"How is it that one encourages and assists the mind set on enlightenment, yet there is nothing that exists and nothing that can be apprehended?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!..."
The mind that provides encouragement and assistance, the fundamental nature of the mind, and the mind of the Way—these are not different minds.
Since there is no mind, one encourages and assists by means of no-mind;
since there is no non-thought, one encourages and assists by means of non-thought.
If one acts with no-mind, then by means of no-mind there is no thought; because there is no thought, this constitutes the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
"If one can encourage and assist a bodhisattva mahāsattva in expounding the Prajñāpāramitā, is it not indeed like this?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for myself, O God among Gods!"
One should repay the Buddha’s kindness by performing acts of reciprocity. Why is this?
Because in the past, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas had their disciples expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas.

In the time of past Buddhas, he exhorted and assisted all bodhisattvas by preaching the six pāramitās, praising, encouraging, and transforming them so that they were established in these factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas).
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the various bodhisattvas, gave rise to the six pāramitās, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and reached the state of abhiṣeka-buddhahood.

Now, I, who am likewise a god among gods, shall also encourage and assist all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to give rise to faith and joy, receive the six pāramitās, and be transformed and established in this Buddha-way.

Having received them all and having encouraged them to find joy in them, I shall earnestly exhort and establish them so that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Listen, Kauśika! As to what you have just asked:"
"How should a bodhisattva dwell within the perfection of wisdom so as to dwell nowhere? "Kauśika!
That which is called 'form'—form is itself emptiness."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise empty.
That which is called a "bodhisattva," that bodhisattva is empty.
Because form is empty, the bodhisattva is empty; there is absolutely no duality, nor is there any multiplicity.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, the bodhisattva is empty; they are entirely without duality, nor are there any distinctions.
This, Kauśika, is what it means.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, that which is called the eye is itself empty of the eye.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
That which is called a "bodhisattva," the bodhisattva is also empty.
Because the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, the bodhisattva is empty; there are not two, nor are there many.
Earth, water, fire, and wind are all empty; for this reason, the bodhisattva is empty.
Within the body, the six elements are entirely non-existent; from beginning to end, they are all empty, neither dual nor manifold.
It is thus, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they understand that ignorance is empty; form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, and suffering are likewise empty. Because the twelve links of dependent origination are extinguished, they are said to be empty.
Because the twelve links of dependent origination are empty, the bodhisattva is empty.
Since the twelve links of dependent origination are empty and the bodhisattva is empty, they are entirely non-dual and without distinction.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
Because the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is empty, the bodhisattva is empty;
it is likewise for the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom.
Because the six pāramitās are empty, the bodhisattva is empty; this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to dwell within the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Because of internal emptiness, external emptiness, proximate emptiness, remote emptiness, true emptiness, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of non-existence, it is called the emptiness of the bodhisattva.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all these, as well as all samādhis and dhāraṇī-doors, are empty; therefore, the bodhisattva is empty.

The six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are empty; the emptiness of emptiness and the emptiness of all Buddha-dharmas are empty; all samādhis and dhāraṇīs are empty—all these are entirely without duality, nor are they manifold.
This, Kauśika, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Kauśika:
Because the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, tathāgata, arhat, and samyaksaṃbuddha are empty, the bodhisattva is empty.

Regarding those four emptinesses—the emptiness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the emptiness of tathāgatas, and the emptiness of bodhisattvas—they are entirely without duality and without distinction.
This, Kauśika, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is empty;
because omniscience is empty, the bodhisattva is empty. This emptiness of omniscience and this emptiness of the bodhisattva are entirely non-dual and not manifold.
"It is thus, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell within the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should not dwell in form; he should not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
One should not dwell within the habitual engagement of the eye; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which likewise have no engagement and nothing in which to dwell.
One should not dwell in the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind, as these too have no habitual engagement and no place of dwelling.
One should not dwell in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the Eightfold Path.
One should not abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
one should not abide in the stages of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, pratyekabuddha, or the path of a Buddha;

one should not abide in the notion that form is permanent or impermanent, nor should one abide in the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are permanent or impermanent.

One should not dwell on form as suffering or pleasure; one should not dwell on form as pure or impure; one should not dwell on form as "mine" or "not mine"; one should not dwell on form as empty or non-empty; one should not dwell on it as tranquil or non-tranquil; one should not dwell on it as vague or non-vague.

One should not dwell on the existence or non-existence of a *srotāpanna*; one should not dwell on the existence or non-existence of a *sakṛdāgāmin*; one should not dwell on the existence or non-existence of an *anāgāmin*; one should not dwell on the existence or non-existence of an *arhat*; one should not dwell on the existence or non-existence of a *pratyekabuddha*;
one should not dwell on the existence or non-existence of a Buddha. One should not dwell on the assembly of the four paths; one should not dwell on the assembly of *pratyekabuddhas* or Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth stage of a bodhisattva."
From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), there is likewise no abiding.

A bodhisattva should not abide in the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); it is the same for the perfections of ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditation (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā).
One should not dwell upon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form such a thought as:
"I am entering the bodhisattva-dharma."
One should not dwell with the thought:
"I have entered the stage of *avaivartika*.

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not dwell in the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), nor should he dwell in the five supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva. Having attained these five supernormal powers, he visits the countless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddha-fields of the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods; there he bows his head in prostration, listens to the Dharma they preach, and as he has received it, he explains that Dharma for the sake of the assembly.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not dwell upon this thought:
"Just as that Buddha, the God among Gods, has manifested his land, I shall likewise transform my world."
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not dwell in this way:
'I shall transform and enlighten all sentient beings.
Nor should they think or say:"
"I shall dwell in countless asaṃkhyeya worlds, behold all the Tathāgatas, and make offerings of flowers, incense, powdered incense, blended incenses, silken canopies, banners, and streamers."
One should not think:
"I shall convert and transform countless *asaṃkhyeya* people, causing them to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form such a thought as:
"I shall establish and perfect the five eyes. What are these five?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
One should not think:
"I shall establish all things in equality, and thereby accomplish the various gates of samādhi to delight myself."
One should not think to oneself:

"I have attained the gateways of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four ways in which nothing needs to be guarded, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
One should not harbor the thought:
"I shall fulfill great loving-kindness and great compassion.

One should not dwell upon the thirty-two marks or the eighty minor characteristics that adorn the body; one should not dwell upon the eightfold noble path, the profound faith, or the upholding of the Dharma; nor should one dwell upon the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha.
One should not abide in the state of a srotāpanna who attains liberation after seven deaths and seven births;
one should not abide in the state of a sakṛdāgāmin or ekabījī, or as a ṛṣi who has exhausted all afflictions;
one should not abide in the state of a srotāpanna who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
One should not abide in the stage of the Sakṛdāgāmin. Why?
Because by returning once more to the world, one exhausts suffering and attains parinirvāṇa.
One should not dwell in the realization of the fruit of anāgāmin. Why is this?
Once one has become an anāgāmin, one enters parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms.
One should not abide in the realization of the fruit of arhatship. Why?

Because once the path of an arhat has been accomplished, one would then abide therein within the realm of nirvana without remainder; one should not enter parinirvāṇa at that point, and for this reason, one should not abide [in that fruit].
The path of the pratyekabuddha surpasses the stage of the śrāvaka, yet it cannot reach the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha-path; therefore, one should not abide within the path of the pratyekabuddha.
One should not abide in the affairs of the Path, remaining within the wisdom of the Path without attachment.
One should not abide in the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Why is this?
Because the wisdom of *sarvajñā* fully comprehends all dharmas and achieves *abhisambuddhi* (perfect enlightenment), severing all hindrances and the fetters of affliction. Why is this so?

When a Tathāgata attains unexcelled perfect enlightenment, he turns the wheel of Dharma, performs the work of a Buddha, and delivers incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings by leading them to parinirvāṇa; for this reason, the Buddha should not abide therein.
Abiding in the four bases of psychic power, by means of this samādhi of form and appearance, one transcends through samādhi and remains for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
One should not abide in an immeasurable lifespan, nor should one abide in the thirty-two marks of a great man.

Each and every mark is accomplished through the merit of a hundred blessings. One should not abide in the worlds of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; one should not abide in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below, nor in a single Buddha-field; one should not abide in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions as being a single land; one should not abide sitting beneath the Bodhi tree. Yet, when such fragrances are emitted from these forms and images, they cause all sentient beings who smell this incense to no longer be bound by lust, anger, or delusion, and to refrain from generating the mind of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, so that they all resolve upon the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When sentient beings have heard this fragrance, their bodies, speech, and minds will all be free from illness; they will not dwell even in that buddha-field, and there will be no sounds of form, nor of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One should not abide in the sounds of *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitā*;

one should not abide in the sounds of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold path (*mārga*), the ten powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*);

nor should one abide in the sounds of the parinirvāṇa of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha*, nor in the sounds of the *tathāgata*, *arhat*, *samyaksaṃbuddha*, or the sounds of all dharmas that constitute the attainment of *anuttarasamyaksambodhi*.
"In this way, Kauśika,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should not abide in any of these sounds of attachment.
At that time, the venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, addressed Śāriputra:
"What do you think? Where does the Tathāgata abide?"
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: “The Tathāgata has no abiding, yet he does not abide in non-abiding. The Buddha is without mind and without form;

he does not abide in form, nor does he abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor does he abide in the realm of the unconditioned. He does not abide in the various emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he does not abide in the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna).”
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should abide in this manner.”
Just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha abides yet does not abide, so should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā abide in this way: abiding in non-abiding.
At that time, the sons of the gods in the assembly each thought to themselves:
"The speech and thoughts of these yakṣas, as well as the sounds they produce and the scripts they employ, can all be understood;
yet the words and phrases spoken by Subhūti cannot be comprehended."
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them:
"Do you not understand? The devaputras replied:
“I do not know. At that time, Subhūti explained to the devaputras:
“There is not a single syllable that can be spoken; it cannot be differentiated, nor is there anyone who hears it.”
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is without words for its exposition, nor is there anyone who hears it. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is without words or letters.
To provide an analogy, O Son of Heaven:

suppose the Tathāgata were to manifest a transformation being, and that transformation being were to manifest fourfold assemblies—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and preach the Dharma for the sake of those fourfold assemblies.
"What do you think, sons of the gods— is there anyone who speaks, or anyone who understands? They replied, "No."
Subhūti said: "So it is, O Devaputra!
All dharmas are likewise illusory transformations; therein there is neither speaker nor listener."
"For example, suppose one hears a Buddha preaching a sutra in a dream. What do you think?
Is there truly anyone who speaks or anyone who listens and understands? He replied:
"No," Subhūti said, "O Devaputra!"
All phenomena are likewise like dreams; there is no speaking and no hearing, and no one who knows.
For example, it is as if two sons of heaven stood at the gate of hell and praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and the voices of these two both emerged.
"What do you think? Does that second sound respond to the first sound? He replied, "No."
“Suppose, for example, a magician at a crossroads were to conjure a Tathāgata and preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
What do you think? Is there actually anyone who preaches the Dharma or anyone who listens and understands it?”
The sons of the gods further thought to themselves:
"The Prajñāpāramitā spoken by Subhūti is exceedingly profound, even most profound, and has reached the pinnacle of subtlety."
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them:
"Is form not very deep, is it not subtle? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness not very deep, are they not subtle?"
Is form not spontaneous, yet profound and subtle?
Are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness not spontaneous, yet profound and subtle?
It is the same for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Are the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and wisdom not spontaneous, profound, and subtle?

Are inner emptiness, outer emptiness, near emptiness, far emptiness, true emptiness, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of non-existence; the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all samādhis, the various doors of dhāraṇī, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) not spontaneous, wondrous, and subtle?
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"Does this teacher of the Dharma not resolve his anger toward form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
Do you not resolve the doubts concerning the six pāramitās, the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the dharmas of all Buddhas?
Do you not resolve the doubts concerning the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha?
"Is it not that the Buddha’s wisdom and his inexhaustible wisdom are indistinguishable?
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them: "It is so, devaputras!"
The Buddha-way is without attainment; the Tathāgata likewise does not preach the Dharma, nor is there anyone who listens, nor anyone who understands.

Those who wish to attain the fruit of srotāpanna or realize the fruit of srotāpanna, or to realize the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat—having failed to endure [the teaching], they depart immediately;
it is the same for those seeking the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha-way is also like this: one cannot bear to depart immediately.
Thus it is, O sons of gods!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening dwells in the prajñāpāramitā, there is no speech, and thus there is also nothing heard.
Chapter 26: The Dharma Teacher as an Illusion, from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Chapter Twenty-Six: The Dharma Teacher as an Illusion. At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"The Venerable Subhūti preaches the Dharma in such a manner; how then should one listen?"
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them:
"The Dharma teacher is like an illusion and the listener is like a transformation; that which they hear likewise does not constitute realization."
The sons of the gods further thought to themselves: "How is it,
Subhūti, that persons are like an illusion and the Dharma-preacher is like an illusion?"
"Are the person [who speaks] like a transformation, and the listener like a transformation? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"
O sons of the gods!
Humans are like illusions, and Dharma-preachers are like illusions;
humans are like transformations, and Dharma-preachers are like transformations.
The self is like a dream, and form is likewise so;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like dreams.
Eye and form are like dreams, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so.
The various contacts practiced are likewise like a dream.
Internal emptiness, external emptiness, near emptiness, distant emptiness, true emptiness, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of non-existence are all likewise like a dream.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise like dreams, like illusions, and like magical transformations.
The fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat are also like illusions and dreams; from the pratyekabuddha up to the samyaksambuddha, they likewise are like illusions and dreams.
The devaputras said to Subhūti,
"Is even the path to buddhahood likewise like an illusion or a dream? Subhūti replied:
"Even Nirvana is likewise like an illusion or a dream.
The devaputras asked Subhūti:
"Is even Nirvana, right up to Nirvana itself, like a dream?"
Subhūti said: “That Dharma of Nirvāṇa, which is supreme from beginning to end, is yet non-existent.
I also say it is like an illusion and like a dream.”
"Why is this? Because illusion, dreams, and nirvāṇa are neither two nor many; they are empty and non-existent.

Thereupon, the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, and an immeasurable multitude of thousands of bodhisattvas questioned the venerable Subhūti:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand, tranquil and subtle.
What kind of person, so deep and wondrous that they are difficult to reach, would be able to receive it?"
Subhūti addressed the disciples and the bodhisattvas:

“Only an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to receive this profound, non-conceptual, and inconceivable practice, which emerges from the remote and mysterious, is difficult to approach and difficult to comprehend, and is tranquil yet majestic; one who abides in the state of the noble ones (*ārya*), possessing clear knowledge and wise discernment, is alone able to receive this *prajñāpāramitā*.”

One who has seen the truths is an Arhat whose aspirations are fulfilled; having performed the practices already established by past Buddhas, having made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and having planted the roots of all virtues, such a son or daughter of good family—being protected and sustained by spiritual friends—is able to receive this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and listen to these teachings. They understand that form is empty and does not conceptualize it; they do not conceptualize that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; they do not conceptualize that the spirit-consciousness is empty, nor do they conceptualize attachment to form.
If one contemplates formlessness, one does not dwell on the signlessness of the five aggregates, nor does one dwell on the signlessness of the consciousness of the self;
one does not dwell on the wishlessness of consciousness, nor does one dwell on the wishlessness of form; and it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One does not contemplate the five aggregates as being without thought, nor does one contemplate them as being without non-thought.
One does not contemplate form as having no arising, nor does one contemplate it as having no ceasing, nor does one contemplate it as being tranquil or elusive;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

One does not contemplate the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being produced or extinguished, but remains tranquil and ethereal; one does not contemplate the various conditions of what is experienced or practiced, nor the *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñā* pāramitās, but remains tranquil and ethereal, neither contemplating their production nor their extinction. This extends even to the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all samādhis and dhāraṇī-gates are likewise such that one does not contemplate their production nor their extinction.

The fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, as well as the pratyekabuddha and the wisdom of sarvajñatā—all are fully understood as empty. The wisdom of sarvajñatā does not conceptualize emptiness, nor does the wisdom of sarvajñatā have any aspiration; that which is without aspiration likewise does not conceptualize.
In the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), that which exists does not conceive of emptiness, nor does that emptiness conceive of existence;
it is likewise for wishlessness and signlessness.
In that realm of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not conceptualize emptiness (*śūnyatā*), nor does emptiness conceptualize the realm of the unconditioned;
the same applies to signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
There is no non-arising and no non-extinction; there is no tranquility, no delusion, and no mental ideation.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound and subtle; it is not something that can be seen or received by those who possess the wisdom of the noble ones."
Why is this so? Because the Dharma is without that which is received, without that which is heard, and without that which is proclaimed.
Since there is nothing heard and no one who proclaims the Dharma, for this reason, there is no person and nothing that is received.
Śāriputra said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Does this Prajñāpāramitā not extensively explain the matters of the vehicles of the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"

They shall protect and sustain the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from those who have newly resolved their minds up to those who have reached the path of the ten stages of bodhisattvahood, including the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the supernormal powers they produce are never lost or forgotten; in accordance with such dharmas, they travel from one buddha-field to another by means of the roots of virtue they have cultivated, desiring to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and they obtain everything exactly as they intend.
Having completed their service, they receive and uphold the sutras and teachings from the Buddhas, never forgetting them, until they personally attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

They are constantly in samādhi, their minds never becoming distracted; they have no discursive thoughts, and their eloquence is unimpeded. Whatever path of Dharma they proclaim cannot be interrupted; their eloquence is appropriate to the occasion, and their meaning and intent are sublime and wondrous, surpassing all the illuminations of the world.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!

Just as you have said, when the *prajñāpāramitā* explains the three vehicles, this constitutes the eloquence and wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva that surpasses the world, being supreme and beyond peer, with a mind free from attachment. He personally understands that his own body is without inversion, nor does he rely upon or cling to what is seen; regarding the views of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he likewise does not rely upon or cling to the six *pāramitās*.

They do not cling to the seven kinds of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, or the dharmas of all Buddhas; nor do they rely upon the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"For what reason does the Prajñāpāramitā extensively expound the three vehicles?
Is it so that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva may attain the eloquence of a bodhisattva, transcend all worlds, and remain without attachment?"
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Because of internal and external emptiness, the three vehicles are extensively taught.
It is the same for the seven kinds of emptiness; because they are all non-existent, the three vehicles are taught."

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have fully realized all forms of emptiness, they preach this protection for practitioners; for this reason, they transcend all worlds, possessing the most supreme eloquence and remaining free from attachment.
Chapter 27: The Rain of the Dharma-Jewel The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Rain of the Dharma-Jewel At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"What the Venerable Subhūti has now spoken is a rain of the Dharma-jewel for the trichiliocosm, from the Four Great Kings above to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven."

Now, as Subhūti preaches the Dharma, he rains down the jewels of the Dharma; I should rather manifest a rain of flowers upon the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, the assembly of noble ones, and upon Subhūti himself.

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the hosts of devas from the great trichiliocosm each manifested flowers and scattered them over the World-Honored One, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the assembly of noble bhikṣus, and Subhūti as an offering; they took refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā.

As soon as these had been scattered, the flowers spread throughout the two thousand Buddha-fields; suspended in the void above, they transformed into multi-storied pavilions, towering and exceedingly high, their splendor beyond description.
The Venerable Subhūti thought to himself:
"In the past, I have traveled through all the celestial palaces, yet I have never before seen flowers such as these.
Those flowers just scattered must be transformational flowers; they do not grow from trees."
"The flowers scattered by the devaputras arise from the tree of the mind; they do not arise from [ordinary] trees.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to Subhūti:
"These flowers have no place of origin; they do not emerge from the tree of the mind."
Subhūti said: "As Kauśika has said, these flowers have no place from which they arise; they do not grow from a mind-tree.
Suppose, Kauśika!"
"That which has no source of arising is not a flower.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to Subhūti:
"A flower is indeed that which does not emerge from anywhere; it is that from which form does not emerge, and from which feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not emerge."
Subhūti said: "Kauśika! These flowers do not arise from nowhere."
Form has no place of origination; that which has no place of origination is not form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have nowhere from which they emerge; that which has no place of origination is not consciousness.
The eye is unarisen; that which is unarisen is not an eye.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The *dānapāramitā* is also unarisen; that which is unarisen is not *dāna*.
The *dāna*, *śīla*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitā* are likewise without arising; that which is without arising is itself the absence of *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, Kauśika, as for the seven emptinesses and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they are nowhere from which they arise;
since they have no arising, there are no seven emptinesses and no thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas are non-arising; that which is non-arising is the absence of all dharmas.

The wisdom of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowing wisdom) of the Buddha are likewise non-arising; that which is non-arising is the absence of *sarvajñatā*.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"The wisdom entered by the Venerable Subhūti is exceedingly profound; the Dharma he teaches is entirely without contention and is never confused."
Then the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas: "It is so, Kauśika!
The wisdom into which Subhūti enters is exceedingly profound; the Dharma taught through the wisdom he has entered is entirely without contention and is never confused."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the Venerable Subhūti has deeply entered into wisdom, such that the wisdom he enters and the sūtras and dharmas he teaches are entirely without contention and without confusion?"
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
"As for that which enters into form, by entering this Dharma, whatever is taught therein is entirely without contention and without confusion;
it is likewise so for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Why is this? That which accords with the Dharma is without harmony and without contention.
What Subhūti has spoken is likewise: it is neither discordant nor confused.
The six pāramitās are likewise thus;
they are neither identical with nor confused with the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the various dharmas of the Buddhas.
