The wisdom of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha’s sarvajñā (omniscience) is likewise thus: they are neither identical nor confused.
Why is this? Subhūti’s teaching of the Dharma is neither harmonious nor contentious; where there is no harmony or contention, there is nothing to contend with.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
"The wisdom into which Subhūti enters and the subtle, sublime discourse he delivers are as magnificent as this.
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Just as the World-Honored One has spoken regarding all dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands them in this way and comprehends all dharmas."
The study of the Prajñāpāramitā should also be like this: when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies in this manner, they are not studying form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive that there is anything to be learned within sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not train in the perfections of giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom.
Why is this? Because they do not see the study of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
nor do they study the seven kinds of emptiness or the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive the seven kinds of emptiness or the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

They do not study the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor do they study the wisdom of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, *pratyekabuddha*, or the *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) of a Buddha.
"Why is this? Because they do not perceive the training in the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Śakra Devānām Indra said to the Venerable Subhūti:

"Indeed, Subhūti! For what reason do you not see form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha’s omniscient wisdom?"
Subhūti said: "Because form is empty;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; and because even up to omniscience (sarvajñatā) is likewise empty."

Kauśika! Because form is empty, one does not study the emptiness of form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, and because consciousness is empty, one does not study the emptiness of consciousness; extending upward to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), because that too is empty, one does not study the emptiness of that wisdom.
Kauśika! This is because it is by means of emptiness; for one who acts through emptiness does not train in emptiness.

If one were to train in emptiness, it would constitute two dharmas rather than one. If one trains in the emptiness of form, it is not one; this continues upward until the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)—if one trains in that wisdom, it is likewise not one.

Therefore, Kauśika! Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, there is no duality; up to and including the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), because all are entirely empty, there is no duality.
The six pāramitās are likewise thus, entirely without duality.

The seven emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the dharmas of the Buddhas—from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to the samyaksaṃbuddhas—are also without duality. The wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is also without duality; one who can study the Buddha’s wisdom of sarvajñatā thereby studies all incalculable asaṃkhyeya dharmas.
Having already been able to study incalculable, asāṃkhyeya numbers of Buddha-dharmas, one then does not study form as having increase or decrease;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so, up to and including the wisdom of sarvajñatā, which neither increases nor decreases.
Having learned that the five aggregates neither increase nor decrease, one is then able to learn the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Having learned that the wisdom of omniscience neither increases nor decreases, one does not learn to grasp form, nor is there anything lost;
one does not learn to grasp feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is there anything lost.
"One does not train in receiving the state of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, nor is there any loss even up to the wisdom of Sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this manner, he does not train in receiving [anything], yet there is no loss."
Subhūti said: "It is so, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way does not train in the grasping of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet there is nothing lost; nor does he train in the grasping of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), yet there is nothing lost."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva neither grasp at the five aggregates nor lose them?
Why does he neither grasp at the training for sarvajñatā nor lose it?"
Subhūti said: "Form is non-existent and cannot be grasped, nor is there anyone who grasps form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna) are all non-existent and cannot be grasped."
"There is no one who receives omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Śāriputra, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through not receiving anything at all regarding all phenomena, achieves omniscience."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, does he train in the *prajñāpāramitā* so as to give birth to *sarvajñatā*?"
Subhūti said: “It is so, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of giving birth to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), because they do not apprehend anything in any dharma.”
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, there is nothing among all dharmas that he receives as a training, nor is there anything that he loses."
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does so for the sake of emerging into sarvajñā (all-knowledge). Subhūti said:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he does not perceive form as having anything that arises or anything that ceases; he neither accepts nor rejects it, neither grasps nor contends with it, and it neither increases nor decreases.”
Why is this so? Śāriputra, because form is by its very nature [empty], there is no such thing as form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not seen to arise, nor do they cease; they are neither accepted nor rejected, without dust and without resentment, without being let go of and without not being let go of, without increase and without decrease.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is spontaneous and entirely non-existent. Therefore, Śāriputra!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding all dharmas, neither produces nor extinguishes anything; there is no grasping and no relinquishing, no defilement and no resentment, no letting go and no non-letting go, and no increase and no decrease. Having studied the Prajñāpāramitā, they give birth to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), precisely because it is without learning and without production.
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:
“Where should a bodhisattva mahāsattva seek the prajñāpāramitā? Śāriputra replied:
"Kauśika! You should seek it from the Venerable Subhūti.
Śakra Devānām Indra then asked Subhūti:
“O Benevolent One of Divine Power, it is by your establishment that you have caused Śāriputra to speak these words:
‘One should seek the Prajñāpāramitā from Subhūti as he speaks it.’”
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"This is not established by my own spiritual power.
He asked again:
"By whose majestic power and grace has this been established? He replied: "Kauśika!
"It is established by the grace of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power.
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"Since all dharmas are entirely without establishment, how can they be thus established by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata?"
Nor is there any other place where [the Tathāgata] is established.
One cannot find the Tathāgata by calculating among all phenomena, nor can the Tathāgata be found in any other place.
The Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

“In this way, Kauśika! The Tathāgata abides nowhere, nor does he abide anywhere else; that which he should abide in is no different from the Tathāgata himself. That which is to be attained does not depart from his abiding.”
The Tathāgata likewise abides nowhere, yet among all dharmas he does not depart from his abiding.

One does not regard form as the Tathāgata; one does not regard the absence of a fundamental basis as the Tathāgata; one does not regard the absence of a fundamental basis in form as the Tathāgata; one does not regard the Tathāgata as having no fundamental basis in form, nor does one regard the dharma of having no fundamental basis in form as the Tathāgata; nor does one regard the Tathāgata as being without a fundamental basis.
Because phenomena have no fundamental basis, all forms have no fundamental basis;
because sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no fundamental basis, the Tathāgata has no fundamental basis.

It is not by means of the Tathāgata having no fundamental basis that sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are established as having no fundamental basis through their lack of consciousness.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata does not take the Dharma of the Tathāgata as a conceptualized dharma.
From the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas up to Sarvajñā (all-knowledge), there is no original Tathāgata, yet one does not [conceive] that the Tathāgata is without an origin.

All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) has no fundamental basis; one does not regard the dharma of all-knowledge as the dharma of the Tathāgata, nor does one regard the dharma of the Tathāgata as the dharma of all-knowledge.

Furthermore, Kauśika! The Tathāgata neither joins with nor disperses from any phenomena of form; he neither joins with nor disperses from the phenomena of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. He does not join with or disperse from anything other than the five aggregates; he does not join with or disperse from the Tathāgata; nor does he join with or disperse from the dharma of sarvajñatā (omniscience).

In sarvajña and the Tathāgata there is neither conjunction nor dispersion; one does not find conjunction or dispersion within the dharma of sarvajña, nor does one find conjunction or dispersion in anything other than sarvajña and the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
These dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they abide by virtue of being established through this majestic spiritual power.
Previously, Kauśika, you asked again:
"Where should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seek the prajñāpāramitā? [The Buddha replied:
"One does not seek it in form, nor does one seek it apart from form; one does not seek it in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one seek it apart from consciousness."

The perfection of wisdom, with respect to all dharmas—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—is neither joined nor dispersed; it is without form and without visibility, and cannot be grasped or maintained. Thus, it is a single mark: the mark of non-existence.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they seek nothing at all, up to and including sarvajñatā (all-knowledge); they do not seek sarvajñatā anywhere else."

Why is this? Because when one seeks the *prajñāpāramitā* and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it is found that among all phenomena there is neither conjunction nor dispersion; it is without form and without visibility, and cannot be grasped or maintained. Thus, it is of a single characteristic: the characteristic of non-existence.
Why is this so? Kauśika!

In the Prajñāpāramitā there is no form, nor is there any other form; there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is there any other consciousness. Consciousness does not differ from the Prajñāpāramitā, nor is there anything other than omniscience (sarvajñatā).

There is no *prajñāpāramitā* that is distinct from *sarvajñatā*; *prajñāpāramitā*, the *Tathāgata*, and *prajñāpāramitā* are one. There is no form (*rūpa*), nor is there anything distinct from form; likewise, there is nothing distinct from sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vijñāna*).

*Prajñāpāramitā* is also not distinct from consciousness. If *sarvajñatā* were not *prajñāpāramitā*, and if *prajñāpāramitā* were not distinct from *sarvajñatā*, then the *Tathāgata-prajñāpāramitā* would have no form, nor would there be anything distinct from form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this: there is no distinct consciousness, nor is there any fundamental basis for it.
In the Prajñāpāramitā, formless phenomena have no distinction from form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

The Prajñāpāramitā is without form and without basis, nor is it different from being without form and without basis; the Prajñāpāramitā has no dharma of form, nor is it different from having no dharma of form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
It is likewise for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to the level of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge): there is no form-dharma that is sarvajñatā, nor is there any form-dharma distinct from sarvajñatā.
The Prajñāpāramitā has no *sarvajña* (all-knowing one) as its basis, nor does it have any other *sarvajña* as its basis.
The Prajñāpāramitā has no *sarvajña* as its basis, nor does it have any other *sarvajña* as its basis.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"This is because for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great perfection of wisdom is undifferentiated; the perfections are limitless."
That which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study is what the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and buddha should study.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas study this Dharma, they transform and enlighten sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, thereby attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: “So it is, Kauśika!
This is the great perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—the peerless perfection, the limitless perfection—and it should be studied in this way.”
Because those of the three vehicles are all born from this, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains for himself anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and reaches the state of an avaivartika buddha.
Form is without limit; this is the boundless perfection of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Why is this?
Because past form cannot be apprehended, intermediate form cannot be apprehended, and future form cannot be apprehended.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Consciousness has no limit, and the pāramitās have no end. Why is this?
Past consciousness cannot be apprehended; there is no intermediate consciousness, nor is there future consciousness.
This is likewise true for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even up to the Buddhas, who are supreme, infinite, and boundless.
Therefore, Kauśika! This is the infinite perfection of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Form is immeasurable, and the prajñāpāramitā is likewise immeasurable.
Why is this so? Because form cannot be delimited. For example, Kauśika!
The limits of space cannot be apprehended; likewise, form is without measure.
Because space is limitless, form is without limit.
Because form is without limit, the *prajñāpāramitā* is without limit.
Extending upward to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is likewise no limit.
Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is without limit; this constitutes the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Why is this so? Kauśika!
It is because the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) cannot be found to have any limits or boundaries.
Just as space cannot have its boundaries apprehended, so too is the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna).
Because space is limitless, the wisdom of omniscience is likewise without limit.
Because *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is limitless, the Prajñāpāramitā is limitless.
Therefore, Kauśika, the Prajñāpāramitā is limitless; this is for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Space is boundless, form has no bottom, and the *pāramitā* has no bottom.
Why is this so, Kauśika?

Form has no limit and no middle; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no limit and no middle. Therefore, the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have neither limit nor bottom.

Why is this so? Because the divine consciousness cannot be fathomed and has no middle; reaching upward to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it likewise has no bottom, and the *pāramitās* also have no bottom. This is the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Why is this so, Kauśika?
Because in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), neither a limit nor a middle can be apprehended.
The perfections are bottomless; this is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Because form (*rūpa*) has no bottom, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) likewise has no bottom.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
"Phenomena have no root; the pāramitās have no bottom.
One who can understand this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason are phenomena without end or bottom, and why are the *pāramitās* bottomless?
Subhūti replied, "Kauśika!..."
Because the matter of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) has no beginning or end, the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are bottomless.
Furthermore, Kauśika,
because dharmas have no beginning or end, the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are bottomless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"For what reason is it that since phenomena have no beginning or end, the *pāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also without end?"
Subhūti said: "Because the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is bottomless, the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are bottomless.
Furthermore, Kauśika, because all things that are without origin are entirely without end or bottom, the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are bottomless."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"For what reason are all things that have no origin entirely without end or bottom, such that the perfections of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are bottomless?"
“Kauśika! It has no beginning and no end; therefore it is without end.
Because phenomena have no starting point, they are without beginning and without end.”
It has no root and no bottom; in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), it is bottomless.
Because phenomena are bottomless, the *pāramitās* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are bottomless.
Furthermore, because persons (*pudgala*) have no bottom, the *pāramitās* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are bottomless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"For what reason is it that because persons have no bottom, the pāramitās of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also have no bottom?"
Subhūti said: "Kauśika, what do you think? Within what dharma is one who gives such instruction called a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to Subhūti:
"This is neither a teaching of dharmas nor a teaching of non-dharmas.
These names come as adventitious conditions; they are entirely non-existent and lack any fundamental form or image, being merely provisional designations, such as what is called a 'person'."
People assign names arbitrarily without any underlying cause or condition.
In your view, Kauśika, do you think that this Prajñāpāramitā serves to proclaim or designate a person?
He replied, “No. Subhūti said:
“Kauśika! If one does not speak of a person, would there not be a bottomless abyss?
What do you think, Kauśika?”

If the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to live for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and were to speak of every single person, would there truly be any person who is born or who perishes?
He replied: "No, Subhūti! Why is that? Because..."
"Human beings are fundamentally pure. Therefore, Kauśika,
because human beings have no bottom, the Prajñāpāramitā has no bottom."
"A Bodhisattva training should understand it thus: the practice of the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā is as follows.
*The Sūtra of Radiant Praise*, Fascicle Ten.
